full_judgment:
Mr. Quazi Reza-Ul-Hoque, J:- The instant Rule was issued on 07.10.2013, calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why diving science papers, namely, Physics, Chemistry, and Biology into three parts namely Objective parts having 35. marks, সৃজনশীল/ creativity part having 40 marks and practical part having 25 marks total 100 marks in H.S.C. Examination, 2013 and imposing undeclared condition to pass in three parts separately in violation of Section 19(1) and (5) of the Intermediate and Secondary Education Ordinance, 1961 should not be declared to have been passed without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect and to direct the respondents to re-examination of the scripts of the petitioner namely, Chemistry (Code 176). Physics (Code 174) and English (Code 107) of the H.S.C. Examination, 2013 and

accordingly intimate the re-evaluated result to petitioner and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court seem fit and proper.

2. The facts necessary for disposal of the Rule, in brief, as has been stated in the petition is that the petitioner is a brilliant student and she appeared in the SSC, 2011 Examination from a reputed school of Dhaka City namely, YWCA Higher Secondary Girls Schools under Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education, Dhaka, bearing Registration No. 447098, Roll No. 109984 in Science group as regular student and passed in the Examination successfully and secured GPA 5.00 (Golden) that means she got grade A+ mark in all subjects. Thereafter she appeared in the H.S.C. 2013 Examination, center name Dhaka- 8, New Model Degree college (Code- 100), Sukrabad, Dhanmondi, Dhaka from another reputed College of Dhaka City, namely, Dhaka City college under Board of intermediate and Secondary Education, Dhaka under control of the notice receiver Nos.2-4 bearing Registration No. 657963, Roll No.115792 in Science Group as a regular student. The petitioner also participated in the different competition such as Science Festival and Debate and she got Certificate of Honour in 2004 and 2006 from Younger Science Club (YWCA) and she also became champion in 5th Debate Competition, 2007 organised by YWCA and rot certificate of Honour from Ideal Debating Club (UDC), sponsored by Prothom Alo. She has successfully completed Bangladesh Debate Federation Certificate Course, 2008 and achieved Grade-A, which proves her talent in science and creativity in different subjects (annexure-A, A-1, A-2, A-3, A-4, A-5 and A-6).

3. The petitioner herein challenges the process of dividing science subjects into three parts namely Objective parts having 35 marks সৃজনশীল/creativity part having 40 marks and practical part having 25 marks total 100 marks in science papers, namely, Physics, Chemistry, Biology illegally and without any legal basis.

4. The Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education, Dhaka, was established under sub-section (1) of section 3 of the Intermediate and Secondary Education Ordinance, 1961 (hereinafter referred to as the Ordinance) for the organization, regulation, supervision, control and development of Intermediate and Secondary Education in Dhaka in accordance with the provision of the Ordinance. Section 9 of the Ordinance, provides that Chairman, Secretary, Controller of Examination and such other officers as may be appointed by Board and shall he the officers of the Board and as per section 31 of the Ordinance and every person appointed for carrying out the purposes of this Ordinance shall be deemed to be a public servant within the meaning of section 21 of the Penal Code.

5. Section 4(1) of the Ordinance prescribed the composition of the Board and section 19 states that the Board shall appoint (i)-(xviii) types of committees, which includes serial No. (vii) Science Education Committee and (xv) Examination committee and (xviii) such other committee or committees as the Board may consider necessary for the purposes of carrying the provisions of this Ordinance and sub-section (2) provides the composition, powers and duties of the committees under sub-section (1) shall be prescribed by regulation.

6. Section 39 of the Ordinance states about the Regulation of the Board for the purpose of carrying into effect the provision of the Ordinance in which sub-section 2(xi) provides of the holding and conduct of all examinations of the Board and sub-section (5) provides that Regulation made under this ordinance shall ordinarily be published in the official gazette. Section 40(1) of the Ordinance says the Regulations set out in the schedule appended to this Ordinance shall on the commencement of this Ordinance be the First Regulations of the Board and shall be deemed to have been framed by the Board under section 39. Regulation 1 of the first schedule prescribed powers and duties of the Chairman of which sub-regulation (5) and (6) of Regulation 1 says that the Chairman shall appoint paper setters, moderators translators, head examiners, assistant head examination, scrutinizers and tabulators in connection with the Examination of the Board and may delegate in writing to the officers of the Board such of his powers as he consider necessary and also withdraw of such delegation without assigning any reason.

7. Regulation 3 of schedule 1 of the Ordinance provides powers and duties of the Controller of Examinations subject to the Control of the Chairman, be in charge of the Examination Sector of the Board and make all necessary arrangement for holding and conducting examination of the Board. As per regulation 3 (2) (III), he shall be responsible for- (a) distribution of question papers and examination materials to all examination centres in time, (b) collection of all answer scripts, surplus examination materials and reports and other documents from all centres; (c) holding of examiners meeting, distribution of answer scripts to them and collection of the marked answer scripts together with mark sheets from all examiners; (d) distribution of the marked answer scripts to the Head Examiners, collection of marks from them and distribution of marks to the respective tabulators (e) collection of tabulated result from the tabulators; (f) publication of results of the examinations in time and as per regulation 3(v) it shall be the duty of the Controller of Examinations to make recommendations to the Chairman; and (g) such other matters as he deem necessary and as may be required of him by the Chairman, who shall perform such other duties as may be assigned to him by the Chairman, and he shall bring to notice of the Chairman all cases of infringement of rules of examination with full report of disposal.

According to section 2 (g)of the Ordinance, "Intermediate Education" means education pertaining to classes XI and XII and includes (i) Arts, (ii) Science, (iii) Technology, (iv) Commerce, (v) Islamic Studies, (vi) Humanities, (vii) Home Economics, (viii) Agriculture, (ix) Industry, (x) Military Science, (xii) Nursing, and (xiii) such other type of (technical) and special education as may be determined by the Board, subject to the approval of the Government and no discrimination be allowed in the aforesaid categories of intermediate education whether it is arts or science or commerce (annexure- B).

8. Respondent No.4 published H.S.C. Examination. 2013 result on 3rd August, 2013, although the petitioner was expecting her result to be as good as S.S.C, i.e. Grade-V (Golden) but surprisingly she found that her roll number was posted with 33 unsuccessful examinees of the Dhaka City College, who have been graded 'F’ but no mark was shown in the subject wise Grade/Mark sheet (annexure- C and C-1).

9. Immediately after publication of H.S.C 2013, result, the petitioner on collecting subject wise Grade/Mark sheet found that she got Grade A+ in Bengali (Code 101), Biology (Code 178), and Mathematics (Code 127), and Grade A in English (Code 107), and Physics(Code 174), and Grade 'F' in Chemistry (Code 176), but petitioner firmly believes that she deserves Grade-V(A+) marks in all three subjects namely, English (Code 1070, and Physics(Code 174) and in Chemistry (Code 176), and therefore, on 04.08.2013 she applied to the Dhaka Board authority i.e. to the Respondent Nos. 2- 4 vide Tracking Number of Recheck: Chemistry P902074P, ENGLISH P 279539P, PHYSICS P 174065P to recheck and re-examination of her aforesaid three scripts but the Dhaka Board authority represented by the Respondent Nos. 2- 4 without rechecking and ex-examination of the script of the petitioner replied on September 11, 2013 vide Teletalk number 880155555 in the terms: HSC RSC 2013 Result: Sarah Tasnim Raisa, Board Dhaka, Roll- 115792 is not changed- Powered by Teletalk, Received on September 11. It is relevant to be mentioned that 24000 of HSC candidates applied for recheck and re-examination total student of 85000 scripts but the Board published Re-scrutiny result of H.S.C Exam 2013, Changes Result only on 10th September signed respondent No. 4 showing only 526 candidates only out of 24000, which is not expected by the students and their guardians. Another student namely, Chowdhury Md, Tariq Aziz, son of Md. Nurul Amin Chowdhury, who secured GP-V (Golden) in the S.S.C Examination, 2011 and all the subjects in H.S.C. Examination, 2013 except in Chemistry as failed which is also unbelievable and unusual (annexure-D, D-2, D-3,D-4, and D-5).

<u>10. The petitioner along with her guardians persuaded the matter with the college authorities, as well as, authorities of the Board including Chairman, Secretary and Controller of Examinations including the Secretary, Ministry of Education but the respondents expressed unwillingness to re-examine the script on the plea that the Regulations of the Dhaka Board does not permit to do so. In the Dainik Amarder Shomoy on 28.09.2013 at page 8 and 7 a report with regard to the same was published (annexure-E).</u>

<u>11. The present HSC examination system in science papers, namely, physics, Chemistry, Biology are divide into three parts, by name Objective part having 35 marks, সৃজনশীল/creativity part having 40 marks, and practical part having 25 marks, totaling 100 marks and internal arrangement has been introduced in HSC Exam-2013 that every candidate of aforesaid science papers have to pass in each part/ component, which creates black hole in the process of passing those subjects, and as a result, if one science student secures full marks in two parts such as 35 in objective and 25 in practical in totaling 60 He/she will not pass in the said paper, if the said student is unable to get 1/3 marks in the সৃজনশীল/ part, whereas in the Group of Humanities and Commerce there is no such black hole and, if they secure only 1/3 marks in the in total they will be considered as passed in the said paper. In comparison with the Group of Humanities and Commerce for the ends of justice considering the huge number of meritorious students who appeared in the H.S.C. examination, 2013 from Science Group fall in the category of Grade- F, which is beyond imagination and hence, it is required to re-examine the said scripts and re-evaluate the answer scripts.</u>

<u>12. Due to denial of re-examination of the answer scripts, education Career of many poor and brilliant students and future faces serious jeopardy, as they have been shown "F", i.e. fail without giving the marks in the said papers in question and the said student is kept in dark about the reasons behind the said result. If the said answer scripts is re-examined, them the said student he would be able to know the exact reality about his fault or mistake, if there any.</u>

<u>13. The system of শৃজনশীল/ introduced by the Education Board Authority in the Science Group of H.S.C. is done without any sanction under Section 39(1) and (5) of the intermediate and Secondary Education Ordinance, 1961 and further facts that the new systems of dividing theoretical portion into two parts namely, Objective parts having 35 marks, শৃজনশীল/  creativity part having 40 marks and imposing new conditions to pass in each part and the said system has not yet been communicated and trained to the concerned teachers and examiners and such practice of the respondent Nos. 2-4 amounts gross violation of the rights of the students.</u>

14. The respondent Nos. 2 and 4 contested the Rule by filing affidavit-in-opposition stating that the Gazette Notification dated 12 March 2001, a candidate would be required to pass in three parts of the science papers, which was to be divided into 3 parts namely, theoretical, creative and practical and that failure in any single part of the divided science would be deemed as failure in that particular science paper.

<u>15. There is no provision of re-examination or re-checking of the answerer scripts of any examinee in the four corners of the Rules and Regulations of the Board but there is a provision under regulation 79 of the Board for re-scrutiny of the answer scripts and the petitioner applied for the same and the respondents scrutinized the answer scripts of the petitioner as claimed and also informed to the petitioner, but after that the petitioner is claiming for re-examination, which are not legal and not practicable.</u>

<u>16. The Regulation 81 of the Board specifically provides that "No answer script of any candidate shall be re-examined, if once the result of the examination of applicant has been published". As such, what these respondents did in regard of the petitioner was done keeping themselves within four corners of the law and Regulations of the Board in the Group of Humanities and Commerce there is no such black hole and so on are not correct and denied by these deponents. In humanities and Commerce Groups there is no necessity of allocating of practical marks but allocation of practical marks in necessity in the Science Group and also for development of that Group. The respondents have such power to do so for betterment of that Group according to sub regulations 1 and 3 of the Regulation 3 of the Ordinance, 1961 and Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh also debars such discrimination.</u>

17. The respondents have already scrutinized the answer scripts of the petitioner as prayed for by the petitioner and the respondents have found that marks have been given to every answer of the petitioner's script and the same has been communicated to the petitioner. Now the petitioner is claiming re-examination of her answer script, which is not possible as thousands and thousands students will apply for re-examination and the respondents will have to be remained busy with the same for, further 3⁄4 months and no result will be able to make final and no student will  be able to make final and no student will be able to take admission in the higher classes. As such, such claim of the petitioner is impracticable and also the law and regulations of the Board does not permit to do so to the respondents thus the Rule is liable to be discharged.

18. Mr. A.J. Mohammad Ali, the learned Senior Advocate with Mr. Mohammad Mehedi Hasan, the learned Advocates appearing for 01'6 petitioner submitted that in reply to the affidavit in opposition submitted by the respondent, Nos. 2 and 4, the petition alleged that the activities made by the respondents in regard of the H.S.C. Examination have been done in accordance with Rules and Regulations of the Board" are not correct. The Science Education Committee might have been constituted under section 19(vii) of the Ordinance but no decision of the said committee to divide the marks of examination in three parts, namely, objective, creativity and practical with the approval of the Government was published in the Gazette, therefore, if there be any decision of the said committee that has got no force of law and such decision can not bind the petitioner and other students like the petitioner. Similarly the claim of the Board that it allocated the marks of examination in said three parts with the approval of the Government has got no legal basis. So far as the petitioner could ascertain that there had been no gazette notification with the backing of any law including the Intermediate and Secondary Education Ordinance, 1961 (hereinafter referred to as "the Ordinance"). There is no provision in the Ordinance and the, Regulation framed there under that debars re-examination of the script of any examinee. Rather combined reading of the provisions of Regulation 3 of First Schedule of the Ordinance show that the concerned authorities of the Board have ample power to order for re-examination of the answer script of the examinee to same himself/ herself from being ruined, if an absurd and improbable result is shown, to have been published or marks are shown to have been secured in a particular subject.

19. He further submitted that the petitioner has collected the copy of the gazette dated 12 March, 2001, published by the Ministry of Education vide notification নং শাঃ 11/10(1)/2001/267/শিক্ষা , on perusal of the same, it prima-facie shows that the same was published by one Mr. Ataur Rahman, Deputy Secretary (Intermediate) of the Ministry of Education without mentioning by the order of the President and without any reference to the Ordinance and the Regulation made therein, therefore the same is in no way can be treated as a law within the meaning of Article 152 of the Constitution. Therefore, decision (S) cannot and has no binding force and therefore the respondents cannot claim the protection under the said decision to justify the division of marks of the subjects, such as, biology, physic and chemistry into three parts, namely theoretical, creative and practical to justify the result of the petitioner. In this regard he further submitted neither in it "(জ)  একাধিক অংশ সম্বলিত বিষয়সমূহ (যেমন তত্ত্বীয়, ব্যবহারিক, রচনামূলক, নৈব্যর্ত্তিক) বর্তমানে প্রচলিত নিয়ম অনুয়ায়ী প্রত্যেক অংশে পৃথক পৃথক ভাবে উর্ত্তীর্ন হতে হবে। উর্ত্তীর্ন সকল অংশে প্রাপ্ত নম্বরের যোগফলের উপর ভিত্তি করে.. .. বিষয়ে Grade নির্ধারন করা হবে। যে কোন একটি অংশে অনুর্ত্তীর্ন হলে… ….বিষয়ে অনুর্ত্তীর্ন বলে গন্য হবে” nor in any other content of the said notification, the word wiw9RM has been mentioned or clarified. Although the said notification dated 12 March, 2001 was published on 13th March, 2001 but so far the petitioner could ascertain the সৃজনশীল পদ্ধতি (creativity) started in ifie year  2009 and thereafter the petitioner could not trace out any gazette notification published in 2009 or thereafter introducing the said সৃজনশীল পদ্ধতি (creativity system) in the H.S.C. examination.

20. He again submitted that the petitioner had to apply for rechecking of her answer script, which definitely also implies re-examination of her answer script, which is absolutely clear from the request made in the last paragraph of the Demand of Justice Notice served upon the respondents (annexure-F). The petitioner and her guardian, namely, the father met the Secretary, of the Ministry of Education, as well as, the answering respondents making request many a time to re-examine the answer scripts and re-evaluate the result of the petitioner. It is absolutely a mala fide plea on the part of the answering respondents to say that the petitioner prayed for scrutinizing the answer scripts but not re examination of the same. So far the petitioner could ascertain there is no Regulation like regulation Nos. 79 and 81 of the Board that "No answer scrip of any candidate shall be re-examined if once the result of the examination if once the result of the examination of applicant has been published", which has no factual and legal basis and the plea taken by the respondents that Regulation 79 there is provision only for re-scrutiny of the answer scripts and that Regulation 81 has specifically provided the aforesaid has mala fide and unjust.

21. Mr. Ali, further submitted that the question of the respondent to be a "benevolent despots" is not at all correct. The question is whether the respondents are acting in accordance with law. Since there is no law authorizing the Board to divide science subjects into three parts as stated hereinbefore the petitioner has every right to approach the Board for re-examination of her answer scripts and re-evaluation of her result. It also does not matter whether Board faces. the difficulties in re-examining the answer script on the plea that if such demand is accepted then the flood gate for re examination of the answer scripts will be open and there will be rush to the Board for re-examination and the Board will not been a position to satisfy the huge number of candidates with the limited man-power and resources, if the law does not permit to an action of the Board and its official, then they are bound to re-examine the answer scripts and re-evaluate the same. In the facts and circumstances of the case the petitioner's grievance for re-examination of the science subjects is legitimate and based on her fundamental right to pursue the education as guaranteed in the fundamental principle of state policy as enshrined in clause (a) of Article 15 of the Constitution.

22. He further submitted that the First Regulations of the Board as appended in the Schedule to the Ordinance shows that there are in total 12 Regulations, therefore it is not understood as to how and on what basis the respondent could rely upon regulation Nos. 78, 79, 80, 81 and 82, of which the respondents have failed to supply any valid Gazette Notification upon which the respondents are baking upon the regulations to justify their decision/action in not re-examining the answer script of the petitioner, they have not mentioned any law under which such regulations were framed and when framed and as to the sanctioned of law.

23. Mr. Ali, by referring to the observations made in University of Rajshahi, Represented by the Vice- Chancellor vs. Md. Abdul Mannan Bhuiyan and others, 10 BLC (AD) 128, submitted that even if there is no such provision in the law, the respondents are to re-examine the script of the petitioner. He then quoted the observations made in the aforesaid judgment of our Apex Court, which inter alia run as follows:

In the overall consideration of the above facts and circumstances of the case are of the view that the University has this petition for leave to appeal only to put respondent No. 1 in further jeopardy, mental and financial, and there is no bona fide on the part of the University in delaying compliance with the direction given by the High Court Division. The University to prolong its inaction and to push the respondent No.1 to a situation of utter frustration and to ruin his future resulting from anxiety and financial loss has filed the present petition. This clearly demonstrates that the University is bent upon continuing its unjust act against the writ petition resorting to all possible steps of delaying the matter of re-examination of the answer script in question. The totality of the matter shows wrath and biasness of the mind of the University to the writ petition. Before parting with the matter we like to observe that the materials on record show things which are highly deplorable and deprecatory. The materials and the totality of the matter show how low the ethics and the values of the highest educational institution have gone and this reflects the prevailing situation in other arena also. The time by now is high to take notice of the matter with all seriousness by the conscious section of the society otherwise, in very near future, persons having respect for ethics and values would choose to be away from the educational institutions financed by the State out of the tax papers' money and by that the educational institutions would be happy home of the persons who have no respect for the ethics and values of the profession.

24. Mr. Ali concluded his submissions by referring to observation made in Abdur Rahman and ors vs. Sultan & ors, 1983 BLD(AD) 129, that:

The procedural laws are grounded on principles of natural justice. It is true that when there is no neither provision nor prohibition, it is to be guided by ordinary principles of common sense, justice, equity and good conscience but then equity will not come to the aid of litigant who is not vigilant.

25.. Mr. Taufiq Newaz, the learned Advocate, with Mr. S.M. Moonir, appearing for the respondent Nos. 2 and 4, submitted that the Respondents cannot be a benevolent despots and there is practical difficulty of the Board to accept such demand because every year about 159045 students from different groups appeared in the examination and about 68381 students fail in the examination and, if such prayer of re-examination is allowed, then flood gate will be opened and administration of Board will collapse and it will be impossible for the Board to conduct any further examination of the innumerable number of candidates. Every candidates will remain Unsatisfied with his/her result and will rush to the Board for re-examination and Board will not be in a position to satisfy the huge number of candidates with the limited manpower and resources.

26. He further submitted that a candidates entitlement to re scrutiny of Answer Scripts and the process of re-scrutiny is governed by Regulation 78 and 79 which are as follows:

"78. If a candidate is aggrieved of the result of is examination, he may apply to the controller of Examinations within 30 days from the date of publication, of the results for re-scrutiny of his answer script or scripts, with such fee as the Board shall prescribe. No application for re-scrutiny of answer script or scripts shall be entertained after the expiry of 30 days from the date of publication of the result.

79. The Chairman shall appoint person or persons according to the necessity as scrutinizers for re-scrutiny.

80. The duties of the scrutinizers for re-scrutiny shall be as follows:

(a) verify whether marks have been awarded to all answer required of the candidate;

(b) whether marks have been awarded to all answer in excess of those required of the candidate'

(c) see if the marks awarded for individual answers have been carried on the front page of the answer script and recorded correctly in the space provided for;

(d) see if the marks recorded in the front page of the answer script have been correctly totaled;

(e) see if the total mark on the front page has been correctly recorded in the tabulation book; submit to the Controller of examination of report on the verification done by him for such action as he considers necessary.

81. No answer script of any candidate shall be re-examined, once the results of the examination in which he appeared, has been published. Answer script and only be re-scrutinised, if demanded or prayed for within 30 days from the date of publication of the result under the provision of Rule 78 of these Regulations.

82. (a) Excepting the answer script for which re-scrutiny had been demanded or prayed for within 30 days from the date of publication of the results, and excepting the answer scripts in relation to which a suit has been instituted in a court of law within 30 days from the date of publication of the results with prior notice to the Board, the Board may dispose of the answer scripts in any manner as it considers fit and proper after the expiry of 30 days from the date of publication of the results.

(b) The answer scripts for which re-scrutiny has been demanded or prayed for within 30 days from the date for publication of the result may be disposed of by the Board in any manner as it consider fit and proper when the re-scrutiny will be over, provided that 30 days have passed from the date of publication of the results.

(c) The answer scripts in relation to which as suit has been instituted in a court of law within 30 days from the date of publication of the results with prior notice to the Board may be disposed of by the Board in any manner as the Board will decide after the final judgment in the case has been given by the court, provided that 30 days have passed from the date of publication of the result.

The petitioner according to the Rule of the Board applied for scrutiny vide TRACKING NUMBER Chemistry P902074P, English P2779539P, Physics P174065P and the Board after scrutiny informed her the result of scrutiny, but the petitioner never applied for re-examination of the answer script till today.

27. He further submitted that according to the circular dated 12.3.2001, a candidate would be required to pass in three parts of the science papers, which was to be divided into 3 parts namely, theoretical, creative and practical and that failure in any single part of the divided science would be deemed as failure in that particular science paper.

28. He again submitted that that by an affirmative covenant under regulation 81, it is embraced that as answer script may only be scrutinized thus where there is a clear provision only for scrutiny, so all other remedies are excluded, as such, the Rule is liable to be discharged.

29. He further pointed out that where regulation 81 provides by a negative covenant that "No answer script of any candidate shall be re-examined, once the results of the examination in which he appeared, has been published. Answer script and only be re-scrutinised, if demanded or prayed for within 30 days from the date of publication of the result under the provision of Rule 78 of these Regulations." And that has already been done, as such; the claim of the petitioner is not backed by any law.

30. He again reiterated that there is no provision of re-examination or re-checking of the answerer scripts of any examinee in the four corners of the Rules and Regulations of the Board but there is a provision under regulation 79 of the Board for re-scrutiny of the answer scripts and the petitioner applied for the same and the respondents scrutinized the answer scripts of the petitioner as claimed and also informed to the petitioner, but after that the petitioner is claiming for re-examination, which are not legal and practicable.

31. Mr. Nawaz, again submitted that Regulation 81 of the Board specifically provides that "No answerer script of any candidate shall be re-examined, if once the result of the examination of applicant has been published". As such, what these respondents did in regard of the petitioner was done keeping themselves within four corners of the law and Regulations of the Board in the Group of Humanities and Commerce there is no such black hole and so on are not correct and denied by these deponents. In humanities and Commerce Groups there is no necessity of allocating of practical marks but allocation of practical marks is a necessity in the Science Group and also for development of that Group. The respondents have such power to do so for betterment of that Group according to sub regulations 1 and 3 of the Regulation 3 of the Ordinance, 1961 and Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh also debars such discrimination.

32. Mr. Nawaz, by referring to some provisions of the Constitution submitted that these provisions are negative covenants to that of the rights guaranteed to the citizens. The statute provided the right to get their scripts re-scrutinised and specifically negated the right to re-examination of the scripts, as submitted earlier, as such, the, claim of the petitioner is not sustainable.

33. He again submitted that the respondents have already scrutinized the answer scripts of the petitioner as prayed for by the petitioner and the respondents have found that marks have been given to every answer of the petitioner's script and the same has been communicated to the petitioner. Now the petitioner is claiming re-examination of her answer script, which is not possible as thousands and thousands students will apply for re-examination and the respondents will have to be remained busy with the same for further 3/4 months and no result will be able to make final and no student will be able to make final and no student will be able to take admission in the higher classes. As such, such claim of the petitioner is impracticable and also the law and regulations of the Board does not permit to do so to the respondents thus the Rule is liable to be discharged.

34. He further submits that if the words of the statute are in themselves precise and unambiguous no more is necessary than to expound those words their natural and ordinary sense, the words themselves in such case best declaring the intention of the legislature. Thus the intent of the legislature is gathered from clear and unambiguous words; or their plain and ordinary meaning; or express words. He referred to the observation made in Abdul Kader vs. Secretary Election Commission & Ors, 58 DLR (AD) 71, wherein amongst others it was observed that:

The Court is to interpret the law as it stands giving the sense its natural and ordinary meaning unless it admits of any other meaning.

The intention of the Regulation of the Board clearly embraces that no re-examination of any answer script will be allowed, once the result is published. And he further cited the observations made in the matter of Reference by the President of Pakistan under Article 162 of the Constitution of Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 9 DLR 1957 (SC) 178, it was observed inter alia that:

One general rule that emerges, and it is an ancient rule, from discussions on the subject is that In the interpretation of written instruments, whether they are constitutional charters or ordinary statutes or older documents, the first object of the Court is to discover the intention of the author and that such intention is to be gathered from the words used in the statute or document.

Reiterating the same principle he asserted by referring to the observations made in Mozibur Rahman Moznu (Md) vs. Abdul Halim and others, 53 DLR (AD) 93.

35. He further referred some observations of our courts that an ordinary meaning of a statute must be applied with its plain interpretation as was observed in Bangladesh vs. Dhaka Steel Works Ltd., 45 DLR (AD) 79,

wherein it was observed inter alia that:

Applied rule of statutory interpretation 'plain and ordinary' meaning to be strictly construed.

And he went on, in Dr. Nurul Islam vs. Bangladesh, 33DLR (AD) 253, it was observed:

Applied the rule that Constitutionality be presumed, that statute should be interpreted in a way that it is saved rather than destroyed signifying:

(a) express words, plain and ordinary meaning;

(b)words (text) not to be rendered idle and/or nugatory.

In, Ahmed Hossain vs. Bashrat Ali, 32 DLR (AD) 57, it was decided inter alia that:

Applied the rule that words in a statute must be given a 'plain and ordinary meaning'.

And son on, in Supdt. & Remembrancer, L.A vs. Jobed Ali, 26 DLR (SC) 7, it was observed that:

Unless very explicit words are used in the statute itself in that behalf such an intention would not be normally imputed to the legislature.

In, Md. Ismail vs. State, 21 DLR (AD) 164, it was reiterated again that:

Applied the rule that statute must be construed in its plain and ordinary meaning if the words are clear and unambiguous.

Bangladesh vs. Mrs. Rehana Kamal & Ors, 25 (2005) BLD (AD) 129, the principle was reaffirmed, by observing inter alia that:

The court is not concerned with any presumed intention of legislature-its task is to get at the intention as expressed in the statute:

36. Mr. Nawaz, again referred to Regulation 78, 79 and 81 that the regulations are unambiguous in their plain reading, as such, those excluded the right to re-examination of the answer scripts, and cited the observations made in Md. Mujibur Rahman vs. Govt. of Bangladesh & Ors, 12 (1992) BLD (AD) 97:

When it is necessary to gather the necessary intendment or manifest interpretation, a court of law will try to gather the same primarily from the language used which must be considerate according to well established rules of interpretation. If the language fails or is inadequate, then as a secondary source, matters outside the language used may be looked into to gather the necessary intendment or manifest intention of a written constitution.

37. He further took us through the observations made with regard to interpretation of Statutes that intention of the legislation be read as it is unless a contrary is meant, and referred to the citation made Taxes vs. Mr. Justice Shahabuddin Ahmed, 10 (1990) BLD (AD) 246, it embraced inter alia that:

It is not the function of a Court of law to give words a strained and unnatural meaning unless the legislative intent is covered by appropriate words.

Abdul Hai Khan & others vs. The State & another, 1988 BLD (AD) 195, it was observed that:

Literal construction when language of statute is clear and unambiguous.

38. He took us through the milestone observation made in Anwar Hossain Chowdhury and Ors Vs Bangladesh, 41 DLR (AD) 191, which contained amongst others, that:

It is well settled principle in interpreting the Constitution, the entire Constitution is to be looked into and if any amendment to the Constitution does not fit in with Constitution itself then the amendment is to be declared ultra vires because Constitution is a logical whole.

39. He again submitted that in interpreting a statute the intention of the legislature be read as a whole and the enactment must be considered. Or Provision is to be considered as a whole not by piecemeal fashion, and referred to the observation made in AKM Ruhul Amin vs. District Judge and Appellate Election Tribunal Bhola and Ors, 38 DLR (AD) 172, wherein it was observed inter alia that:

While interpreting statues Judges are not expected to apply pre-conceived notions nor can they be expected to arrive at the conclusion by considering the provisions concerned in an isolated or piecemeal fashion. While considering a statute, its provisions should be considered as a whole, bearing in mind its object and purpose.

Ahmed Hossain & ors vs. Basharat Ali and ors, 32 DLR (AD) 57, embracing inter alia that:

When phraseology of an enactment is clear and unambiguous and capable of one and only one interpretation, it is not open to the Court to give a different interpretation, with a view to carry out which is supposed to be the intention of the legislative. But it the phraseology used in the Statute or in a section of the interpretation which is consistent with the object of the enactment is to he preferred to the interpretation that would nullify that object. In interpreting a word or phraseology used in a Statute the Court is to presume that the legislature has used the word with a purpose. It is an accepted cannon of interpretation that the words in a Statute must be taken to be used correctly and exactly, and not loosely or inexactly. Dictionary may he referred to just find out the ordinary meaning of the word used in the English language, but interpretation by relying on dictionary has been deprecated. To find out the sense "contiguous" carries, it is to be considered in what context the word has been employed in the Statute, and in doing so, if necessary, dictionary may be referred only to find out the ordinary meaning of the word.

He further submitted by referring to the point of interpreting constitutional provisions that every like interpreting the Constitution every statute should also be interpreted in the same way by giving it a dynamic spectrum and referred to the observation made in Mofizur Rahman Khan vs. Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, 1982 BLD (AD) 120.

Constitution should be interpreted as an organic instrument keeping its dynamic character in view, more specifically regard may be had to the political, social and economic conditions and their place in the historical setting and the present international milieu.

Mr. Nawaz, further took us. In the purview of interpretation that constitutional or statutory provision must not render idle or nugatory another provision nor denude other constitutional provisions by referring to the observation made in NCTB Vs Shamsuddin, 48 DLR (AD) 188:

Presumption always in favour of Constitutionality of an enactment, i.e. (a) express words will prevail.

He further submitted that the rule of interpretation requires that only when interpreting words of statute leads to absurdity, a construction may be put upon it which modifies the meaning of the words and cited the observation made in M. A. Hai vs. TCB, 40 DLR (AD) 211:

Applied the rule that, only when interpreting words of statute leads to absurdity, a construction may be put upon it which Modifies the meaning of the words.

41. He again submitted that statutes in Pari Materia can be used to assist in interpreting language of another Rule of Interpretation invoking the applicability and referred to the citation Mohammad Julfikar vs. Abul Kalam Chowdhury and Ors, 42 DLR (AD) 83;

Two Acts in pari materia Whether "Conclusive and binding authority for the proposition that in construing a provision of an earlier Act, the propositions of a later Act cannot be taken into account except in a limited class of cases, and that rule applies although the late Act contains a provision that it is to be read as one with the earlier Act or purports to declare its meanings in such cases." (relied on 1928 AC 143).

He further submitted that when a conflict between law and regulation, law will prevail as was decided in Bangladesh vs. Shafiuddin Ahmed, 50 DLR (AD) 27:

If there is a conflict between law and regulation, law will prevail.

He further reiterated his submission by referring to the observation made in Col. Md. Hashmat Ali vs. Bangladesh, 41 DLR (AD) 5:

If there is conflict between law and regulation, law will prevail.

And further relied on the decision made in Sheikh Abdus Sabur vs. Returning Officer & Ors, 41 DLR (AD) 43:

In conflict between law and regulation, law will prevail.

Mr. Nawaz, again submitted that the Constitution must be read progressively and liberally and referred to the observation made in Momtaz vs. Chief Settlement Commr, 18 DLR (SC) 188:

Constitution must be read progressively and liberally.

And on point of Stare Diesis, he referred to the observation made Registrar, University of Dacca vs. Dr. Sajjad Hossain and University of Dacca V. Dr.  Mohor Ali,1981 BLD (AD) 349:

Constitution should be interpreted as an organic instrument keeping its dynamic character in view.

And he concluded by submitting that since there is no provision in the Ordinance or in the Regulations of the Board to re-examine any script, once the result is published, so the Rule is liable to be discharged.

<u>42. On perusal of submission of the learned Advocates of both the sides, the petition, affidavit-in-opposition and the documents annexed thereto, it appears that the petitioner appeared in her HSC examinations and when the result was declared, she found herself in the "fail" category, which let her and her parents to ask for re-scrutiny and re-examination of some of her answer scripts including the paper-Chemistry. The Dhaka Education Board authority declined to re-examine the paper on the plea that there is no provision in the Ordinance, as well as, in the regulations to re-examine any paper once the result once the result is published. The petitioner also challenged that dividing the science papers into three components and an examinee shall have to pass individually in all those components, are illegal, as such division and regulation/ circular is not backed by law.</u>

<u>43. The respondent Nos. 2 and 4 have referred to the regulations and on query of this Court, they could not show us the gazette notification of the said regulations, which in fact has never been published in the gazette notification. The regulation Nos. 78, 79 and 81 therefore have any enforceability in the eye of law and further reference to those regulations therefore is not applicable in the instant case.</u>

44. The Ordinance did not provide for any ouch provision with regard to re-examination or scrutiny of answer scripts, which are creations of the authority. Furthermore, the Education Ministry by its Notification dated 12.03.2001, in the official Gazette Notification have made provisions for grading system as well as for the theoretical, practical, creative and objective components of every subject. And every student shall have to pass individually in every component. This Gazette notification have been issued by the Ministry of Education, who in fact is not the authority to do so, since the authority to do such thing have been delegated to the Education Board by the Bangladesh Intermediate and Secondary Education Ordinance (Ordinance No. XXXIII) of 1961. Section 3 of the Ordinance clearly stipulates that:

3.(1) Under this Ordinance a Board shall be established for the organisation, regulation, supervision, control and development of Intermediate and Secondary Education in accordance with the provisions of the Ordinance.

(2) The Board shall, by the name of the Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education, Bangladesh, be a body corporate with perpetual succession and a common seal and shall have, subject to regulations, power to acquire and hold movable and immovable property, to transfer such property, when held by it, to contract, and to do all other things necessary for carrying out the purposes of this Ordinance, and shall by the said name sue and be sued.

(3) The powers of regulation, supervision, Control and development of Intermediate and Secondary Education Shall vest in the Board.

Provided that the Universities of Dacca nd Rajshahi shall have authority to conduct Intermediate Examinations to he held in 1961 and 1962 and to frame courses of studies thereof,

(4) The entire funds, all properties movable and immovable, all assets and liabilities and all records of the East Pakistan Secondary Education Board established at Dacca by the East Bengal Secondary Education Act, 1955, shall stand vested in the Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education, Bangladesh.

So, the Education Ministry, though is the supervising authority, does not have the authority to by pass this Ordinance. Apart from that nowhere in the Notification the name of the Ordinance is mentioned, so that it could be presumed that the Gazette Notification have been made within the authority of the Ordinance. As mentioned by the learned Advocate for the petitioner that every such Gazette Notification, which ought to have a force of law must be made in the name of the President of the Republic, unfortunately, it is totally absent as was required under the provisions of Article 152 of the Constitution. And the same flaw has been done by the Education Ministry in passing another Gazette Notification on 30.04.2008, which was done by a Deputy Secretary, Project Director, Secondary Education Sector Development Project, Ministry of Education, by referring to the previous Notification dated 12.03.2001. A project Director under any circumstance does not have any such authority overtake the authority of the Education Board.

<u>45. Now let us come to the point as to whether a student shall have to pass every component. For the development of education, every education board have the authority to undertake programmes and every such programme, when binds the students shall have to be put through Gazette Notification. In the instant case, the petitioner have failed to obtain required pass marks in the practical component and apart from that she has pass in all other components of the subject Chemistry, so we are of the view that since making provision for passing in every component is not backed by an enforceable law, as such, she should he deemed to have passed in Chemistry.</u>

<u>46. Now let us "see the provisions with regard to re-examination and re-scrutiny of the scripts. A re-scrutiny is to recount the marks given on each answer script and re-examination is re-examining the requested answer script. Sections 39(5) of the Ordinance requires every rule, regulation be published in the official Gazette, as such, regulations 78, 79, 80, 81 and 82 as embodied in regulations which were never notified in the official gazette and the notifications dated 12.3.2001 and 30.04.2008, which falls short of legal requirements, are no laws at all to bind a student and the education board.</u>

<u>47. Further the plea taken by the respondents that remaining thousands of- scripts will take long time and that will delay the 'process of declaring the result, as a shameful plea when thousands of students' educational career and for some that may even cause end of an education career, such a plea is absolutely unjust. Now-a-days, the results are declared within two months of completing the examinations, so re-examining will just take a few more days and that will certainly change the education career and future of many students.</u>

48. A student is a citizen of this country and they do have legitimate expectation that their scripts be examined properly, when they are sure that they did well in the exams to pass, so failing in a single or couple of papers puts their whole future in jeopardy. As in the instant case, the petitioner have secured GPA A+ in her SSC examination and she was expecting same result in the HSC, in such a situation when the statute is silent about re- examination , it should be construed in her favor. There must be responsibility in declining re- examination of her answer script.

A citizen always expect that his/ her right must be protected and since education is a matter of right, though not specifically guaranteed in the Constitution, however, its denial cannot be construed to be justified. The actions of the respondents, so far gathered as opposed to the spirit of the constitution and constitutional norms, Ordinance and the spirit of modern democracy. In the instant case, denial of the petitioner's claim is a synonym of denail of her right to  education and opposed to all forms of natural justice, legitimate and reasonable expectation.

The doctrine of legitimate expectation has been judicially recognized by the apex courts of the different comparable Commonwealth jurisdictions and that has paved the way for the development of a broader and more flexible doctrine of fairness.

In the Common law jurisdiction the doctrine had been traced to an obiter dictum of Lord Denning M.R in shehmidi vs Secretary of Home Affairs,(1969) 1A II E.R 904, wherein Lord Denning observed inter alia that:

The speches in Ridge v Baldwin show that an administrative body may, in a proper case, be bound to give a person who is affected by their decision an opportunity of making representations. It all depends on whether he has some right or interest or I would add, some legitimate expectation of which it would not be fair to deprive him without hearing what he has to say....

And its model clucidation came from the observation of Lord Paser in Council of Civil Service Unions vs. Minister for the Civil Service ("GCHQ"), 3A11. E.R. 935, wherein it was held inter alia that:

Legitimate, or reasonable, expectation may arise either from an express promise given on behalf of a public authority or from the existence of a regular practice which the claimant can reasonably expect to continue.

The governing principles was laid down by the Court of Appeal in R, North and East Devon Health Authority exp Coughlan (2001) QB 213 at paragraph 57, wherein three categories of case were identified:

(i) Those where the public authority was only required to bear in mind its previous policy giving weight, but no more, if it thinks right to the promise before deciding to change course.

(ii) Those where the promise is of consultation before a particular course is adopted.

(iii) Those where the promise has induced a legitimate expectation of a benefit which is substantive.

In the first category of case the Court of Appeal held that it could only intervene on traditional Wednesbury [1948] IKB 223, sense. In the second category of case the consultation has to be given unless there is an overriding reason to resile from the promise. Here the Court judges the requirement of fairness. In the third category of case the Court will require the promise to be performed, if it frustrates the promise, which is so unfair as to amount to an abuse of power. The Court will weigh upon the requirement of fairness against any  overriding interest relied upon for the change of policy.

In R (on the application of Nadarajah) and Abdi v Secretary of State for the Home Department, [2005] EWCA Civ 2363, the Court of Appeal after reviewing the authorities suggested that the applicable test as follows:

The principle that good administration requires public authorities to be held to their promises would be undermined if the law did not insist that any failure or refusal to comply is objectively is stifled as a proportionate measure in the circumstances. The Court of Appeal went on to state, at paragraph 69 that: "Proportionality will be judged, as it is generally to be judged, by the respective force of the competing interests arising in this case. Thus where the representation relied on amounts to an unambiguous promise where there is detrimental reliance, where the promise is made to an individual or a specific group; these are instances where denial of the expectation is likely to be harder to justify as a proportionate factor".

49. There is a recent and significant decision of the Court of Appeal in R (Bhatt Murphy) and Others v Secretary for the Home Department, (2008) EWCA Civ 755, wherein it was held that:

The power of public authorities to change policy is constrained by the legal duty to be fair (and other constraints which the law imposes). A change of policy which would otherwise be legally unexceptionable may be held unfair by reason of prior action, or inaction, by the authority.

The Supreme Court of India referred to its earlier decision in Union of India vs. Hindustan Development Corporation, (1993) SCC 499, wherein the Court observed amongst others that:

It is generally agreed that legitimate expectation gives the applicant sufficient locus standi for judicial review and that the doctrine of legitimate expectation is to be confined mostly to right of a fair hearing before a decision which results in negativing a promise or withdrawing an undertaking is taken.

In a very recent case, Sethi Auto Service Station vs. Delhi Development Authority, (2000) 1 SCC 180, it has been retreated inter ilia that:

... that the golden thread running through all these decisions is that a case for applicability of the doctrine of legitimate expression, now accepted in the subjective sense as part of our legal jurisprudence, arises when an administrative body by reason of a representation or by past practice or conduct aroused an expectation which it would be within its powers to fulfill unless some overriding public interest comes in the way.

In the case of Golam Mostafa Vs. The Bangladesh Supreme Court Bangladesh, 2007(XV) BLT (HCD)128, the High Court Division explained the concept of legitimate expectation. The crux of the decision is that a judicial review may be allowed on the plea frustration of legitimate expectation in the following situations:

i) If there is a promise by the authority expressed either by their representations or by conducts.

ii) The decision of the authority was arbitrary of unreasonable within the Wednesbury principle.

iii) There was a failure on the part of the concerned authority to act fairly in taking the decision.

iv) The expectation to be crystallized into a legitimate one, it must be based on clear facts and circumstances leading to a define expectation and not a mere anticipation or a wish or hope and also must be reasonable in the circumstances.

v) Judicial review may allow such a legitimate expectation and quash the impugned decision even in the absence of a strict legal right unless there is an over reading public interest to defeat such an expectation.

50. Let us revisit the realm of Wednesbury Principle [Associated Provincial Picture Houses Ltd v Wednesbury, Corporation (1948) 1 KB 223)]. This principle is a concept used by the courts when a judicial review case is taken to it and states that public bodies should be reasonable in its, decision making process, i.e. that a public body was not reasonable in its decision making process. This principle came about in the Wednesbury Corporation's case in 1948. The only exception in history was in the case of Council of Civil Service Unions v Minister for the Civil Service, 1985 (GCHG Case). However, this English law case has set down the standard of unreasonableness of public body decisions which render them liable to be quashed on judicial review. So, the courts will not intervene to correct a bad administrative decision on grounds of unreasonableness, unless such decision is, as was articulated in Council of Civil Service Unions Vs.  Minister of State for Civil Service (1984) 3 All ER 935 the (GCHQ Case) Lord Diplock, observed inter alia that:

So outrageous in its defiance of logic or accepted moral standards that no sensible person who had applied his mind to the question to be decided could have arrived at it.

The House of Lords rationalized the grounds of judicial review and ruled that the basis of judicial review could be highlighted under three principal heads, namely- illegality, procedural impropriety and irrationality. Illegality as a ground of judicial review means that the decision maker must understand correctly the law that regulates his decision making powers and must give effect to it. Grounds such as acting ultra virus, errors of law and/of fact, onerous conditions improper purpose, relevant and irrelevant factors, acting in had faith, fettering discretion, unauthorized delegation, failure to act etc. fall under the heading "illegality". Procedural impropriety, may be due "to the failure to comply with the mandatory procedures, such as breach of natural justice such as audi alteram partem, absence of bias the duly to act fairly, legitimate expectations, failure to give reasons etc.

In A.K.M. Kawser Ahmed and others vs. Bangladesh, 65 DLR(2013)277, wherein it was observed inter alia that:

... The potentially important point is that change of policy should not violate the substantive legislative expectation and if does so it must be as the change of policy which is necessary and such a change is not irrational or perverse.

51. From the above observation our own and persuasive, we can safely draw the line that a public and/or constitutional authority must act reasonably required to do within the ambit of the concerned law. The reasonableness and rationality can be read together in the instant case, Wherein the Education Board is given the responsibility to act fairly diligently and reasonably in applying the law. It never had the authority to override the metes and bounds of law, which it did. So, a legitimate expectation cannot be deleted by a public/constitutional body which is set by law to be followed by a public functionary. In this regard our Court have set its own standard in the light of decisions made in other jurisdictions; and of our own, such as, in Bangladesh Soya-Protein Project Ltd. Vs. Secretary, Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief 22 BLD (2000) HCD 378; The Chairman, Bangladesh Textile Mills Corporation vs. Nasir Ahmed Chowdhury 22 BLD (AD) (2002) 199: Dhaka WASA vs. Superior Buildings and Engineers Ltd. 51 DLR AD 1999.

<u>52. So, as we already have discussed above that in the absence of any provision of law to re-examine an answer script, it must be construed in favour of the petitioner, and therefore negating her request to re-examine her answer script is denied without lawful authority and is of no legal effect, apart from that since Gazette Notification dated 12.3.2001 and 30.4.2008 falls short of legal requirement to have the force of law, so she should be deemed to have passed in all the papers, since she was shown just to have failed in practical component of Chemistry, otherwise, she would have passed, as such she reserves the right to ask for re-examination, if she yet chooses to do so.</u>

53. With the above observations, the Rule is made absolute.

54. There is no order as to costs.

End.
