full_judgment:
Mr. A. N. M. Bashir Ullah; .J:- This Rule, on an application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure (in short, the Code) at the instance of the defendant petitioners was issued calling upon the opposite party nos.1-7 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 26.04.2006 (decree signed on 02.05.2006) passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Patiya, Chittagong in Other Appeal no. 492 of 1994 allowing the same and setting aside those dated 30,07.1994 (decree signed on 06.08.1994) passed by the teamed .Assistant Judge, Additional Court, Banskhali (Satkania Chawki), Chittagong in Other Suit no. 174 of 1992 dismissing the suit should not he set aside and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

2. The facts leading to the issuance of the Rule, in short, is that Kamini Bala Das, the 
predecessor of opposite party nos. 1-7 and 1 I as plaintiff filed Other Suit no. 28 of 1992. subsequently, the same was renumbered as Other Suit no. 174 of 1992 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Banskhali, Chittagong for declaration of her title. Later on, through amendment the further declaration was sought for that the deed of relinquishment dated 1 1.04.1933 is illegal, forged and not binding upon the plaintiff contending inter-ilia that 40 acres or land appertaining to R.S. khatian no. 705 of Chechoria mouza originally belonged to Joy Kumar who died leaving wife Kamini Bala Das having no son. 

3. Kamini Bala Das gave birth of 3 daughters namely Shanda Rani, Indu Rani and Nimoy Bala and at the time of death of Joy Kumar they were also alive. Shanda Rani and Indu Rani got married during the lifetime of their father. Shanda Rani was issueless while Indu Rani had 5 sons. Nimoy Bala got married under the auspices of her mother after the death of her father. 

4. Kamini Bala Das has been possessing the suit land after the death of her husband Joy Kumar. The P.S and B.S khatian have been rightly recorded in the name of Kamini Bala Das though inadvertently Joy, Kumar has been shown as the father of Kamini Bala Das instead of her husband. In the B.S khatian there appears a wrong entry into the column of possession that the defendants are in possession of the suit land. But the said entry is erroneous. Kamini Bala Das did not induct them as her permissive possessor. Joy Kumar did not execute and register any deed of relinquishment in favour of Pran Hari Acharja and Sree Hari Acharja and on the basis of the said deed of relinquishment, Pran Hari Acharja and Sree Hari Acharja did not get possession of the suit land. The defendants taking the ad~ antaucs of the wrong entry in the column of possession of B.S khatian threatened Kamini Bala Das with dispossession on 25.02.1992, hence the suit. 

5. After filing of the suit, Kamini Bala died, accordingly the plaintiffs who arc the grand sons of Kamini Bala through her daughters Indu Rani and Nimoy Bala were substituted as plaintiff nos. 1 (ka) to I (j a). 

6. The suit was contested by 3 sets of defendants. The defendant nos. 1/3, 5 and 6/7 filing 3 separate written statements contested in the suit. Though they have filed separate written statement, but their case appears to be similar with each other. The common case of the defendants may be narrated as that the suit is not maintainable in its present from, the plaintiffs have no right, title and interest into the suit land, the substituted plaintiffs have long-standing enmity with the defendants and those substituted plaintiffs in order to cause harm to the defendants field the original suit using the name of their grand mother Kamini Bala Das. 

7. The further case of the defendants are that the suit land originally belonged to Mohendra Chandra Acharja who met with a prematured death leaving two sons Pran Hari Acharja and Sree Hari Acharja and wife Sarat Kumar Acharja. Sarat Kumar Acharja in order to pay the loan and also for some other legal necessity created a benami transaction dated 23.03.1925 in the name of Joy Kumar. But Sarat Kumar Acharja as the mother of minor sons had no legal capacity to execute and register the said deed. Sarat Kumar Acharja did not seek permission from the learned District Judge or such execution. As such, the deed of the settlement dated 23.03.1925 was an illegal document. But for the said deed of patta the continuous possession of Pran Hari Acharja and Sree Hari Achat ja has not been affected. Since Pran Hari Achaija and Sree Hari Acharja were minors at the time of R.S record of right, Joy Kumar using the said opportunity got the said land recorded in his name. But at the attaining majority Pran Hari Acharja and Sree Hari Achaija raised objection against the deed of patta dated 23.03.1925 and Joy Kumar being convinced that ultimately the patta will not stand executed and registered a deed of relinquishment dated 11.04.1933 in favour of them. 

8. Pran Hari Acharja and Sree Hari Acharja on the same date, that is, on 11.04.1933 settled the suit land with Pan Mohan Das, Sukumar Das and Lalit Mohan Das. Pad Mohan Das gifted his portion to East Chechuria Primary School by a deed of gift dated 28.03.1941. Sukumar Das died leaving the defendant nos. 2 and 3. The defendant no.2 gifted four gandas of land from his share to the defendant no.3 on 11.06.1989. Shamsul Islam has been living on the said land. Lalit Mohan Das died leaving son Amar Keton who sold one ganda land to Shamsul Islam by a registered kabala dated 11.08.1991. Thus Shamsul Islam has purchased five gandas of land in to the suit land. 
9. The P.S khatian of the suit land is wrong which had just followed the R.S khatian. At the time of preparation of B.S. record of right, the defendants could not show their title deeds to the concerned officer, as such, though their possession into the suit land has been recorded but their names were not recorded in the columns of tenants. The plaintiffs have tiled a false suit and they are not entitled to get any relief in the suit and the suit is liable to be dismissed with costs.

10. Upon the above pleadings the trial Court framed as many as four issues to dispose of the suit at trial. The plaintiffs examined two witnesses and filed some documentary evidences that have been marked as exhibits. The defendants examined 6 witnesses in all and filed some documentary evidences duly marked as exhibits. The trial Court considering the evidences and other materials on record dismissed the suit holding that though Joy Kumar had acquired the suit land through the settlement dated 13.03.1925 but Joy Kumar relinquished his title in favour of Fran Hari Acharja and Sree Hari Acharja executing and registering a deed of Mukti-patra or Nadabi-patra dated 11 .04.1933. 

11. The plaintiffs of the original suit against the said verdict of the trial Court filed Title Appeal being no. 492 of 1994 in the Court of District Judge, Chittagong which has been ultimately heard by the learned Joint District Judge, Patiya, Chittagong, who by his impugned judgment and decree dated 26.04.2006 reversing those of the judgment and decree of the trial Court came to a conclusion that through the deed of relinquishment dated 11.04.1933 the title which was acquired by Joy Kumar has not gone in favour of Pran Hari Acharja and Sree Hari Acharja and ultimately he decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiffs. The defendant-petitioners being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the said judgment and decree moved this Court and obtained the present Rule. 

12. Mr. Probir Neogi along with Mr. Hassan M.S. Azim, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners supporting the Rule submits that the trial Court on the right assessment of the evidence and on the right evaluation of the facts of the case came to a very fair conclusion that through the deed of relinquishment dated 11.04.1933 Joy Kumar had lost his title and interest into the suit land. But the appellate Court below very erroneously found that through the deed of relinquishment dated 11.04.1933 Pran Hari Acharja and Sree Hari Acharja did not acquire title in to the suit land. The appellate Court below wrongly relied upon the decision of 19 DLR 33 but he has failed to take notice of the fact that though in the reported case it was held that Mukti-patra can never create title to any party unless it is supported by a registered deed of transfer but by the subsequent development that decision has been overruled by the Appellate Division. 

13. He referring the case of Government of Bangladesh-vs-Aziz Molla being dead his heirs Md. Mozibur Rahman and others reported in 44 DLR (AD) 90 submits that such type of deed whatever they are named like Nadabi-patra or Mukti-patra etcetera ultimately confers title to the recipient of the deed. But the appellate Court below without noticing the development of the law in respect of the Mukti-patra and Nadabi patra as the case may be came to a very wrong conclusion resulted into an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice to the defendant-petitioners. 

14. He further submits that in fact in this Rule the main points to be considered by this Court whether by the deed of relinquishment dated 11.04.1933 the land was again gone back to Pran Hari Acharja and Sree Hari Acharja or-not and since our Apex Court in the reported case held that by such type of deed of release or nadabi patra the recipient will acquire title and possession in the suit land. So, Pran Hari Acharja and Sree Hari Acharja got the land back in 1933 and in exercise of their such ownership they have settled the land on the same date to Pali Mohon Das, Sukumar Das and Lalit Mohon and from them the present defendants acquired the suit land. 

15. He further submits that in recent record of right which is known as B.S record of right; the possession of the defendants have been rightly recorded in B.S khatian no. 572. So, the B.S record of right ultimately shows that the predecessor of present defendants i.e. PanMohon Das, Sukumar Das and Lalit Mohon got the suit land by the patta dated 11.04.1933 from Pran Hari Acharja and Sree Hari Acharja. But the appellate Court below on the wrong application of law came to a wrong conclusion that they did not acquire any interest into the suit land. So, the Rule is liable to be made absolute setting aside the impugned judgment and decree of the appellate Court below restoring those of the judgment passed by the trial Court. 
16. On the other hand, Mr. H. S. Deb Brahman, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-opposite party nos. 1-7 opposing the Rule very strenuously r submits that Joy Kumar acquired the land through patta from Sarat Kumar Acharja on 23.03.1925 and on the basis of the said settlement the land was recorded correctly in the R.S record' of right in the name of Joy Kumar. But Joy kumar did never return back the said land in favour of Pran Hari Acharja and Sree Had Acharja as claimed by the defendants. Had, there been any such relinquishment in favour of Pran Hari Acharja and Sree Hari Acharja by Joy Kumar that would have been reflected in the subsequent records of right particularly in P.S and B.S records of right. In both the subsequent records of right the land was correctly recorded in the name of Kamini Bala Das, the wife of Joy Kumar who was the original plaintiff of the suit. The defendants did not challenge the R.S and P.S records of right at any point of time though they had the ample opportunity for the same. 

17. He also submits that it is fact that in the B.S record of right the names of the defendants have been recorded in the column of possession but they being shrewd and cunning got their names recorded with the help of the field officer but in the column of tenants the name of Kamini Bala Das has been recorded rightly. So, the subsequent record of right clearly indicates that the land was never gone back to pran Had Acharja and Sree Hari Acharja. 

18. He further submits that in the written statement the possession of Kamini Bala Das has been admitted and it surely indicates that Kamini Bala Das was never ousted from the suit land and the possession of Kamini Bala Das has been considered from the date of patta on 23.03.1925'. But the trial Court on the misconception of law very illegally dismissed the suit. The appellate Court below rightly held that .by the Mukti-patra dated 11.04.1933 no title was conferred to Pran Hari Achada and Sree Hari Acharja. The appellate Court below on the right assessment of the oral and documentary evidence decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiffs which does not call for any interference from this Court. So, the Rule is liable' to be discharged with costs. 

19. I have considered the above submissions and arguments of the learned Advocates of both the parties with profound attention and have gone through the materials on record. 
20. On going to the materials on record it is found that the patta dated 23.03.1925, exhibit-4 is an admitted fact in this suit. Sarat Kumar Acharja the wife of Mohendra Acharja and
mother of Fran Hari Acharja and Sree Hari Acharja settled the suit land in favour of Joy Kumar by exhibit-4. It is the definite case of the defendants that Sarat Kumar Acharja for some legal necessity settled the said land to Joy Kumar but the settlement was always under a question as Sarat Kumar Acharja had the lifetime interest into the suit land. After the death of Mohendra Chandra Acharja, the real owner of the suit land would be his sons Pran Hari Acharja and Sree Hari Acharja. Though, she had the right to transfer the land for some legal necessity subject to permission from the learned District Judge as her sons were minor at that time. But since there was no permission from the learned District Judge for such patta, so Fran Hari Acharja and Sree Hari Acharja attaining their majority demanded the suit-land and as a result Joy Kumar relinquished the land in favour of Fran Hari Acharja and Sree Hari Acharja by a deed of Mukti-patra dated 11.04.1933. In my consideration, the fate of the suit rests upon the said Mukti-patra dated 11.04.1933. 

21. The trial Court though without any reference of law or precedent of the higher Court simply came into a conclusion that by the deed of said Mukti-patra exhibit-Ka, the right, title and interest which was available in favour of Joy Kumar had gone to Pran Haig Acharja and Sree Hari Acharja. As such, neither Kamini Bala I) as nor his grand sons who became the plaintiffs on her death 'acquired nothing in to the suit land. 

22. But from the judgment of the appellate Court below it is found that the appellate Court below relying on the decision of 19 DLR 33 found that by the deed of Mukti-patra, Pran Hari Acharja and Sree Hari Acharja acquired nothing into the suit land. In the case of Bangladesh-vs-Aziz Molla being dead his heirs Md. Molibur Rahman and others reported in 44 DLR (AD) 90 it was held that by a Muktinama or Mukti-patta the -title and interest confers upon the recipient of the Mukti-patra or Mukti-nama as the case may be and in that case the case of Abdul Gafur Sander and others-vs-Wazedali Talukdar and another reported in 19 DLR 33 was also considered by the Appellate Division. 

23. The Appellate Division hi answering the question whether the recipient of a Mukti-nama and Mitkti-patra will acquire title into the land through the said Mukti-nama and Mukti-patra considered the decisions of the numerous eases of Indian jurisdiction. It will he beneficial for all of us if the valuable observations and findings made in the said case (para 7 to 13) are reproduced here, which runs as follows:
In Jadu Nath Poddar-Vs-Rup Lal Poddar, ILR 33 Cal. 967 (983-984), Dharam Chand- Vs-Mauji Saha, 16 CLJ 436, Naraklal-Vs-Thagoo Lal, AIR 1915 Cal. 819, Mathura Mohan Saha-Vs-Ramkumar Saha. AIR 1916 Cal. 136(141), Mookerjee, J held that a deed of release or relinquishment could not operate as a conveyance and could at most be taken as an admission that the executant had no interest in the property. 

After considering aforementioned cases in Thayil Manno and another- Vs-Kottiath Ramunni and others; AIR 1966(SC) 337 the Indian Supreme Court held that those cases do not lay down a proposition of universal application that a deed styled as a deed of release cannot operate as a conveyance. It further noted Hemendra Nath Mukedi-vs-Kumar Nath Roy, 12 CWN 478. In that case it was held that by a registered deed or disclaimer the executants relinquished all their right, title and interest and claim in the properties in favour of the release upon the condition that the release would discharge certain debts and the executants would be under no liberty to pay those debts. Maclean, CJ held that the deed or release, on its true construction, was a transfer though it was stamped only as a release and not with ad valorem stamp. 
The Indian Supreme Court then concluded: 
"We think that a registered instrument styled a release deed releasing the right, title and interest of the executant in any property in favour of the releasee for valuable consideration may operate as a conveyance, if the document clearly discloses an intention to effect a transfer.
This principle was extended in Kuppuswami Chettair-Vs-ASPA Arumugam Chettiar and another AIR 1967(SC) 1395, to a registered instrument of release executed without any consideration. After considering that under section 123 of the Transfer of property Act, 1882, a gift may be effected by a registered instrument signed by or on behalf of the doper and attested by at least two witnesses, it was held that a registered instrument releasing the right, title and interest of the releasor without consideration may operate as a transfer by way of a gift, if the document clearly shows an intention to effect the transfer and is signed by or on behalf of the releasor and attested by at least two witnesses. 
I am in respectful agreement with the above two decisions of the Indian Supreme Court. These decisions have been followed in a number of decisions of different High Courts of India, namely. Lakshman Naik and another-Vs-Smt. Sushila Swain, AIR 1968 Part 274 and Satyesh Chandra Banerjee- Vs -Smt. Rani Banedee and others, AIR 1977 Cal. 509. In Sanjukta Chatterjee-Vs Mrinmoy Chatterjee and others, 84 CWN(1979-80) 688 a deed of release, executed by the husband in favour of his wife and attested by their two sons, was construed as a gift. 
In the instant case the release is executed by plaintiff no. 2 on demand of plaintiff no. l. It is a registered document valued at Tk. 2000.00. Plaintiff no.2, the promisor agreed to compensate plaintiff no. 1, the promise, in case the latter suffers any loss, and held out that on the basis of the document plaintiff no.2 shall have the right to get his name recorded and enjoy all other rights of property. In view of the unassailable finding of the last court of fact that the father of plaintiff no.2 was the real owner and not a name-lender, as alleged in the plaint, it is clear that plaintiff no.2 had right in the property and was competent to pass on that right to plaintiff no.2". For all practical purposes the document is a document of transfer. Even if it is not construed as a document of conveyance under section 6 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, its nature as an agreement cannot be ignored. The document is a kind of contrivance that comes within the broad spectrum of definition of 'transfer' in clause(e) of section 2 of the Act." 
24. The Appellate Division considered the developments of law in respect of Mukti-patra from 1915 till pronouncement of the judgment and the last conclusion was drawn by the Appellate Division that for all practical purposes the document is a document of transfer. Here the document means the Mukti-nama or Mukti-patra as the case may be. Thus, I find that the appellate Court below simply relied upon the case of 19 DLR 33. However, at the relevant time the decision of 44 DLR (AD) 90 was prevailing in the arena of the law. As such, the appellate Court below should have not relied more upon the decision of 19 DLR 33 bypassing the decision of 44 DLR(AD) 90. 
25. As I have noticed it earlier that the fate of the present Rule would be decided relying on the deed of relinquishment dated 11.04.1933 and relying on the decision of 44 DLR (AD)90. It can safely be said that Joy Kumar executing and registering the deed of relinquishment has become nobody for the suit land and the suit land ultimately had become the property of pran Hari Acharja and Sree Hari Acharja. So, the Kamini Bala Das as the wife of Joy Kumar inherited nothing from Joy Kumar after 11.04.1933. 
26. The learned Advocate for the plaintiff-opposite parties put much emphasis on the record of right. It is fact that the R.S record of right stands in the name of-Joy Kumar. It is pertinent to point out here that in between 1925 to 1933 Joy Kumar was exercising his right, title and interest into the suit land and that was the time when the R.S record of right was prepared in that particular locality. So, in that view of the matter, there appears no harm and wrong in recording the name of Joy Kumar in R.S record of right of the suit land and it is known to us that at the time of preparation of P.S khatian or S.A khatian after the acquisition of rent receiving interest by the Government, the S.A record of right was prepared relying on the previous record of right and in that view of the matter it is very much natural and probable that the P.S or S.A record of right will be prepared in the name of,/ Joy Kumar as R.S record of right stands in his name. 
So far the B.S record of right is concerned it has blessed and favored both the plaintiffs and the defendants. In the column of tenants the record was prepared in the name of Kamini Bala Das but in the column of possession the land has been recorded in the name of Amar Kesh Das, Sudhir Kumar Das and Modhu Sudhan Das. This Amar Kesh Das is not an outsider but son of Lalit Mohan Das who took settlement of the suit land from Pran Hari Achada and Sree Hari Achada on 11.04.193.3 and Sudhir Kumar Das and Modhusudhan Das are the sons of Sukumar Das who also got the land through settlement dated 1 1.04.1933 from Pran Hari Achatja and Sree Hari Acharja. 5o, the presence of the names of the defendants into the column of possession is consistent with the case of the defendants that on the date of relinquishment by Joy Kumar, Pran Hari Acharja and Sree Hari Acharja settled the suit land with Pari Mohan Das, Sukumar Das and Lalit Mohan Das. Thus from the materials on record I find that all the defendants whose possession have been recorded in the B.S. of record of right has the reasons for the same. 

27. In the written statement of the defendant nos. 1-3 they have admitted that Kamini Bala Das being their relation and since she had no any financial capacity she was allowed to stay into the suit land during her life time. This sorts of statement though indicates the possession of Kamini Bala Das into the suit land but at the same time it was stated in the written statement that she was given a simple shelter into the suit land. I find nothing in the suit as a whole that after the deed of relinquishment dated 11.04.1933 the Joy Dr. Kumar or the plaintiffs had exercised their right, title and interest into the suit land. 

28. Having regards to the above discussion I find that the appellate Court below not justified In holding that the Mukti-patra or Mukti-nama did not confer any title to its recipient in fact he without taking into the notice of the case of 44 DLR(AD) 90 came into a wrong conclusion committing an error of law resulted into an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice to the defendants-petitioners. So, the judgment and decree of the appellate Court below are liable to be set aside. 

29. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. The judgment and decree of the appellate Court below dated 26.04.2006 and 02.05.2006 passed in Other Appeal no. 492 of 1994 is hereby set aside and those of the judgment passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Additional Court, Banskhali, Satkania Chawki, Chittagong is hereby restored. 

30. Let a copy of this judgment and order he sent to the Court concerned with the lower Courts record for information and necessary action. 


End.

lawyer:
Ms. Zubaida Gulshan Ara, Advocate -----for the petitioner 
Ms. Kashefa Hossain, A.A.G. (with leave of the Court) ----- for the respondents
parties:
Shahina Begum ----- Petitioner
Versus
Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Mr. Md. Kabul Quddus, J:- This Rule at the instance of a Lecturer of a Private College was issued for a direction to accord permission for her promotion and thereby to ensure her seniority and other benefits including salary and other remunerations. 

2. It is contended in the writ petition that the petitioner is a Lecturer. of Philosophy in Alhaj Mokbul Hossain University College, Dhaka. She joined the College on 25.9.1993 and was enlisted in the monthly pay order (M.P.O.) on 1.4.1999. While she was serving the College with utmost sincerity and diligence, the Principal of the College illegally dismissed her from service on 10.6.2001, challenging which she filed an appeal before the Vice-Chancel tor of National University, Gazipur (herein respondent 3). On receipt of the appeal the National University authority formed a three member committee to enquire into the matter. After completion of enquiry the said committee submitted a report on 17.7.2002 (annexure-B) terming her dismissal to be illegal. On the said report, the National University authority directed the College authority to reinstate the petitioner in service and pay her hack wages. Accordingly, the Governing Body of the College in its meeting held on 6.8.2002 reinstated the petitioner and communicated her its decision by a letter as contained in Memo No.A.M.H. Co/600/02/(Kha) dated 11.8.2002. In pursuance thereto, the petitioner joined the College on the same day. 

3. It is pertinent to mention that by the same report dated 17.7.2002 (annexure-B) the enquiry committee proposed suspension and departmental proceeding against Mr. Md. Mohibullah, the then Principal of Alhaj Mokbul Hossain College. Pursuant thereto he was put under suspension on 8.8.2002. Mr. Md. Mohibullah filed Writ Petition No. 4309 of 2002 challenging both the said report dated 17.7.2002 and the order of suspension dated 8.8.2002. Meanwhile, the decision of the Governing Body for reinstatement of the petitioner was acted upon. 

4. The High Court Division ultimately made the rule absolute in the said writ petition by
its judgment and order dated 29.11.2006. Relevant portion of the judgment is quoted below: 

"Under the circumstances we are of the view that the direction contained in the University letter dated 17.7.2002 and the order of suspension passed on 8.8.2002 under the direction of the University authority have been made without lawful authority and this is of no legal effect" 

5. Against the said judgment and order of the High Court Division, the college authority filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 277 of 2007 before the Appellate Division, which was also dismissed on 30.10.2007. The petitioner Ms. Shahina Begum was made a party neither in the said writ petition nor in the civil petition for leave to appeal. 

6. In the meantime considering the seniority of the writ petitioner, the Governing Body of the College, recommended her for promotion to the post of Assistant Professor and forwarded the matter to the Director General, Directorate of Secondary and Higher Education, Dhaka. While the matter was in progress, Mr. Md. Mohibullah, the Principal of the College taking advantage of the judgment passed in Writ Petition No. 4309 of 2002 raised objection against the proposal of her promotion. 

7. In a supplementary affidavit (affirmed on 19.2.2013) filed by the writ petitioner it has been stated that initially she was prevented from joining in service, but ultimately could join on 1 1 .1 1 .2002 and got her back wages. After forwarding the proposal of her promotion, she along with her another colleague Mahmud Mostafa Al-Mamun made a joint representation dated 12.4.2008 to respondent No.2 and served notice demanding justice upon all the respondents on 2.4.2010, but without any result. It has 41 also been stated that during pendency of the Rule no one was promoted to the post of Assistant Professor in the Department of Philosophy and the post is still vacant. 
8. The President of the Governing Body, Principal in charge and concerned public functionaries are made respondents in this writ petition but no one has appeared and controverted the facts placed in the writ petition as well as in the supplementary affidavit. 

9. It appears from the relevant portion of the judgment as quoted above that Mr. Md.  Mohibullah moved Writ Petition No. 4309 of 2002 so far it was related to the proposal of his suspension and commencement of a departmental proceeding against him. The present petitioner was not made a party therein. Moreover, she was reinstated in service on the basis of the report dated 17.7.2002 and was allowed to draw her salaries and back wages. In such a position we do not think that the judgment passed in Writ Petition No. 4309 of 2002 is a barrier on the way of her promotion. 

10. In the present case, the writ petitioner has sought for a direction to promote her on the basis of tenure in service as a lecturer i.e. seniority. Seniority alone does not create the right to promotion. Some other factors like sincerity, honesty, integrity, efficiency, commitment, service record etc. are also taken into consideration and as such this Court would not be within its jurisdiction in directing the respondents to promote the petitioner. It is within the domain of the authority concerned to make decision in the matter of her promotion in the facts available to them as well as upon due compliance of the applicable Rules and Regulations. But it is definitely her right to be considered for promotion on the basis of seniority as well as other factors. [reliance placed on the Chairman, Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education. Jessore Vs. Nazir Ahmed, 16 BLT (AD) 2641. We have already held that in considering the petitioner's promotion, the judgment as referred to above is not a barrier. 

11. Under the above facts and circumstances, we are of the view that justice would be met if the respondents arc directed to consider the proposal of promotion of the writ petitioner subject to fulfillment of all other legal requirements. 

12. Accordingly, the Rule is disposed of. The respondents are directed to consider the promotion of the writ petitioner in accordance with law and dispose of her representation dated 12.4.2008 (annexure-I) within three months from receipt of this judgment. 

13. Communicate a copy of this judgment. 

End.

full_judgment:
Mr. Syed Refaat Ahmed, J:-  In this Application under Section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure ("Code") a Rule was issued calling upon the Opposite Parties to show cause as to why Order No. 28 dated 31.5.2009 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Moulvibazar in Title Slat No. 6 of 2007 adding the Opposite Party No. 1 as Defendant in the Suit should not be set aside and/or such other or further Order or Orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

2. The petitioner as Plaintiff instituted the original Suit for declaration that the Suit land was purchased benami by the plaintiff in the name of his wife, the Defendant No.1. It is contended that the plaintiff purchased the Suit land vide deed No. 4110 dated 18.7.1958 and came to possess the same along with other suit properties also purchased by the plaintiff benami in the name of the Defendant No. 1. The Defendant No.1, It is further contended having no title in the Suit land but having nevertheless refused to give kabala to return the said land, the Plaintiff had no other recourse but to file the Suit. 

3. It is noted that the Defendant No.1 entered appearance in the Suit and incidentally both the parties on 21.9.2008 filed a petition for Compromise of the Suit and consequently both parties deposed before the learned Court in support of the said compromise. The plaintiff-petitioner states that prior to filing the Compromise Petition, the Defendant No. 1 filed a Written Statement denying material allegations made in the plaint contending that there is no cause of action and that the Suit is not maintainable and disavowing the plaintiff-petitioner's statement that he is the owner and in possession of the Suit land. 

4. It so transpired that the Defendant No.1 passed away issueless on 10.10.2008 leaving the plaintiff-petitioner as her widower husband and seven siblings as her heirs, all of whom figured in an Application dated 26.11.2008 made by the plaintiff-petitioner for addition as parties to the Suit. 

5. It is evident to this Court from documents on record and, in particular, Annexure-E to this Application, that consequent upon the Compromise petition of 21.9.2008 the Defendant No. 1, however, filed a petition dated 23.9.2008 seeking a postponement of issuance of any Order on the Compromise petition on account of an alleged breach of trust by her husband the plaintiff-petitioner in duly complying with his undertaking in her favour evidenced in the Compromise petition. It is on the heels of these developments that the Defendant No. 1 passed away on 10.10.2008. It is against this backdrop that the Opposite party being Md. Moklisur Rahman, given the apparent transfer pendente lite of the Suit land to hint on 26.12.2007 and 20.4.2008, filed an Application under Order 1, Rule 10 of the Code seeking to be added as a party and further reinforcing that prayer by bringing forth the fact of being a necessary and proper party stemming from title and interest in the Suit land on account of the transfer pendente lite. 

6. The learned Joint District Judge after hearing the parties passed an Order on 31.5.2009 allowing the said Application for addition of party on the ground that though the Applicant purchased the Suit land pending the disposal of the Suit, in the interest of avoiding further complication and multiplicity of proceeding there is no legal bar to allow Mr. Rahman to be a party. The plaintiff-petitioner now impugns that Order in this Revision Application. The focal issue, as submitted by the plaintiff-petitioner, is that the learned Joint District Judge in so allowing for addition of party gravely erred in law by ignoring the fact that the transferee pendente lite had no interest in the Suit land as indeed dictated by the Doctrine of Lis pendens. 

7. In making that argument further by reference to the Application itself, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-petitioner Mr. Md. Zakir Hossain submits that the governing principle here is of a subordination of the rights and interests, if any, of a transferee pendente lite to those of the parties in a pending suit by reason of which such transferee shall take, if at all, any benefit stemming from such right and interest but subject to the outcome of such a suit. It is submitted that by that reason, in the present instance, the transferee pendente lite shall have his fate determined finally upon the disposal of the Suit commensurate with the fate as befalls the claim of the now deceased Defendant No. 1. Mr.Hossain substantiates that argument by reference in particular to Section 52of the Transfer property Act ("the Act") that is submitted to incorporate a specific bar for someone as the opposite Party No. 1 transferee pendent elite to be added on as a party to the Suit. Citing decisions in Jamal Uddin vs. Raheya Begum reported in 32 DLR (1980), 63. Nesmohammad & Ors vs. M. Jamil Khatun & Ors reported in 6 BLT (AD) (1998), 276, Tozammel Hossain vs. fatema Khatun reported in 15 DLR (1993), 697 and Sree Nath Paul vs. Sachindra Kumar Bashu reported in 20 DLR (1968), 97, Mr. Hossain submits that upon a true construction of Section 52 any transfer of land that is otherwise the subject- matter of any suit awaiting disposal is hit by the Doctrine of Lis Pendens, thereby, leading such transfer liable to be declared as invalid in law. Consequentially, Mr. Hossain submits, any transferee pendente lite is law to seek any recourse to the provisions of Other I. Rule 10(2) to be impleaded or added on as a party to such a Suit. 

8. The learned Advocate for the Opposite party No. 1 Mr. Chanchal Kumar Biswas, in responding to the Rule, highlights that the issue of title to the Suit land was a highly contested one between the plaintiff-petitioner and the now deceased Defendant No. l. This, Mr. Biswas explain, is evident, for example, from the Written Statement filed on 10.8.2008 that in disputing the plaintiff-petitioner's claim to the Suit land instead asserts the ownership and possession of the same to lie with the Defendant No. 1 by her own right and in her own name. Submitting on the fact of the compromise struck as above stated by and between the plaintiff-petitioner and the Defendant No. 1, Mr. Biswas lays stress, however, on the developments of 23.9.2008 reflected in an Order of that date whereby the Defendant No. 1 sought to put a halt to effect being given to the Compromise Petition of 21.9.2008 on account of breach of its terms already committed by the plaintiff-petitioner. Mr. Biswas submits as dubious the effort thereafter of the plaintiff-petitioner to, however, contrive to convince the Court that the Defendant No. 1 was in that regard not pressing her above referred petition of 23.9.2008. In doing so, the plaintiff-apparently prayed concomitantly for the suit to be decreed on the terms of the very Compromise petition that the Defendant No. 1 had earlier so raised an objection to. 

9. It is against the above factual backdrop that the Application for addition of party under Order 1, Rule 10(2) appears to have been made with concern evidently raised by the applicant Opposite party No. I of the above developments compounded by the fact of the demise by then on 10.10.2008 of the Defendant No. 1 vendor further giving rise to the spectre of the rights and interests of the Opposite party No. 1 vendee not being duly represented in the pending suit proceedings. 

10. Upon a consideration of the facts and circumstances as above cited, this Court at the outset has deemed it prudent to dwell on the parameters of the Doctrine of Lis pendens as has through the years gone through a continuous exercise of common law enunciation in various jurisdictions. 

Indeed, as argued by Mr. Md. Zakir Hossain, the core principle still remains of a sale pendente lite resulting in sub ordinate rights relative to the rights decreed upon ultimately in the suit proceeding s. In broadening, however, the scope of the application of the Doctrine in a beneficial sense it has equally been judicially endorsed that the effect of section 52 of the Act, however, is not to completely wipe out a sale pendente lite. It is from that notion that there emerges the concept, in certain circumstances at least, of the adequate protection of interests and rights pendent elite keeping nevertheless within the broader framework of the principle of subordination as above stated. Accordingly, the Supreme Court of India in Nagubai Ammal and others vs. B Shama Rao and others reported in AIR 1956 (SC) 593 ruled in simple terms thus: 

"The effect of section 52 is not to wipe out a sale pendent elite altogether but to subordinate it to the rights based on the decree in the suit." 

11. Predicated on that reading of the core concept of the Doctrine of Lis Pendens the supreme Court, thereafter, referred to view the operation of section 52 of the Act in terms that a transfer pendente lite is indeed "good except to the extent that it might conflict with rights decreed under the relevant decree or order." The Indian supreme Court's decision further Sm Saila Bala Dassi vs. Sm Nirmala Sundari Dassi and another reported in AIR 1958 (SC) 394 takes the beneficial application of the Doctrine a notch further in that since the transferee pendente lite shall in any event be bound by proceedings initiated by the parties in whose favour a decree is passed in execution of the decree it would indeed be in the interest of justice that such transferee pendente use by given on opportunity to protect his/her rights. 

12. This Court notes that these pronouncements and elaborations on the Doctrine of Lis pendens has, for example, informed the ratio of the Judgment in Mokther Masum vs. Nironjan Kumar Mondol reported in 50 DLR (1998), 341. The Court in that Case found the beneficial application of the Doctrine favouring a transferee pendente lite to stem from the judicial recognition as indeed comes forth in the Nagubai Ammal Case that transfers pendente lite are to be deemed to be valid and operative as between the parties thereto notwithstanding that a transferee pendente lite acquires interests and rights otherwise of a subordinate nature in the general scheme of the Doctrine. 

13. Turning to the provisions of Order 1, Rule 10(2) of the Code, this Court appreciates that first and foremost it reflects a judicial discretion that has to be exercised with regard to impleading a party or not in view of the fact and circumstances of each individual case. It is equally to he borne in mind that any applicant under order 1, Rule 10(2) may either qualify as a necessary and/or a proper party. Hence, should the facts and circumstances merit identifying an applicant as one or the other kind of party then that would merit a favourable exercise of judicial discretion. Here, this Court is reminded of the fact that a necessary party is one whose presence in a suit is otherwise enjoined by law or in whose absence no effective decree can be passed. Contradistinctively, a proper party is one whose presence though not necessary for passing an effective decree, may nevertheless remain central in order to facilitate a more effectual and complete adjudication of all the disputes and thereby necessarily help avoid a multiplicity' of Proceedings (See Mahmudul Islam and probir Neogi "The Law of Civil procedure" Volume-1, page, 519). Upon a perusal of the impugned order of the learned Joint District Judge it is evident that it is the latter rationale of impleading a proper party that appears to have been the guiding force in his arriving at the decision that he did. It is here that Mr. Biswas has satisfactorily established certain compelling circumstances in this Case under which the Opposite Party No. 1 would indeed qualify to be added on as a proper party. It is noted that the Opposite party No.1, since the demise of the Defendant No. 1 on 10.10.2008, has been virtually the only interested party in place of the deceased Defendant No. 1 to agitate and deliberate upon the competing rights and interests in the Suit land. This is so given that the Defendant No. 1 passed away without leaving any children but instead certain of her siblings who in the facts, have not acquired as direct a right and interest in the Suit property as the Opposite Party No. 1 has. Accordingly, the Opposite party No I now reasonably apprehends that without being impleaded as a party a decree may ensile that, will not ensure justice overall. These facts manifest in effect some of the tests that can be discerned from the various judgments cited by Mr. Biswas, these being chiefly the judgments in the mokthar Masum Abedin Case and in Anil Ranjan Ghosh vs. Assistant Custodian reported in 49 DLR (1997), 296. It is noted that in the Anil Ranjan Ghosh Case the notion subscribed to was that of the necessity of impleading a party (like the Opposite party No. 1 in this instant Case) in circumstances where a court finds itself unable to rule on an effective remedy in the absence of a party. Subscribing to the notion, as above expound that the Doctrine of Lis Pendens does not make a transaction pendent lite invalid, the court in the Anil Ranjan Ghosh Case ruled that a purchaser assignee of suit land being interested in the result of the suit can indeed be added as a party given his presence is necessary in the suit. Mr. Biswas has also drawn our attention to the judgment in Nathu Dhoju vs. Ramchand Balchand reported in AIR (33) 1946 Bombay 462 that addresses the risk that a transferee pendente lite may be exposed to in circumstances where a compromise is struck between the original litigants and there arises in the facts a fear that the compromise may not have been fairly and reasonably struck. In the Nathu Dhoju Case in fact it was held that if the final decision in any pending litigation is brought by any means less than fair then such decision shall not operate to affect the rights of the transferee pendente lite. 

14. The facts in the instant Case of themselves necessitated in this Court's view the addition of the Opposite Party No. 1 at the very least as the proper party, as rightly found by the learned Joint District Judge, in the interest of ensuring a fair outcome of the pending litigation filed against the backdrop of highly contested and divisive claims to the Suit land of both the Plaintiff-Petitioner and the now deceased Defendant No.1vendor as the predecessor-in-interest of the Opposite Party No. l. Indeed, the Opposite Party No.1, we note, having claimed interest though the Defendant No.1 vendor will not get any better right than the deceased Defendant No.1-vendor. But that does not detract from the fact that his coming on board as an Added party will indeed ensure his rights and interests to be properly addressed by the Court and, thereby, contribute to the more effectual and complete adjudication of the dispute at hand. It is this Court's view, therefore, that the learned Joint District Judge aptly and duly appreciated the somewhat compelling circumstances in this Case that reasonably merited the Application under Order 1, Rule 10(2) to be allowed in the manner that was done. Having, therefore, not erred in law in any manner and having not contributed to the failure of justice in any sense, the impugned order merits no interference by this Court as otherwise prayed for. 

15. Accordingly, we find no merit in this Application and no substance in the Rule issued. 

16. In the result, the Rule is discharged. 

17. There is no Order as to costs. 

End.

lawyer:
Mr. Md. Abdul Hai, D. A. G. ----- For the Petitioner. 
Mr. Probir Haider, Advocate. ----- For the opposite party No. 3.
parties:
Government of the people's Republic of Bangladesh, represented by the Divisional Forest Officer, ----- Plaintiff-petition.
Versus
Md. Abdur Sobahan and another. ----- Defendant-Opposite parties.
full_judgment:
Mr. Sheikh Abdul Awal, J:- This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the delay of 1477 days in filing the Revision application should not be condoned and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

2. Material facts of the case, briefly, are that the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, represented by the Divisional Forest Officer, Mymensingh as plaintiff-petitioner being aggrieved and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree dated 09.08.2007 (decree singed on 16.08.2007) passed by the learned Additional District judge, 2nd Court, Mymensingh Other Appeal No. 301 of 2000 dismissing the appeal, preferred a Revision application under section 115 (1) of the Code of Civil Procedure before this Court, which is out of time by 1477 days and hence, the Rule. 
3. It is contended in the application that after passing the impugned judgment and decree the petitioner received the same from the conducting lawyer of the case in the year 2008. Thereafter, the petitioner sent the certified copy of judgment and decree to the retainer, Mymensingh for opinion on 07.07.2010. Thereafter, the petitioner sent the file to Solicitor Wing on 20.07.2010, as the petitioner sent photocopy of the judgment and decree passed by the appellate court the Solicitor Wing on 16.08.2010 sent a letter to the petitioner for sending the original certified copy of the judgment and decree which was subsequently received on 27.9.2010. by the Solicitor Wing, Ministry of Law and justice and then Solicitor Wing sent the case file to the office of the learned Attorney General on 23.01.2011, and then the Attorney General Office handed over the case file to the learned Assistant Attorney General for drafting the Revision application, who after preparing the Revision application filed the same on 28.12.2011 and in this way the delay of 1477 days has been caused in filing the Revision application. 

4. It is further contended that the delay of 1477 days has been caused in filing the Revision application is unintentional and bonafide. The petitioner graves mercy and apology before this Court for such unintentional delay in filing the Revision application and if the delay is not condoned the petitioner will suffer irreparable loss. 

5. Mr. Md. Abdul Hai, the learned Deputy Attorney General appearing for the petitioner submits that the delay of 1477 days has been caused due to the movement of the case file from one officer to other officer within usual normal gap of time for observing various formalities. He further submits that the delay of 1477 days in filing the Revision application is unintentional, which was beyond the control of the petitioner, unless the delay is condoned, the petitioner will suffer irreparable loss and injury resulting in the loss of the public. 

6. Drawing support for his submission, the learned Deputy Attorney General referred to a decision reported in 10 BLT (AD)-79. 
7. Mr. Probir Halder, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party No. 3, on the other hand, by filing counter affidavit contested the Rule. He submits that the settled proposition of law is that each day's delay has to be explained by the applicant, be it a private person or the Government and in the instant case the petitioner has miserably failed to explain each day's delay. The learned Advocate drew my attention to the statements of facts made by the petitioner in paragraph Nos. 1-2 of the application and thereafter, submits that the Government petitioner after being unsuccessful in both the Courts below preferred Civil Revision under section 115 (1) CPC without any sorts of explanation from 9.8.2007 to 3.9.2007=24 days, 30.9.2007 to 7.7.2010 = 2 years 9 month 07 days, 20.7.2010 to 27.9.2010= 2 month 07 days and from 23.01.201 Ito 28.12.2011=11 month 05 days, that is, total 3 years 11 months 13 days. He next upon referring to a decision reported in 6 BLD (AD) 101 submits that if this sort of inordinate delay is condoned that will encourage the officers of Solicitor Office and law officers as well to be irresponsible and negligent in their official duties. 

8. Finally, Mr. Probir Haider submits that in this case Government petitioner as plaintiff lost in both the Courts below and there is no merit in the connected revisional application inasmuch as Forest Settlement Officer has already been released the property through Misc. case No. 9(XIV)/2010 which has been affirmed by the Divisional Commissioner vide judgment dated 28.3.2011 passed in Misc appeal No. 218 of 2010. 

9. I have considered the submission of the learned Deputy Attorney General and the learned Advocate for both the sides and perused the application under section 5 of the Limitation Act Rule petition and other materials on record. It appears from the record that the certified copy of the judgment and decree dated 09.08.2007 (decree singed on 16.08.2007) was made ready on 11.09.2007 and the petitioner took delivery of the same on 30.09.2007 and the petitioner sent the certified copy of judgment and decree to the retainer, Mymensingh for opinion on 07.07.2010 without any sort of explanation over a period of 2 years and 9 months and thereafter, solicitor wing and the office of the Attorney General took more than I year to prepare and file the Revision application without any reasonable explanation whatsoever. In the instant case even if all the latches are brushed aside the petitioner has failed to explain the delay of more than 10 months which took place in the office of the learned Attorney General. The endorsed Assistant Attorney General knew that the Revisional application was already barred by limitation but for the reasons best known to him as to why he took more than 10 months for preparing the Revisional application which clearly indicates that the Government officials dealt with the matter in gross negligent and callous manner. 

10. It is true that concerned authorities of the Government require longer time in making the decision to file Appeal or Revision and then in processing the matter for acting on it and if reasonable explanation of delay in the relevant matter is given, there is no reason why such reasonable explanation of delay should not be accepted. 

11. In this case it appears that the Government petitioner having knowledge of the limitation and without sufficient cause slept over the matter and allowed the period of limitation to run out. If this sort of negligence is condoned by the Court then the litigant public will be at the mercy of the state functionary since in this application the Government-petitioner has utterly failed to explain the delay. It appears to me that the petitioner had acted in negligent way and as such there is no scope whatsoever to condone the unexplained delay. 

12. Further, the learned Deputy Attorney General in the facts and circumstances of the case finds it difficult to refute the contention raised by Mr. Probir Halder that there is no merit in the connected revisional application inasmuch as Forest Settlement Officer has already been released the suit property through Misc. case No. 9(XIV)/2010 which has been affirmed by the Divisional Commissioner vide judgment dated 28- 3.2011 passed in Misc appeal No. 218 Of 2010. Thus, I do not find any substance in this Rule. 

13. The rule is, therefore, discharged. Since the delay of 1477 days is not condoned, the connected Revision application is rejected summarily. 

End.

lawyer:
Mr. Md. Jafor Ali, Advocate ----- For the petitioner 
Mr. S.N. Goswami, Advocate ------ For the Opposite Parties
parties:
Mosammat Hasina Begum.-----Pre-emptee-Appellant -Petitioner
Vs
Durga Charan being dead his heirs: Basu Deb Mondal and another. ----- Pre-emptor-Respondent Opposite Parties.
full_judgment:
Mr. Soumendra Sarker„ J :- The Rule issued calling upon the opposite party Nos. 1(ka) and I (kha) to show cause as to why the judgment and order dated 29.05.2001 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Artha Rin Adalat, Faridpur in Miscellaneous Appeal No.43 of 1999 should not be set aside and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this court may seem fit and proper. 

2. The facts leading to the issuance of the Rule in a nutshell can be stated thus, the father of the present opposite-parties namely Durga Charan (now dead) filed an application for pre-emption of the case land under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 against the present petitioner who purchased the case land by a registered sub-kabla deed dated 08.11.1994 being preemption Miscellaneous Case No.33 of 1996 in the court of learned Senior Assistant Judge, Madhukhali, Faridpur contending inter alia that the pre-emptor is a co-sharer by inheritance in the case holding. The opposite-party No.2 & 3 who were other co-sharers of the holding transferred their share in favour of pre-emptee-opposite party No.1 a stranger to the case holding behind the back of the pre-emptor. The pre-emptor is an agriculturist having OS(five) bighas of land and knowing about the case kabla the pre-emptor filed the case for getting the land pre-empted. 

3. The contrary case of the pre-emptee-appellant-petitioner is such that the pre-emptor have no locus standi to prefer the Miscellaneous Case and the case is hit by the principle of estoppel, waiver and acquiescence and that the case land is the home-stead in which the pre-emptee have got his dwelling house and a husking Mill which is within the knowledge of the pre-emptor. That the pre-emptee purchased the land at the negotiation of the pre-emptor & while he refused to purchase the land the pre-emptee purchased and that the pre-emptor filed the case on false allegation suppressing the truth. 
4. The learned trial court after taking evidence from the sides of the respective parties allowed the Miscellaneous Case of pre-emption by his judgment and order dated 26.04. 1999. 

5. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the impugned judgment and order the pre-emptee preferred a Miscellaneous Appeal being No.45 of 1999 in the Court of Learned district Judge, Faridpur which was heard and disposed of by the learned the then Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat. Faridpur and the learned appellate court by the impugned judgment and order dated 29.05.2001 disallowed the appeal affirming the judgment and order passed by the trial court. 
6. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the impugned judgment and order the pre-emptee-appellant-petitioner has preferred this revisional application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the Rule with an interim order of stay. 

7. Mr. Md. Jafar Ali, the learned Advocate appeared on behalf of the petitioner while Mr. S. N. Goswami, the learned Advocate appeared on behalf of the opposite parties. 

8. The learned advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner during hearing of this Civil Rule submits that the learned lower appellate court committed illegality in deciding the fate of the appeal. The learned Advocate further submits that the learned court of appeal below failed to consider that the case is hit by the principle of waiver, estoppel and acquiescence; as during purchase of the land by the pre-emptee-petitioner the pre-emptor-opposite party expressed his unwillingness to purchase the land in dispute. Furthermore; the preemptor-opposite party have no necessity of the case land but to deprive the pre-emptee in enjoying the land instituted the original case. The following conduct will prove that the pre-emptor had no necessity of land. In the year 1993 A.D. the full brother of the pre-emptor sold the contiguous land of the same plot in favour of the pre-emptor at that time was totally silent in filing such miscellaneous Case for getting the land pre-empted. Mr. Md. Jafar Ali, the learned Advocate in support of his argument submits an application under order 41 Rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure so-that; the pre-emptee-appellant-petitioner can get an opportunity to adduce additional evidence to substantiate her case. A photo copy of the kabla deed dated 23.11.1993 executed by one Sukumer Mondal, son of late Nedu Ram Mondal in favour of Most. Hasina Begum, wife of Md. Nasir Uddin is annexed herewith as Annexure-"A". The learned Advocate lastly submits that during trial of the original case the pre-emptee-petitioner was not in a position to file this application supported by the sub-kabla deed as it was not known to her during pendency of the original case and as a result of that the petitioner deserve an order of sending the case on remand. 

9. As against the aforesaid submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioner the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite-party opposing the Rule controverted the arguments advanced from the side of the pre-emptee-petitioner and submits that during passing the impugned judgment and order the learned appellate court below committed no wrong or illegality. There is no misreading or non-reading of evidence and non-consideration of material facts resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. The learned Advocate further submits that there is no scope to entertain the application filed under order 41 Rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure since the pre-emptee petitioner was totally silent in her pleading about the content of the application which is brought at present. In the written objection the pre-emptee-appellant-petitioner never raised any such plea that the pre-emptor-opposite party has no necessity of the case land and as a result; under the purview of order 7 Rule 18 of the Code of Civil Procedure the pre-emptee-appellant petitioner is now debarred from taking any advantage which is beyond her pleading. The learned Advocate lastly submits that the order of remand can not be allowed to fill up the lacuna under order 41 Rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

10. Heard the learned Advocates of both sides. Perused the case record, exhibited documents, deposition of the witnesses and all other connected papers. 

11. On perusal of the case record it transpires that the original Miscellaneous Case under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 was preferred by the pre-emptor-opposite party alleging that he is a co-sharer by inheritance in the case holding and within the statutory period of limitation he has instituted the case for pre-emption complying all provisions of law. 

12. Vis-a-vis; the pre-emptee-opposite party No. 1 to the case after filing a written objection therein states that she purchased the case land with the consent of the pre-emptor and the case land has been developed subsequently by her after purchase at a cost of Tk.40,000/and in the presence of the pre-emptor the vendor-opposite party Nos.2 and 3 transferred the case land in favour of the vendee-opposite party No.1 The learned trial court and thereafter the appellate court in it's findings and observation concurrently held that the pre-emptor is co-sharer by inheritance in the case holding and while the other co-sharers of the property i.e. the opposite-party Nos.2-3 transferred the case land in favour of the stranger opposite-party No. 1 the pre-emptor filed the original Miscellaneous Case invoking section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 within the period of limitation. After proper sifting of evidence and analysis of connected papers both the courts below concurrently decided that the contention of the preemptor is proved by credible evidence but on the other hand the case of the pre-emptee not at all established by any tangible evidence. It appears that the assessment of evidence and appreciation of law which was done by the courts below is proper in its true perspective. 

13. In this context; under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act it is to be remembered that mere presence or knowledge of the pre-emptor while transferring the land under pre-emption cannot take away the statutory right of a pre-emptor to pre-empt the land and in that case the principle of acquiescence and waiver is not attracted. 

Maulana Abdul Karim vs. Nur Jahan Begum and others, 38 DLR 371, Akhlasur Rahman and others vs. Safurullah and others, 14 BLD (AD) 20 and Fazaruddin vs. Maijuddin and others, 44 DLR(AD) 62 ref. 

14. In view of the submissions of the respective parties I have scrutinized the written objection of the pre- emptee-appellant-petitioner along with the testimony given by her and consulting the evidence on record no where it is noticed that during pendency of the original case or in the written objection the preemptee ever raised any such plea that the pre-emptor has no necessity to purchase the case land by way of pre-emption. In this regard Order VII Rule 18 of the Code of Civil Procedure reads as follows: 

"A document which ought to be produced in Court by the plaintiff when the plaint is presented, or to be entered in the list to be added or annexed to the plaint, and which is not produced or entered accordingly, shall not, without the leave of the Court, be received in evidence on his behalf at the hearing of the suit. 

Provided that the court shall not grant such leave save in exceptional circumstances. 

Nothing in this rule applies to documents produced for cross-examination of the defendant's witnesses, or in answer to any case set up by the defendant or handed to a witness merely to refresh his memory." 

Furthermore; order VII Rule 14 of the Code direct the party concerned that he shall produce the documents in his possession on which he relies upon, at the time of presenting the plaint and shall give the list of such documents which are not in his possession or power in support of his claim. Rule 15 further directs the plaintiff that he shall state, if possible, in whose possession or power those documents are. 

Therefore; it is obvious to note that under order 41 Rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure the pre- emptee-appellant-petitioner have got no scope to get any opportunity to adduce further evidence by way of the sending the case on remand. 

16. Under order XLI, Rule 23 of the Code of Civil Procedure the order of remand as prayed for is not to be granted as a matter of course [vide the case law reported in 41 DLR (AD) 124; 3 BLC (AD) 38;] or to fill in the lacuna in any party's pleading. [vide Akitullah vs Zafala. 54 DLR(AD) 74.] 

17. Having regard to the facts, circumstance and decisions referred to above I am constrained to hold such a view that since the lower appellate court in disposing the appeal committed no illegality and no misreading or non-reading of evidence on record resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice the Rule have got no substance to succeed. 

18. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and order dated 29.05.2001 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Artha Rin Adalat, Faridpur in Miscellaneous Appeal No.43 of 1999 is hereby affirmed. 

19. The order of stay granted earlier by this Court at the time of issuance of the Rule stands vacated. 

20. Communicate the judgment and order at once & send down the lower court's record immediately. 

End.

lawyer:
Dr. Mohammad Abul Bashar, Advocate -----for the petitioners 
No one appears ----- for the opposite parties
parties:
Md. Mazam Ali and others ----- Plaintiff-respondent-petitioners
Versus
Mir Khurshed Ali and others ----- Respondent-appellant-opposite parties
full_judgment:
Mr. A.K.M. Shahidul Huq, J:- The Judgment of reversal has been called in question by invoking the revisional Jurisdiction of this Hon'ble Court on laying an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure at the instance of the plaintiff against the judgment and decree dated 11-11-1999 passed by the Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Tangail allowing the Appeal and thereby reversing the judgment and decree dated 23-9-1998 and 29-9-1998 respectively passed in Other Class Suit No. 8 of 1997 should not be set aside or such other or further order or orders passed as to this court may seem tit and proper

2. The short facts for disposal of the revisional application is that the petitioners as plaintiffs instituted Other Class Suit No. 8 of 1997 in the Court of the Assistant Judge, Madhupur for decree of permanent injunction against the defendant opposite parties restraining from disturbing their peaceful possession stating inter alia, that. the land of C.S. Plot no.4 1 1 under C.S. Khatian No. 155 corresponding to S.A. No. 276 of mouja Madhupur belonged to Roy Mohan Tepal who was succeeded by his son Kokaram Tapal. Kokaram Tepal sold entire plot No. 411 measuring 1.01 acres of land while exercising title and possession Manindra, Amarendra and Upendra Chandra Bhowmik by registered sale deed dated 25.2.1943.

3. Upendra Chandra Nath Bhowmik, Amarendra Nath and Mahendra Nath Bhowmik while exercising right title and possession sold the entire land or case plot No.41 1 and other land measuring 2.15 acres to the plaintiffs petitioners by 3 sale deeds dated 7.2.1965 handed over possession. The case land was correctly recorded in S.A. operation of 1962 in the names or the plaintiffs petitioners who have been in peaceful possession paying regular rent and taxes to the Government and other authorities. The plaintiffs have 4 residential houses in the case land with 25 dwelling huts.

4. The defendants have no title or any possession in the suit land but they threatened the plaintiffs for dispossession on 12-1-1997 hence they constrained to file the instant suit for permanent injunction against the defendants opposite parties.

5. The defendant nos. 1-2 and 4-6 contested the suit by filing written statements contending inter alia, that the plaintiffs suit was not maintainable and the plaintiffs have no title and interest in the suit land that the original owner Kokaram sold the entire 1.01 acres of land of suit plot no. 411 to Manindra, Upendra and Amerandra on 25.2.1943 and they appointed peari Mohan as constituted attorney and the said constituted attorney sold .12 decimals of land of case plot along with another 1.15 decimals to Mir Muksed Ali on 7.2.56 and said Moksed Ali being dead the defendant nos. 1-3 and 4 sold .01 decimals of land to defendant no. 6 and defendant nos. 4 and 5 sold .02 '/2 decimals to defendant no.6. In this way defendants have been possessing .12 decimals of case land the purchase of the plaintiffs are illegal and invalid and they cannot get decree in the suit and their suit is liable to be dismissed with costs.

6. The trial Court framed as many as five issues which are as follows:

১। অ্রত্রাকারে ও প্রকারে গঠিত বর্তমান মোকদ্দমা আইনত চলতে পারে কি?

২। নালিশী ভূমি সুনির্দিষ্ট ও সুচিহ্নিত কি?

৩। অত্র মোকদ্দমায় নালি্শের কারণ যথাযথভাবে উদ্ভব হয়েছে কি?

৪। নালিশী ভূমিতে বাদীর স্বত্ত্ব স্বার্থ ও ধখর বিদ্যমান আছে কি?

৫। বাদী তার প্রার্থীত প্রতিকার পেতে পারে কি?

7. At the trial four witnesses were examined in support of the plaint case and four DWS were examined in support of the defence case.

8. The trial Court on perusal of the oral and documentary evidences of PWS and DWS was pleased to pass a decree in favour of the plaintiffs restraining the defendants from disturbing the plaintiffs in exercising their title and possession by judgment and decree dated 23.09.1998.

9. Being aggrieved by the impugned judgment and decree of the trial Judge the defendants preferred Title Appeal before the District Judge and the same was heard and disposed of by the Subordinate Judge, Tangail and who by his Judgment and decree dated 11.11.1999 and 19.11.1999 respectively was pleased to allow the Appeal and set aside the judgment and decree of the trial Judge by his impugned Judgment and decree dated 11.11.1999 and 19.11.1999 respectively.

10. The impugned judgment and decree of the last court of fact was challenged by the plaintiffs before this Hon'ble Division by invoking the revisional jurisdiction of this Hon'ble court as laid down in section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present Rule.

11. Dr. Md. Abul Basher, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners submits that petitioners prima facie proved their title, possession and interest over the suit land by adducing oral and documentary evidence in accordance with law.

12. He also submits that all the P.WS proved the title and possession over the suit land.

13. He next submits that the exhibited documents of the plaintiffs in respect of their title and possession clearly proved their title and possession over the suit land on the basis of the S.A. Khatian and subsequent Khatians. The rent receipts and other Taxes in the name of the plaintiffs also proved the title and possession of the plaintiffs in the suit property.

14. The learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners further submits that the last court of fact though found the deed of the defendants opposite parties is earlier than  the plaintiffs but in no where of the alleged deed it was mentioned from which portion 12 decimals of land was sold to Mir Moksad Ali vide deed No.969.

15. The learned Advocate also Submits that the very finding of the last court of fact about cause of action is perverse.

16. He further submits that the findings of the trial Judge was not properly reversed by the final court of fact under order 41 Rule 31 of the Code of Civil procedure.

17. The learned Advocate in course of his submission draws my attention to the fact that the witnesses of the defendants are not impartial and independent as because DW.2 Md. Delwar Hossain is related to the defendant and is highly interested witness and also DW.3 Shahadat is an employee of the defendant and as such he is not an independent witness.

18. The learned Advocate for the petitioner lastly submits that the judgment of the trial Judge is ambiguous, perverse but the Judgment of the trial Judge is very much well reasoned judgment as such the judgment of the trial Judge does not suffer from any legal infirmity, perversity and material irregularity for which the very reversal of the last court of fact under its Appellate Jurisdiction was not proper and not in accordance with law and the same is liable to beset aside.

19. The learned Advocate for the petitioner relied his submission on the basis of the citation in the case of Besarat Mollah and others-Vs-Bangladesh and others reported in 20 BLD (HCD) 258 where a single Judge of this Hon'ble Division held that:-

"The provisions of Order XLI Rule 31 of the Code enjoins that either reversing or affirming the decision of the trial Court it is incumbent upon the appellate court as a final court of fact to consider, assess both oral and documentary evidence in order to come to his own independent finding particularly when it reverse the finding, of the trial court. But in the instant case the Court of appeal below having failed to comply with the said mandatory provision of law and as such the judgment and decree of the court of appeal below cannot be sustained in law."

He next relies his submission on the basis of the citation in the case of Shamsunnahar Vs. Md. Afzal Patwary and others, reported in 12 BLT(AD)204

"The learned Additional District Judge who reversed the judgment of the Trial Court had not controvert the facts and did not reverse the findings of fact arrived at by the trial court. The Additional District Judge did not discuss the oral or documentary evidence and therefore it was held that the appellate court arrived at an illegal and unsustainable finding that the property was a vested property.

<u>20. Heard the learned Advocate, perused the impugned Judgment and decree of the final court of fact, considered the statements as made in the application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the submissions as advanced by the learned Advocate as well as the citations as referred by the learned Advocate in course of his submission. On perusal of the impugned judgment and decree. I find at the trial the plaintiffs examined four witnesses P.W.1 Majum Ali is plaintiff No.1 who deposed in support of the plaint case and proved the plaint case. P.W.2, Madhushudan Rajbangshi is the Mohorar of Tangail District record room who at the direction of the court produced volume No. 10 in which at page 102 ad 103 deed No. 965 is written where the name of the Vendor is shown as Manindra Nath Bhowmik and the Vendees are Majam Ali Saker, Md. Sukur Ali Saker, Md. Yead Ali Saker, Md. Amjad Ali Saker and Md. Amjad Ali Saker and Schedule of the land has been clearly mentioned including the area the quantum of land and boundary has been well demarcated in the said deed. P. W. 3 is Baktar Ali Kha who is the adjacent land owner of the suit property who deposed.</u>

<u>‘‘ মোকদ্দমার বাদী বিবাদীদের চিনি। নালিশী জমি চিনি। নালিশী জমির পাশে আমার বাড়ী। নালীশি জমিতে বাদীদের বাড়ি। বিবাদীগণ দক্ষিনাংশের কোন ১২ শতাংশ ভূমি দখল করেন না।" who corroborated the plaint case and supported the statements of P.W.1. PW.4 is Arfar Ali who deposed " আমি নালিশী জমি চিনি। বাদী বিবাদীদের চিনি। নালিশী জমিতে মাজম আলীদের বাড়ি। নালিশী জমিতে বিবাদীদের কোন দখল নাই।” according by supported the plaint case.</u>

<u>21. The final Court of fact at the time of disposal of the appeal did not at all consider the aforesaid averments of the PWs who categorically was able to prove .the case of the plaintiffs, In order to reverse the findings of the trial Judge the last court of fact must reverse the finding specifically and must show that such findings of the trial Judge were perverse not in accordance with law, based on total non consideration of evidence which resulted in erroneous decision occasioning failure of justice but as a matter of fact the final Court of fact did not follow the principles as laid down in Section 115 of the Code of Civil. Procedure at the time of reversal of the findings of the trial Judge the aforesaid principle has been well settled in the case of Nurul Abser Chowdhury Vs. Jesmin Akhter reported in 51 DLR P-352. The same principle of law has also been followed in the case of Waliullah Vs. Hasina Begum and others reported in 23 BLD(HCD)( 2003) page-67.</u>

<u>22. On perusal of the judgment of the trial Judge I find that the trial Judge arrived its finding on due and proper consideration of the oral and documentary evidence on record and rightly arrived at its finding on due consideration of the exhibits which on appeal the last court of fact arrived its finding on very perfunctory manner and according to me the said finding of the appellate Court is based on serious miscarriage of justice, perversity and not a proper judgment of reversal. I also find the appellate court in passing the impugned judgment has totally misconceived, misdirected in arriving its finding. The final court of fact passed the impugned judgment and decree in violation of the mandatory provisions of law as contained in section 115 of the Code of .Civil Procedure and also in violation of the provisions of law as contained in Order 41 Rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure. I also find the impugned Judgment and decree of the final court of fact is not a proper judgment of reversal and the same has suffered' from serious miscarriage of justice. I also find the last court of fact failed to give its reasoning’s on due consideration of the materials on record and arrived at its own independent findings on the issues involved in the case while reversing the decision of the trial Judge in violation of the settled principles of law as laid down in the case of Md. Ibrahim Vs. Md. Alauddin and others reported in 27 DLR page 413 and also in the case of Rostom Ali Dhakua being dead his heirs Rustom ali Dhakua and others Vs. Abdur Rahman dead his heirs Razia Khatun and others reported in 14 BLD (AD)(1994) page- 229 where it is clearly held that "affirming the decision of the trial court must independently consider the evidence on record. But in the case of "affirming the findings of the trial court the narration of the entire evidence and reiteration of the reasons given by the trial court are not essential. In such a case expressions of general agreement with those of the trial court are generally considered sufficient. But in the case of a reversal of the judgment, the consideration of the evidence of necessity has to be through and more elaborate." On record here in the instant case the final court of fact at the time of reversal of the judgment of the trial court failed to assess and consider the evidence on record independently as such the impugned judgment and decree of the last court of fact is not a proper judgment in accordance with law. In view of the submissions citations and the attending circumstances of the case.
