full_judgment:
Mr. Soumendra Sarker, J.:- The Rule have been issued calling upon the Opposite Parties to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 20.09.1993 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Rajshahi in Title Appeal No.60 of 1991 affirming those dated 28.02.1991 passed by the Assistant Judge, Upazilla Puthia, District Rajshahi in Other Suit No.25 of 1990 should not be set-aside and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this court may seem fit and proper. 

2. The facts leading to the issuance of the Rule, in brief, are that the suit property along with other properties originally belonged to one Ram Krishna Sarker, Sree Krishna Sarker and Bijoy Krishna Sarker. By amicable family arrangement the suit property had been in exclusive share and possession of Ram Krishna Sarker. Ram Krishna Sarker setting up idol of the deity, Radha Ballav Deb Thakur in his dwelling house had been performing daily worship (Deb puja) and other rituals with utmost devotion. At the age of 71 years Ram Krishna Sarker dedicated the suit property as described in the schedule of plaint as debuttar property to the plaintiffs by a registered deed of endowment (Arpannama) dated 13' Karthik, 1349B.S. corresponding to 30' October, 1942 A.D (exhibit-5) and he himself as shebait had been performing Deb puja and other religious rites. As per terms of the deed of endowment, after the death of Ram Krishna Sacker his son Kanakadri Krishna Sacker became shebait and continued to perform Deb puja of the plaintiff's deity regularly. In 1945 Kanakadri Krishna Sarker left this country for India. Thereafter Niladri Krishna Sarker became shebait and has been performing Deb puja and other rituals of the plaintiff deity regularly. The further case of the plaintiff-appellant-petitioners is such, that the suit property was wrongly recorded in the names of Niladri Krishna Sarker and his brothers in S.A. Khatian. But Niladri Krishna Sarker has been performing functions as shebait and enjoyment and possession of the suit property by the plaintiff deity had never been affected or obstructed in spite of such wrong recording. In R.S. Khatian the suit property has been recorded in the name of plaintiff deity, but in remark column of the R.S. Khatian it has been noted as 'Vested Property'. On 05.09.1979 A.D. the local tahsilder threatened to lease out the suit property as vested property necessitating institution of the suit. 

3. Vis-a-vis; the case of the defendant-respondent-opposite parties in brief, is thus, that the original owners of the property described in the schedule of the plaint having left for India for good, the suit property was enlisted as vested and non-resident property and taking lease from the Government one Md. Elahi and Abdul Latif have been possessing the same. The further -case of the opposite parties is such, that there was no temple or bigraha in the suit property and had any bigraha been there, it was sent to India and the plaintiffs cannot be shebait. The suit lands had not been properly managed and as shebait the plaintiffs to grab the property filed the original suit on false allegations on the basis of some forged papers. The plaintiffs are not the heirs of ex-shebait and Niladri Krishna Sarker sold some portion of debuttar property as of his paternal property. The plaintiff-petitioners having no manner of right, title, interest and possession over the suit property are not entitled to get relief as prayed for. 

4. The learned trial court after examining witnesses from the sides of the respective parties dismissed the suit on contest and being aggrieved the plaintiff-appellant-petitioners preferred Title Appeal No.60 of 1991 in the Court of learned District Judge, Rajshahi which was heard and disposed of by the learned Subordinate Judge, Rajshahi and the learned appellate court vide the impugned judgment and decree dated 20.09.1993 and 26.09.1993 respectively dismissed the appeal affirming the judgment and decree of the learned Assistant Judge. 

5. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the impugned judgment and decree of the learned Appellate Court the Plaintiff-Appellant-Petitioners have preferred this revisional application under Section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the Rule. 

6. Mr. Prabir Neogi, the learned Advocate appeared on behalf of the plaintiff-appellant-petitioners while Mr. Gopal Chandra Saha and Mrs. Suchorita Sen Gupta, the learned Assistant Attorney Generals appeared on behalf of the defendant-respondent-opposite parties. 

7. The learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners submits that the impugned judgment and decree is neither proper nor in accordance with the provisions of law. The learned lower Appellate Court during disposal of the appeal committed error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice and both the courts below illegally decided the merit of the suit against the plaintiffs and in favour of the defendants on the basis of surmise and conjecture. The learned Advocate Mr. Prabir Neogi on behalf of the petitioners further submits that the trial court as well as the appellate court were totally failed to assess the evidence on record properly and appreciate the actual position of law and there has-been no sifting of evidence rightly by the learned trial court as well as lower appellate court. The learned Subordinate Judge, Rajshahi committed error of law in not considering that Trust Board as mentioned in exhibit-5 and all the members of Trust Board either died or left this country the last shebait Niladri Krishna Sarker being died during the pendency of the suit his son Samirandra Krishna Sarker having all the qualifications of becoming a shebait performed Deb puja of Sree Radha Ballav Deb Thakur and looked after and managed the affairs of debuttar properties and others since of late shebait Niladri Krishna Sarker also having performed Deb puja & all the 6(six) sons of late shebait were substituted in his place. The learned counsel for the plaintiff-petitioners also submits that Ram Krishna Sarker got the suit properties in his `Saban' by amicable settlement and as such he had legal rights to endowment the suit properties as debuttar for the purpose of `Deb sheba and Deb puja' as described in the deed of endowment (exhibit-5) and as such the findings of the lower appellate court that Ram Krishna Sarker had no legal right to donate the suit properties as debuttar is absolutely baseless. The learned Advocate lastly submits that the learned- lower appellate court erred in law in not considering that from the evidence on record Radha Ballav Deb Thakur is still in the `Mandie at the residence of Rant Krishna Sarker at `Baneswar' and as such even if anyone of all the shebaits have migrated for India the properties of the bigraha cannot be declared as an enemy or vested and non-resident properties. It is from the evidence of the plaintiff's witnesses that Samarendra Kumar Sarker with other brothers has been possessing the suit properties on behalf of Radha Bailey Deb Thakur and the defendants have hopelessly failed to prove the possession of the defendants by giving lease. The learned counsel for the plaintiff-appellant -petitioners has drawn much emphasis to the following submissions that Sub-Section (6) of Section 9 of Act No.16 of 2001 (as amended by অর্পিত সম্পত্তি প্রত্যর্পণ (সংশোধন) আইন, ২০১১, (Act No.23 of 2011) which provides that the properties which is not enlisted in the `Ka' or `Kha' schedule of Bangladesh Gazette cannot be treated Vested and non-resident properties and in the said properties the Government has no manner of title, interest, right and liabilities as contemplated by law. The suit properties excepting .08 acres of land in R.S. khatian No.44/2 in Plot No. 296 out of total 14.80 acres of land is not enlisted in the `Ka' or 'Kha' schedule of the respective localities and the Government (Ministry of Land) published the list of `Ka' schedule vested properties of the concern Puthia Upazilla under Rajshahi District by Notification dated 08° February, 2012 in the Bangladesh Gazette, Extraordinary Issue, dated 08° April, 2012. In the said list in Serial No.102 only .08 acres of land appertaining to A.S. Khatian No.44/2, R.S. Plot No. 296 has been included out of 14.80 acres of land which is the subject-matter of the instant suit. The Government published list of "kha" schedule vested properties of the concern Puthia Upazilla by Notification dated 08th March, 2012 in the Bangladesh Gazette, Extraordinary Issue, dated in May, 2012 wherein the suit Property is not at all included. Act No. 16 of 2001 provides that under Section 13 Sub-section 1(kha) the suit which is pending in respect of such properties which is not enlisted as vested property in the Official Gagette is automatically abated to the extent of that portion of land. 

8. As against the submissions of the learned counsel for the plaintiff-appellant-petitioners the learned Assistant Attorney General Mr. Copal Chandra Saha on behalf of the Govemment opposing the Rule submits that the suit of the plaintiffs is concocted and manipulated and papers produced are forged, created and not acted upon. The plaintiff's title paper i.e. the 'Arpannania' is a forged document which is not acted upon and by virtue of this 'Aipannama' no possession was delivered in favour of the plaintiffs as alleged and in fact, both the courts below concurrently found that the plaintiff-petitioners are not able to prove its case of possession of the suit property and there exist defect of parties in the suit which is apparent from the face of the records. The learned Assistant Attorney General Mr. Gopal Chandra Saha for the opposite parties further submits that there is no scrap of paper and a single witness from the side of the plaintiff-petitioners to substantiate that the plaintiffs have got possession in the disputed properties and it is evident from the papers on records that there are some left out parties whose presence are necessary for proper adjudication of the suit and both the trial court as well as the appellate court rightly decided that the suit is not maintainable under Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act for want of possession and defect of parties. The learned Assistant Attorney General in support of his submissions referred some decisions of our Apex Court reported in 43 DLR (AD) 87 upon maintainability of the suit, 47 DLR (AD) 95 upon Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 4 BLT (AD) 150 upon Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 56 DLR 427, 39 DLR (AD) 237, 43 DLR 551 upon identification of the suit property, 28 DLR (AD) 57 and 51 DLR (AD) 55. The learned Assistant Attorney General lastly submits that the alleged shebait as stated from the side of the plaintiffs since not functioned properly the property in dispute is under the control and possession of the Government and the Government by leasing out the property to its lessee managing the some rightly and the learned trial court & the appellate court during disposal of the suit and appeal after proper sifting of evidence and appreciation of law decided the merit of the suit and appeal respectively and the Rule having no substance is liable to be discharged. 

9. Heard the learned Advocates of both sides, perused the case records, deposition of the witnesses, exhibited documents and all other connected papers including the series of decisions referred from both the sides of the respective parties. 

10. On perusal of the case 'record it transpires that the learned trial court during disposal of the original title suit being no.25 of 1990 decided the merit of the suit against the plaintiffs on the plea  that there exist defect of parties in the suit and two necessary parties namely Kanakadri Krishna Sarker and Amadri Krishna Sarker, 2(two) sons of Ram Krishna Sarker who are residing in India has been left out from the pleadings and the plaintiffs did not implicate them as parties to the suit whose presence are necessary to adjudicate the matter in dispute. In the last portion of the decision the learned Assistant Judge, Puthia opined that as per evidence adduced from the side of the plaintiffs the plaintiff's title to the disputed properties appears to be proved but only because the suit is bad for defect parties the plaintiffs are not entitled to get declaration of title. The learned appellate court vide the impugned judgment and decree upheld the decision of the trial court and it was further observed by the learned lower appellate court that the plaintiffs had no locus standi to file the suit as their title document the 'Arpannama' was not properly acted upon and since the suit is bad for defect of parties there is nothing to interfere with the judgment and dismissal decree of the trial court. It was also observed by the lower appellate court that after payment of rent no rent receipts were obtained year to year and submitted to prove the bonafide of the appellant-petitioners and the property in dispute cannot be treated debuttar for want of proof. 

11. In the aforesaid context from the papers on record it appears that it is the specific case of the plaintiff-appellant-petitioners that the suit property by amicable family arrangement had been in the exclusive share and possession of Ram Krishna and Ram Krishna setting up idol of the deity Radha Ballav Deb Thakur in his dwelling but had been performing daily worship there. At the age of 71 years he dedicated the suit properties as debuttar property in favour of the plaintiff deity by a registered deed of endowment (Arpannama) on 13u Karthik, 1349 B.S. corresponding to 30th October, 1942 A.D. (Exhibit-5), After the demise of Ram Krishna his son Kanakadri Krishna Sarker became the shebait and continued to perform 'Deb puja' of the plaintiff deity regularly. In the year 1945 A.D. Kanakadri left this country for India and thereafter, Niladri Krishna ,Sarker became shebait and has been performing 'Deb puja' and other rituals of the plaintiff deity regularly. It is also the specific case of the plaintiff-petitioners that despite during the S.A. Operation the S.A. khatian was wrongly recorded in the names of Niladri Krishna Sarker and his brothers but in the R.S. khatian the suit property has been recorded in the name of plaintiff deity, but in the remark column it has been noted as 'vested property' and for that noting while the concerned Tahsilder tried to lease out the property in favour of third party plaintiff's title to the suit properties has been clouded. To dispel that cloud plaintiff instituted the original suit for declaration of title. The very documentary evidence as adduced from the side of the plaintiff-petitioners marked as exhibit-3 series supports the contention of the plaintiffs. In the concern R.S. khatian in it's remark column the property is mentioned as vested property but the names of the plaintiffs has been duly recorded. The prayer for relief by the plaintiffs as cited in the prayer portion of the plaint is for declaration that the schedule properties appertaining to:C.S. khatian no. 164 and R.S. khatian no. 187 including other khatians as described in the schedule of the plaint comprising an area of 14.80 acres is liable to be declared 16 (sixteen) annas title in favour of Sree Sree Radhaballabh Deb Thakur seen as plaintiff no. 1 in the plaint and the time of cause of action cited therein is 05.09.1975 A.D. while the concerned Tahsilder tried to lease out the property in favour of third party. To substantiate the case of the plaintiffs they have adduced 5(five) witnesses. The witness no, 1 is Samarendra Krishna Sacker son of late Niladri Sarker. This witness deposed in support of the plaint case and the witness no. 2 Md. Ekramul Hoque is a `Maharar of the concern District Registry Office who after getting summon of the court brought the concerned volume book to prove the title document of the plaintiffs which is identical with the suit properties marked as 'exhibit-5'. The witness no. 3 for the plaintiffs is Vhim Charan Paul who deposed corroborating the case of the plaintiffs. The witness no. 4 Debendra Nath also states supporting the plaintiff's case. The last witness Suvash Kumar being one son of Niladri Kumar specifically states in his deposition that the suit properties are being possessed and looked after by proper management and they are as sons of Niladri Kumar Sarker being full-brothers do possess the property in dispute and they are performing all the religious activities concern to deity within the knowledge of all. 

12. On the other hand the witness no. 1 is the sole witness on behalf of the defendant-opposite parties namely Md. Abdul Ezaj who is a Tahsilder of Baneswar Tahsil Office. This witness states in his deposition that in the S.A. record of rights the land has been recorded in the names of Niladri Sarker and others and in the corresponding R.S. record it has been recorded in the name of Radha Ballav Deb deity which is not correct. In his cross-examination it was admitted by the witness for the defendants that the C.S. recorded tenants possessed the suit property in 'Ejmali' and it is within his knowledge from his predecessors. He also admits that no paper has been produced from their side showing the property as enemy or vested property. This witness at a stage of his deposition specifically states to the effect that he does not know the suit properties personally and never went there and as such, he cannot say whether there is any deity in the suit property. 

13. I have come across from the connected papers that the learned trial court in his judgment and decree opined that the plaintiffs have successfully proved title in the disputed properties but for defect of parties they are not entitled to get the relief as prayed for. In this context the learned Advocate Mr. Probir Neogi on behalf of the plaintiff-petitioners referred some decisions of our Apex Court reported in 49 DLR (AD) 151 & 10 BLC (AD) 41 and regarding burden of proof under the purview of Evidence Act's Sections 102 and 103 the decision reported in 1987 BLD (AD) 103 and 54 DLR (AD) 26. Consulting the relevant decisions of our Apex Court it is obvious to note that it is a settle principle of law that the suit shall not fail for reason of mis-joinder and non-joinder of the parties. No suit can fail by reason merely of non-joinder of parties. Order I Rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure makes this legal position clear. Apart from this on careful scrutiny over the case records it is evident that Abdul Latif and Elahi are not the necessary parties of the suit. As lessee under the defendant No.1 their presence is not required for proper adjudication of the matter in dispute and it is within record that the defendant Government of Bangladesh is well within the plaint of the suit and they are contesting the case. The exhibited documents as it appears go to show that the rent receipts starts from Puthia Zomindari Estate upto the Government which has been duly marked as Exhibits 4-4(35) from the side of the plaintiffs. In view of the materials on record it is a glaring misconception of law as to onus probandi in a civil proceeding. Cumulatiye effect of Section 101, 102 and 103 of the Evidence Act is that unlike criminal cases, the fate of a civil suit is decided by the preponderance of evidence, in other words, comparative weight and worth of evidence led by the parties. In the instant case, the plaintiffs have established their case by producing unimpeachable documentary and credible oral evidence. All the documents forming the basis of the claim of the plaintiffs on the suit property were admitted into evidence and marked exhibits without objection. The testimony of P.W. 1 was corroborated by four other competent, credible and independent witnesses whose testimony remained unshaken in cross-examination. 

14. On the contrary the sole witness for the defendant-Government is the witness no. 1 Tahsilder, Baneswar Tahsil Office who had no personal knowledge about the suit properties. He could produce the official records, if any, relating to the suit property, but admittedly he could not produce any scrap of paper. As I have stated earlier that the burden of proof to discharge onus of proving the respective case lies entirely on the concern party and the decision as referred from the side of the petitioners carries much weight to arrive at a correct decision. In the case of Chinivash Pramanik Vs. Md. Nurul Hossain Molla reported in 1987 BLD (AD) 103 it has been held, when both the parties adduced evidence in order to set up their respective cases, the question of onus losses significance and the provisions laid down in Section 101 and 102 of the Evidence Act is required to be judged. Consulting the nature and character of each and every suit when both the parties lead evidence question of onus as well as the matter in dispute is to be decided on the evidence adduced from the sides of the respective parties. 

15. Consulting the important documentary evidence `Arpannama'(exhibit-5) it is apparent that it is a registered document of the year 1942 and it was produced before the court of law from the proper custody and admittedly it was marked exhibit after due process of law. The legal presumption of its genuineness under Section 60 of the Registration Act and under the purview of Section 90 of the Evidence Act (I of 1872) lies in favour of the plaintiffs and the very aspect has been totally ignored from the side of the learned courts below. Let as now look into the Vested Property Act which is prevailing at present in the country. 

অর্পিত সম্পত্তি প্রত্যর্পণ আইন, ২০০১ (Act No.16 of 2001) contemplates a non-obstacle clause giving overriding effect to this Act over any other law for the time being in force in following terms: 

“৩. আইনের প্রাধান্য-আমাততঃ বলবত অন্য কোন আইনে ভিন্নরূপ যাহা কিছুই থাকুক না কেন, এই আইনের বিধানাবলী কারযকর থাকিবে।”

Sub-section (6) of Section 9 of Act No. 16 of 2001 (as amended by অর্পিত সম্পত্তি প্রত্যর্পণ (সংশোধন) আইন, ২০১১, (Act No.23 of 2011) provides-

“(৬) এই ধারার অধীনে ‘ক’ ও ‘খ’ তফসিলে বর্ণিত এবং গেজেটে প্রকাশিত সম্পত্তির তালিকা অন্তর্ভূক্ত নহে এমন কোন সম্পত্তি অর্পিত সম্পত্তি বলিয়া গণ্য হইবে না এবং উহাতে অর্পিত সম্পত্তি হিসাবে সরকারের কোন স্বত্ত্ব, স্বার্থ, অধিকার বা দায়-দায়িত্ব থাকিবে না।”

16. The Government in the Ministry of Land published list of "ka" scheduled vested properties of Upazila- Puthia, District-Rajshahi by Notification dated 08 February , 2012 in the Bangladesh Gazette, Extraordinary Issue, dated April 8, 2012 . In the said list in serial No.102 only .08 acre of land appertaining to A.S. Khatian No.44/2, A.S. Plot No.296 has been included out of 14.80 acres of land which is the suit properties of the instant suit. 

17. The Government published separate list of "kha" schedule vested properties of Upazila- Puthia, District- Rajshahi by Notification dated 08 March, 2012 in the Bangladesh Gazette, Extraordinary issue, dated 17 May, 2012 The suit property or any part thereof has not been included therein. 

18. Therefore; save & except .08 acre of land of R.S. khatian No.44/2 and R.S. plot No.296, the suit property i.e. remaining 14.17 acres of land is not vested property according to the provisions of Sub-section (6) of Section 9 of অর্পিত সম্পত্তি প্রত্যর্পণ আইন, ২০০১ and the Government has no right, title, interest and obligation in respect of the said land and nothing to say anything about that portion of property. Thus, the sole basis of the defendant-Government's claim on the suit property falls through and the Government is estopped by law to raise any claim on the suit property except the said .08 acre of land, and that .08 acre of land also has to be returned to the real owner/claimant through the procedure as contemplated in Sections 10-15 of অর্পিত সম্পত্তি প্রত্যর্পণ আইন, ২০০১ 

19. I may not be out of place to advert here that the legal consequence of inclusion of .08 acre out of the suit land measuring 14.80 acres in the list has been incorporated in Section 13 of অর্পিত সম্পত্তি প্রত্যর্পণ আইন, ২০০১ which runs as follows: 

“১৩। প্রত্যর্পণযোগ্য সম্পত্তি সংক্রান্ত মামলার abatement, কারযধারা রুদ্ধ ও ট্রাইব্যুনালে দাবী উত্থাপন। 

(১) প্রত্যর্পণযোগ্য সম্পত্তির তালিকা সরকারী গেজেটে প্রকাশের তারিখে যদি কোন আদালতে এমন দেওয়ানী মামলা অনিস্পন্ন থাকে যাহাতে উক্ত তালিকায় অন্তর্ভূক্ত কোন সম্পত্তিতে স্বত্ত্ব দাবী করিয়া বা উহা অর্পিত সম্পত্তি মর্মে দাবী করিয়া কোন প্রতিকার প্রার্থনা করা হইয়াছে বা যদি তত্ত্বাবধায়কের নিকট এমন কোন কারযধারা অনিষ্পন্ন থাকে যাহাতে উক্ত সম্পত্তিকে অর্পিত সম্পত্তির তালিকা হইতে অবমুক্তির আবেদ;ন করা হইয়াছে তাহা হইলে-

(ক) প্রত্যর্পণযোগ্য সম্পত্তির তালিকা সরকারী সরকারী গেজেটে প্রকাশের তারিখে উক্ত মামলায় উক্ত সম্পত্তি যতটুকু জড়িত ততটুকু বাবদ মামলাটি আপনা আপনি abated হইয়াছে বলিয়া গণ্য হইবে। 

(খ) এইরূপ abatement এর জন্য সংশ্লিষ্ট আদালত কর্তৃক আনুষ্ঠানিক আদেশ প্রদানের বাধ্যবাধকতা থাকিবে না, এবং উক্ত তারিখের পর এইরুপ সম্পত্তির বিষয়ে উক্ত আদালত প্রদত্ত কোন আদেশ (আনুষ্ঠানিক abatement আদেশ ব্যতীত) এর কার্যকারিতা থাকিবে না.

(গ) উক্ত তালিকা সরকারী গেজেটে প্রকাশের তারিখে তত্ত্বাবধায়ক উক্ত কার্যধারা কার্যক্রম বন্ধ করিবেন এবং উক্ত তারিখের পর এইরূপ সম্পত্তি বিষয় তত্ত্বাধায়ক প্রদত্ত আদেশ (কার্যক্রম বন্ধ করণের আদেশ ব্যতীত) এর কার্যকারিতা থাকিবে না। 

(২) উপ-ধারা (১) এ উল্লেখিত সম্পত্তির মালিক উহা প্রত্যর্পনের জন্য বা উক্ত সম্পত্তির ক্ষেত্রে ধারা প্রযোজ্য হইলে সংশ্লিষ্ট স্বার্থবান ব্যক্তি উহা প্রত্যরপণযোগ্য সম্পত্তির তালিকা হইতে অবমুক্তির জন্য বা জনস্বার্থে অধিগ্রহনকৃত অর্তি সম্পত্তির বিপরীতে প্রদেয় ক্ষতিপূরণের জন্য ট্রাইব্যুনালের নিকট এবং প্রত্যর্পণযোগ্য জনহিতকর সম্পত্তি হইলে উক্ত ধারায় উল্লিখিত ব্যক্তি জেলা প্রশাসকের নিকট আবেদন করিতে পারিবেন। 

(৩) এইরূপ আবেদন উপস্থাপন ও নিস্পত্তির ও সংশ্লিষ্ট ডিক্রী বাস্তবায়নের ক্ষেত্রে ধারা ১০, ১১ এবং ক্ষেত্রমত ধারা ১৫ এর বিধানাবলী প্রযোজ্য হইবে।”

Hence, the instant suit is deemed to have been abated to the extent of that .08 acre of land appertaining to A.S. Khatian No.44/2, R.S. Plot No.296 as mentioned in Item No.6 of the Schedule of the plaint. And the suit which has been culminated in the proceedings of the instant Civil Revision will continue in accordance with law except to the extent of the said .08 acre of land. Furthermore, the Government has no legal right/locustandai to claim the present suit land measuring (14.80-0.08). 14.72 acres as per provisions of Section 9(6) of অর্পিত সম্পত্তি প্রত্যর্পণ আইন, ২০০১. 

20. I have already come across that the trial court found title and possession in the suit land of the plaintiff. It dismissed the suit on the sole ground of defect of parties.
Firstly, the defect of parties is not a correct finding inasmuch as once the property is found to be not a vested property, lessees, if any, are neither necessary nor proper parties.

Secondly, it is the finding of both the courts below and apparent on the face of the deposition of D.W. I that the defendant- Government could not produce a scrap of paper to show that the suit property or any part thereof has been leased out

Thirdly, Order 1, Rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides and it is settled by a long line of decisions handed down by the superior courts of the sub-continent including our Appellate Division that a suit cannot fail solely on the ground of defect of parties. 

21. The court of appeal below dismissed the appeal on the ground that though the Government could not produce any documentary evidence to show that the suit property is a vested property, but that does not absolve the plaintiffs of the burden of proving their case. 

22. Having regard to the facts, circumstances arid evidence referred to above I have every reason to inclined such a view that both the courts below were totally failed to assess the evidence on record properly and appreciate the actual position of law. There is no sifting of evidence in the true perspective of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. The appellate court during disposal of the appeal misread and misconstrued the evidence on records and misinterpreted the material evidence specially the exhibited documents which is an apparent error in law on the face of the papers. This submissions with regard to the respective case of the Plaintiff-Appellant-Petitioners from the side of the learned Advocate Mr. Probir Neogi carries much weight as well as consistent with the nature & facts of the suit and I have the reason to appreciate the decisions referred to but the case laws cited from the side of the learned Assistant Attorney General have got no nexus in the instant suit due to different facts & circumstances. 

23. Consulting the connected papers it is obvious that for the aforesaid illegalities as well as irregularities done by the learned courts below the impugned judgment & decree deserve interference of this court and accordingly, the Rule have got much substance to succeed. 

24. In the result; the Rule having merit is made absolute. 

25. The impugned judgment and decree dated 20.09.1993 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Rajshahi in Title Appeal No.60 of 1991 affirming those dated 28.02.1991 passed by the Assistant. Judge, Upazilla Puthia, District Rajshahi in Other Suit No.25 of 1990 is hereby set-aside. 

And the original Suit be decreed hi `part on contest save and except in respect of .08 acre of land appertaining to H.S. Khatian No.44/2 in H.S. Plot No.296 as mentioned in the schedule of the plaint in item no.6. 

26. However, there will be no order as to cost. 

27. Communicate the judgment and order at-once to the court concerned for information and necessary action. 

28. Send back the Lower Court's Record immediately.

End.

full_judgment:
Mr. A.H.M. Shamsuddin Choudhury J: As many as four Writ Petitions, registered as Writ Petitions no. 7236 of 2010, 826 of 2011, 1048 of 2011 and 1059 of 2011 respectively had been filed challenging the validity of the (0 Proclamation dated 20th August, 1975, whereby the whole of Bangladesh was placed under Martial Law, (ii) the Martial Law Regulation No. XVI of 1976, published in the Bangladesh Gazette Extraordinary dated 14th June, 1976 and (iii) the judgment and order dated 17th July, 1976 passed by the Special Martial Law Tribunal in Special Martial Law Case No. I of 1976, convicting all the petitioners in all the four petitions and the deceased husbands of Petitioner Nos. 2 and 3, in WP 7236/10 under section 121 A of the Penal Code. 

2. All the Petitioners were sentenced to suffer imprisonment for varying terms while Lt. Col. (retd.) M. A. Taber, Biruttam, husband of the Petitioner No. 2 in WP 7236/10, was sentenced to death, which was executed on 21st July, 1976. Flight Sergeant Abu Yusuf Khan, Bir Bikram, husband of the Petitioner No. 3, in WP 7236/10, was sentenced to suffer imprisonment for life. 

3. Since the basic theme and the relief craved in all these petitions are identical, they are taken up for adjudication as a lump. 

4. Professor M. Anwar Hossain, an eminent personality in our academic horizon, endowed with exquisite academic achievements gained from various educational institutes of universal acclamation, who attained wide spectrum notoriety, not merely by dint of his intellectual pursuit but also because of his active participation in our Glorious War of Liberation, filed the first cited petition before us along with two other Petitioners, one of whom is his sister in law, invoking Article 102 of the Constitution. 

5. Salient parts of the averments that emerge from the first aforementioned petition, i.e. the Writ Petition no. 7236 of 2010, run as follows; 

6. On 20th August 1975 the whole of Bangladesh was purportedly placed under so-called "Martial Law", following a purported proclamation to that effect on the same day. One Khandakar Mushtaque Ahmed purportedly took over "all and full powers of the government of the People Republic of Bangladesh." 

7. A succession of actions by the then so-called government followed the said proclamation, which included the arrest of the husband of the Petitioner no. 2 on 23rd November 1975 and the arrest of the Petitioner no.1 himself on 15th November 1976. They were apprehended following the lodgance of a so called first information report (FIR) with the Mohammadpur Police Station on 4th June 1976. Section 121 A of the Penal Code was cited in the said FIR along with some other provisions of the said Code. 

8. The FIR led to the purported, commencement of a case that was recorded as Special Martial Law Tribunal Case no. 1of 1976. Both the Petitioners were purportedly found guilty following a so-called trial and the spouse of the Petitioner no. 2, a Valiant Freedom Fighter, named Lt. Colonel (Rtd), M.A. Taper, who was decorated with the Gallantry Award, Bir Uttam, the highest award for a surviving Freedom Fighter, for his spectacular contribution in the Liberation War, was purportedly sentenced to death, while, Flight Sergeant Abu Yusuf Khan, who was also honored with another Gallantry Award, namely Bir Bikram, the spouse of the Petitioner No. 3, was purportedly sentenced to life imprisonment, while the Petitioner No. 1 was purportedly sentenced to a term of ten years imprisonment and to pay a fine or to suffer an additional term of 2 years in default of payment. The purported verdicts were delivered on 17th July 1976. 

9. The so-called special tribunal was set up under the purported martial law regulation no XVI of 1976, section 3(4) which equipped the so-called tribunal with power to try any offence, whether committed before or after the commencement of the regulation. Crimes under Chapter VI and VII of the Penal Code were also brought within the so-called tribunal's jurisdiction by section 3(4)(a) of the regulation. The so-called regulation empowered the tribunal to sit in camera at the so-called chair's discretion. 

10. The so-called regulation placed a total clog on appeal, stipulating, "No appeal shall lie to any authority from any decision or judgment of the tribunal". 

Section 4(10) thereto stipulated that when the tribunal would sit in camera, the chair would require persons attending or otherwise participating in the trial to subscribe to an oath of secrecy against disclosure of anything in connection with the trial. 

11. The so-called special tribunal was composed of one Army Colonel, named Yusuf Haider (who chaired it), one Air Force Wing Commander an Acting Commander of the Navy and two Magistrates. 

12. A handout dated 18th June 1976, issued by the chair of the so-called tribunal, required some II persons to surrender before the tribunal on or before 21st June 1976 in connection with the case in which Lt. Col. M.A. Taher, Bir Uttam, Flight Sergeant Abu Yusuf Khan, Bir Bikram and the Petitioner No.1 were purportedly impleaded as accused.

13. The so-called trial of the so-called Special Martial Law Tribunal Case no. 1 of 1976 proceeded in total secrecy inside Dhaka Central Jail. 

14. Although the Petitioner No.1, and the spouse of the Petitioners no. 2 and 3 were allowed to be represented and defended by Advocates, the Petitioners No. 2 and 3 were never allowed to attend. Because of the so-called oath of secrecy, participants in the trial could never divulge any information on the so-called trial to the Petitioners no. 2 and 3. 

15. The Petitioner no. 2 was never allowed, despite incessant requests, to meet her husband. Her written request to that effect was never responded to. It is only from the newspaper reporting that she came to know of the purported conviction and the sentence that was passed on her husband. 

16. On learning of the purported passage of death sentence on her husband, the Petitioner No. 2 preferred an application to the so-called president, to the so-called chief martial law administrator and to Major General Ziaur Rahman, the so-called deputy chief martial law administrator, seeking an abeyance on the confirmation of the sentence and to put the same on halt. 

17. She was, however, told in reply, that the president has not been able to accede to her prayer. 

18. The purported death sentence on Lt. Col. M. A. Taher, Bir Uttam, was executed on 21st July 1976, where after his corps was removed from Dhaka Central Jail in a pickup and then was flown by a helicopter to his village named Kula, under Purbadhala Police Station in Noakhali. 

18A. The Petitioner No. 1 and the spouse of the Petitioner no. 3 were released from the prison in June 1980, yet they were not supplied with any official document as to their release at any point of time, not even today. No document or certified copy on the trial, the charge, deposition, proceeding, judgment or any other matter quo the trial was ever given to the Petitioner No.1 although he tried heaven and earth to procure the same. 

19. Through a purported Act of Parliament, purportedly passed on 06th April 1979, the so-called 5th Amendment Act, all so-called proclamations, proclamation order, martial law regulations, martial law orders and other laws (henceforth collectively cited as martial law instruments) as well as all amendments modifications, substitutions made thereof, including amendments to the Constitution brought about by such proclamations and regulations and all actions and proceedings taken or purportedly taken under those proclamations during the period between 15th August 1975 and 9th April 1979, were ratified and confirmed. 

20. That purported amendment, had, however, been declared void and non-est by this Division in the case of Bangladesh Italian Marble Works Ltd-V-Government of Bangladesh, best known as the 5th Amendment Case, reported in the Special Issue of Bangladesh Law Times 2006. 

21. A leave petition filed with a view to challenge the said Judgment of this Division, was turned down by the Appellate Division, though certain minor modifications were infused into this Division's Judgment. 

22. It is the Petitioners' emphatic assertion that since the Supreme Court has declared the so-called 5th Amendment to the Constitution illegal and void ab-initio, and has, thereby, wiped out the purported ratification, confirmation and validation of the so-called martial law instruments, the impugned purported trial and all the proceeding leading to the impugned judgment and order dated 17th July 1976 in the so-called special martial law tribunal were but devoid of legal sanction and as such, of no effect in law as being repugnant to the. Constitution. They also assert that the whole notion of camera trial, oath of secrecy, embargo on appeal are palpably abhorrent not only to our Constitutional Scheme, but also to minimum tenet of Justice. 

23. By a supplementary affidavit the Petitioner No. 1 stated that one Mr. Lawrence Lifschultz, who was the South Asian correspondent of the Far Eastern Economic Review, is possessed of invaluable and, otherwise unobtainable and untraceable information on the whole episode by having been in Bangladesh to cover the so-called trial for his named Journal, although he was, subsequently expelled from Bangladesh by the government headed by General Ziaur Rahman. It has also been revealed through the said supplementary affidavit that Mr. Lifschultz had unveiled plenitude of precious and, hitherto, undisclosed, information on the trial, he gathered through his investigative journalistic pursuit, which was first published in 1977 in the Special Edition of an India based Journal, named "Economic and Political weekly" (Bombay) under the caption "Taher's Last Testament". It has further been stated that on 28th January 2011, two treatises authored by him on the so-called trial were published in Daily Prothom Alo and that they contained elaborate factual analyses of the said trial as well as the author's personal account on Col. Taher. 

24. The Petitioners went on to narrate that Col. Taher, Bir Uttam, inspired his entire family to actively participate in the Triumphant Liberation War. He himself fled Pakistan to join the War being propelled by his own conscience to fulfill his long cherished dream, rather than being forced to do so by subordinates. As a Sector Commander he led many historic battles to capture a strong Pakistani outpost, named Kamalpur, which was known as the "Gateway to Dhaka," and it was his strategy which was followed by the Freedom Fighters of Sector II along with the allied forces of India to mark their maiden entry into Dhaka on 16th December 1971. Although Col. Taher himself could not be present to witness the historic event due to the injury he sustained during the war, Flight Sergeant Abu Yusuf Khan, Bir Bikram, the spouse of the petitioner No. 3, represented Col. Taher on the occasion. Indeed, it was Ft. Sergeant Khan, who, along with the Indian Army went to the Eastern Command Head Quarters of the occupying Pakistani Army at Dhaka Cantonment on 16th December in the morning to negotiate the terms of surrender with the Pakistan Army and, as a member of the Victorious Liberation Army, it was him who plucked the flag from the staff car of Lt. General Niazi, the defeated chief of the Eastern Command of the Pakistani Army. 

All of the eight siblings, six male and two female, of Col. Taher directly participated in the War of Liberation, of whom four received Gallantry Awards. 

25. The career of the Petitioner No. I as a Lecturer at the Department of Biochemistry in Dhaka University, came to an abrupt impasse with the arrest of his two brothers, Col. Taher and Ft. Sergeant Yusuf Khan, which event plunged his family into turmoil. The whole family found themselves at a paradoxical jeopardy, they fell prey to the vengeance of General Ziaur Rahman. The Petitioner No. I had to go to the ground. On arrest, he was interned in a clandestine torture cell known as "Safe Hole", located inside Dhaka Cantonment, and was kept there until 15th June 1976, the day on which he was handed over to the Dhaka Central Jail authority. The period in the said torture cell was kept concealed. 

26. The so-called accused persons, 33 in number, included revered Sector Commanders and front line organizers of the Liberation War. It was a conglomerate of Politicians, Military Personnel, Writers, Journalists, Teachers, Economists and People engaged in intellectual cultivation, who volunteered to stake their lives to secure the emancipation of their mother land after the Pakistan Army unleashed genocide on the Bengali People.

27. The person who chaired the so-called special tribunal, Col. Yusuf Haider, was one of those who collaborated with Pakistani Army of occupation. Mr. ATM Afzal, subsequently prized with elevation to the High Court Bench, acted as the special public prosecutor. Although the martial law regulation, by which the purported tribunal was formed, was itself promulgated on 14'" June 1976, it is that very day on which the tribunal personnel visited Dhaka Central Jail and, indeed it was on 12th June that the office of the Deputy Inspector General of Prison was vacated to accommodate the tribunal. 

In his book, titled, "Democracy and the Challenge of Development: A study of Political and Military Interventions in Bangladesh", Barrister Moudud Ahmed, a close associate of General Ziaur Rahman, wrote; "Why did Zia allow Taher to be hanged, the person who freed him from captivity" In the difficult situation after independence, Zia had to strike a balance with repatriated officers to strengthen his own position in the army. The officers who had not taken part in the liberation war, had found a new ally in Zia after the killing of Mujib and removal of
Mushtaque. They needed each other to survive both as a class and a force in the Civil-Military structure of the country. When it came to sentencing of Taher, the repatriated officers wanted him hanged. উপযুক্ত বিষয় ও সূত্রোক্ত পত্রের আলোকে জানানো যাচ্ছে যে লেঃ কর্ণেল এম এ তাহের বীর উত্তম-কে মৃত্যুদন্ড প্রদানকারী সামরিক ট্রাইব্যুনালের রায়ের আদেশ/ডকুমেন্টস অনুসন্ধানপূর্বক এতদসংস্পন্ত ফলাফল সেনাদের জেএজি বিভাগ-কে এ সংকান্ত তথ্যাদি প্রেরণের জন্য অনুরোধ করা হয়। সেনাসদর জানিয়েছেন লেঃ কর্ণেল এম এ তাহের বীর উত্তম কে দি স্পেশাল মার্শাল ল ট্রাইব্যুনাল রেগুলেশন ১৯৭৬ বলে গঠিত স্পেশাল মার্শাল ল ট্রাইব্যুনাল বিচারের মাধ্যমে মৃত্যুদ্ড প্রদান করা হয়েছিল।তিনি বিচারের অনেক পূ্র্বেই ৬ অক্টোবর ১৯৭২ তারিখের এল পি আর এ গমণ করেন েএবং ৬ জুলাই ১৯৭৩ তারিখে সেনাবাহিনী খেকে অবসর গ্রহন করেন। যে কারণে লেঃ কর্ণেল এম এ তাহের বীর উত্তম এর বিচার স্পেশাল মার্শাল ল ট্রাইব্যুনালের সেহেতু উক্ত বিচার সম্পর্কিত কোন নথিপত্র অথবা রায়ের আদেশে সেনাদের মওজুদ নেই।

In the backdrop of the dismaying messages on the traceability of trial records as depicted above, we reckoned that people who were, at the time under scrutiny, placed as the relevant government functionaries, should be directed to disclose, through affidavits, whatever information they are possessed of. 

51. Before that, however, we asked ourselves about the permissibility of taking evidence in a judicial review matter and, on perusal of some authorities and instruments came up with the following finding; "A proceeding of the kind we are adjudicating upon is a civil proceeding and hence, although provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure should generally apply, a proceeding, whereby judicial review of administration or legislative action; is craved, is a proceeding of extra-ordinary nature. Unlike other civil proceedings the fate of the petition in a judicial review case is determined by reference to in dispullable, facts as are narrated in the affidavit, where evidence on facts, as a matter of general norm, cannot be taken. The proceeding is of summary nature and factual questiont4f0'ldf, remain beyond controversy. ThiPlAti0til1P however, does not reflect a rule of- thrtinbe6 and there are cases, very sparing though where the Courts can, if the integer of justice so warrant, take evidence, and Ail ask a deponent to proceed with verbal elaboration and that is consistent with the High Court Rules which provide; "all questions arising for determination of such petition shall be decided upon affidavits. But the Court may direct that such questions, as it may consider necessary, be decided on such other evidence and in such manner as it may deem fit and in that case it may follow such procedure and make such Orders as may appear to it to be Just" (Rule 11). Hence it is envisaged by the Rules that the Court may, in the interest of Justice, take oral evidence at its discretion.  

52. The Indian Supreme Court in ITO-V-MIS Seth Brother (AIR 1970 SC 292) ordained that it is within the competence on the High Court to take or call for appropriate evidence at any stage of the proceeding when such a course appeal's 'to the Court to be essential for a just decision of the case and the exercise of such power is certainly called for where the Court feels that such a move is necessary for the protection of the" Court against any farud and deception attempted to be practiced upon it. 

53. In Smt. Guwant Kaur and others-V-Municipal Committee, Bhathnda and others (1969(3) SCC 769), the Indian Supreme Court expressed; "The High Court is not deprived of its jurisdiction to entertain a petition under Article 226 merely because in considering the petitioners' right to relief questions of fact may fall to be determined In a petition under Article 226, the High Court has jurisdiction to try issues both of facts and law. Exercise of the jurisdiction is it is true, discretionary, but the discretion must be exercised on sound Judicial principles. When the petition raises questions of fact of complex nature, which may, for their determination require oral evidence to be taken, and on that account the High Court is of the view that the dispute may not appropriately be tried in a writ petition, the High Court may decline to try a petition. Rejection of a petition in limine will normally be justified, where the Hgih Court is of the view that the petition is frivolous as because of the nature of the claim made, dispute sought to be agitated or that the petition against the party against whom relief is claimed, is not maintainable or that the dispute raised thereby is such that it would be inappropriate to, try it in the Writ Jurisdiction, or for analogous reasons." 

54. In Century Spg. And Mfg. Co Ltd-V-Ulhas-nagar Municipal Council (1970 I SCC 582), the Supreme Court of India observed "merely because a question of fact is raised, the High Court will not be justified in requiring the party to seek relief by the somewhat lengthy, dilatory and expensive process by a civil suit against a public body. The questions of facts raised by the petition ,-are elementary" 

55. In ABL International Ltd and Another—V-Export Credit Guarantee Corporation of India Ltd and Others (2004 3 SCC 553), the Indian Apex Court came up with a clear finding that in an appropriate case the Writ Court has the Jurisdiction to entertain a writ petition involving disputed questions of fact and there is no absolute bar for entertaining a writ petition even if the same involves some disputed questions of fact. 

56. In mofsin Sharif-V- Bangladesh 27 DLR 186, it was held that the Court may allow one party to cross examine the other with a view to ascertain the veracity of the deponents sworn statement In APSRT Corp.-v-Satya Narayan (AIR 1965 SC 1303), the top Court of India expressed the view that to ascertain the truth from conflicting stories figured in two countervailing affidavits, cross examination of the deponents may be desirable. 

57. The factual matrix that the petitions before its invite are to be decided on the anvil of the above cited authorities, because it can be said with all certitude that this is one of the most apposite cases where we ought to exercise our discretion to take evidence given that no document pertaining to crucial fact on the trial under review could be located, and the petitions can, by no means, be termed, vexatious. 

58. Mostafa Kamal J stated "Writ Petitions are generally disposed of on affidavits and on facts admitted or accepted by opposing contenders" (Page 143, Bangladesh Constitution: Trends and Issue). What we deduce from the above quoted observation is that facts narrated through affidavit and facts admitted or accepted by adversaries can be taken account of in judicial review proceedings. In the petitions before us statements made by the deponents are (a) in the form of affidavits and (b) they have either been admitted or at least been accepted as true by all the parties. In other words no dispute had been raised as to their authenticity and as such, no question of determination of the veracity of those statement through examination and cross examination, cropped up. 

59. As Mr. Rokanuddin Mahmud rightly opined oral statement made by some deponents at our instance, were in elaboration of their affidavit statement, not by opening any new window of evidence.

67. Averments Mr. Lifschultz figured in his affidavits are recorded below, verbatim; 
1. My name is Lawrence Lifschultz. I am an American citizen and a writer by profession. I am resident of Stony Creek, Connecticut in the United States. 
2. On January 21,2011 I was contacted by email by M. K. Rahman, the Additional Attorney General of Bangladesh and informed that the Supreme Court had made a request that I appear before it by January 26, 2011 in order to share with the Court "necessary information as to the so-called trial and conviction of Colonel Abu Taher by a Special Military Tribunal in 1976." 
3. This is a request I had hoped to receive for more than 30 years. I would consider it one of the great honors of my life to stand in Justice Shamsuddin's and Justice Hossain's court room in Dhaka. In my view a tragic crime was committed in Dhaka during June and July 1976. I was one of the few witnesses to what happened in this case. On June 28, 1976 I stood in front of Dhaka Central Jail. It was the day the "so-called trial" of Abu Taher and his Colleagues began in 
secret hidden, behind the walls of a prison. When I arrived that morning. the security around the prison appeared as if the Army was preparing for a war. Machine gun nests were set up all along the prison walls with their guns pointing outwards. What were these guns defending? Secrecy? Who were they prepared to shoot? Why Was a trail taking place in a prison instead of in Court? 
4. As one of the only independent witnesses at the prison that day, I believe it is my responsibility to describe what I saw and why I believe these events transpired as they did. In a letter to Justices Shamsuddin and Hossain I explained it was impossible for me to travel to Dhaka at this moment. My son was recently in a serious accident. He was badly injured. He is in the process of recovery and has passed a critical point in a three month process of recuperation. My presence is required for at least another month. Furthermore, another matter has also made it impossible for me to travel to Dhaka until the end of February. Thus, not wishing to delay the proceedings of the Supreme Court in this matter, 1 am submitting an affidavit. 
5. In 1976 I was South Asia Correspondent of the For Eastern Economic Review (Hong Kong). I had been based in New Delhi. Two years earlier I lived in Dhaka, where I was the Bangladesh Correspondent of the Review. Thus, I knew many of turmoil and conflict then roiling Bangladesh society. 
6. In June of 1976 I arrived in Dhaka from Katmandhu. Abu Taher had been arrested following the November 7th Uprising. As South Asia Correspondent of the Review, I reported on the tragic events of august 1975 when Sheik Mujib was murdered. I also returned to Dhaka following the insurrection and Sepoy Mutiny of November 7th. This is not the place to review these events. I have written elsewhere in detail about these matters. 
7. In my view the critical issue which faces the Supreme Court is whether Abu Taher's constitutional and human rights were fundamentally violated, by a military regime that had no democratic or constitutional legitimacy. On what legal basis was "Special Military Tribunal No. I" constituted? Were those facing trial before this Tribunal given adequate time to prepare their defense? Or, in fact were they denied access to legal representation until only a few days before the proceedings began? What standing did this Tribunal have constitutionally or morally to pass a death sentence? Would it be accurate to describe the Tribunal headed by Colonel Yusuf Haider as simply a kangaroo court which implemented a sentence pre-determined? These are the questions that need to be addressed and answered. Furthermore, those need to be answered within the framework of rights defined and ostensibly guaranteed to all the citizens of Bangladesh by the country's Constitution. 
8. I with to place before the Court an important point of evidence that I believe may assist in answering these questions. When I arrived in Dhaka in early June 1976, I contacted General Mhd. Manzur. I indicated that I was in Bangladesh. At the time Manzur was Chief of General Staff. I had previously met General Manzur in New Delhi in the summer of 1974 when he was Bangladesh's military attache in India. At that time I was curious to speak with him about his experiences in the Liberation War and his escape as a junior officer from Pakistan following the Pakistan army's violent crackdown in Dhaka on March 25, 1971. 
9. Manzur, together with Abu Taher and Mohammed Ziauddin, bravely crossed the border into India administered Kashmir in order to join the Liberation War. Within weeks all three would become sector commanders. Taher, who I had already met in Dhaka, suggested that summer of 1974 I meet Manzur in New Delhi on my way back to the United States. 1 was in the process of moving to New Delhi to become the Review's South Asia Correspondent. The day I met Manzur, the two of us spent most of a long afternoon talking about history. 
10. Thus, two years later in June 1976, when I called and told him I was in Dhaka he was pleased to hear I was in town. However, I was soon to discover he had a great deal on his mind. He told me that he would send someone to meet me in order to make arrangements for as to get together. He insisted that we meet late at night at his headquarters in the Cantonment. I arrived about nine in the evening. I stayed for nearly three hours. 
11.During the evening, General Manzur focused most of all on speaking to me about Taher who by then had been in prison for more than six months. He told me Taher had been kept mostly in solitary confinement. He asked me about my travel plans. I told him I was expected in the United States by the end of June. He urged me not to leave. He feared that Zia would go through with plans to put Taller on trial. Manzur and other officers who participated in the Liberation War were trying to dissuade Zia but in early June Manzur was uncertain he could stop the trial proceeding. He spoke of repatriated forces that had not participated or supported the independence movement as having a growing influence in the Army. He again emphasized to me that I should stay in Dhaka. He said if there was a trial someone should report on it in the international press. I could see he was worried. I changed my travel plans and stayed. 
12.1 did not see General Manzur again that June. Tension was mounting in Dhaka. I attempted to interview General Zia. His staff asked me to write out a list of questions. They covered many issues such as the Farraka Barrage which at the time was emerging as a crisis between India and Bangladesh. But, the list also included several questions concerning the November 7th Uprising and Abu Taker's arrest. I asked Zia, among other matters, to confirm that Taker and forces under his command had saved Zia's life that evening. If that were the case, why had he arrested Taber and freed those who had, in fact, detained him. I was not granted an interview by Zia. This was not surprising. The General had other plans and they did not include being asked troubling questions. 
13.1 was arrested and deported in the midst of Taher's trial. On the 30th Anniversary of Taker's execution I spoke at a memorial gathering at Dhaka University in which I described how an effort was made to impose complete and total censorship of the trial. (See "The Trial of Colonel Abu Tatter" by Lawrence Lifschultz, The Daily Star, July 24, 1976. See also "The Taber I Knew" by Lawrence Lifschultz, The Daily Star, July 23, 1976. Both articles are attached as exhibits to this affidavit.) 
14. The reason I have brought up my meeting in early June 1976 with General Manzur is because of what happened later. The night I met Manzurat the Cantonment he clearly feared that Zia would go ahead with Taker's trial but he did not say that he feared this would end with Taper's execution. I don't think at that stage such a thing was quite imaginable. However, several months after the trial Manzur sent me a message through an intermediary. I was then living in Cambridge, England. Manzur's emissary told me that Manzur wanted me to know that he had tried to stop the trial but clearly had been powerless to do so even though he ranked third in the Army's High Command. His opposition to Taper's trial had made him a marked man inside the Army among those who wanted Taller dead. Although many of us had suspected it, Manzur's representative told me that General Manzur also wanted me to know one thing above all else: Manzur knew with absolute certainty that Zia had personally taken the decision before the "so-called trial" even began that Taher would be hanged. SubSeguently, this fact was also confirmed to me by two high ranking military officers who were close to Zia at that time. 
15. What are the implications of such a fact within the framework of the judicial review taking place today by the Supreme Court? Can what happened in Dhaka Central Jail in July 1976 even be termed a trial? If the death sentence was determined prior to the Tribunal convening, then was the Tribunal in reality simply a mechanism used by extra-judicial forces to stage an execution. If this is the case, then Special Tribunal No. I which sat only once, and was never convened again, should be named for what it truly was. In reality it was an illegal entity established to commit murder and to imprison men and women who were denied their constitutional rights. Hopefully, the Bangladesh Supreme Court will today, in an atmosphere largely free of the fear, threat and coercion that so pervaded the past, find its way to overturning a verdict of a Tribunal which in every respect was a negation of the principles underlying Bangladesh's Constitution and the rights guaranteed to its citizens by law. 
16. I believe independent of the fact that the verdict was pre-determined before the Tribunal convened there are ample grounds to overturn Taher's so-called conviction and to vacate the verdict. Taher's execution ought to be called not only a miscarriage of justice but "a crime committed by the state". Such a crime ought to be remedied by an institution of the State that has power and capability to look back historically on crimes of the past. This has been done by several societies in modern times including Germany, Argentina, Chile and South Africa, to name only a few. One institution that has that capability is Bangladesh's Supreme Cows. 
17. Those on trial were denied access to adequate legal representation. Their fundamental rights under the Bangladesh constitution were violated. The trial was in secret before an illegal entity which had no foundation in law. The trial was held in a prison, not a Court of Law. The press was shackled so public anger at the injustice being carried out in camera would be contained. Journalists were threatened and deported. Imagine the public response. If Taher's closing speech before the Tribunal had been published the day after he spoke? 
18. Here, being tried in secret, was a Sector Commander of the Liberation War who lost his leg in a battle for his country's independence and who was awarded the highest military distinction, Bir Uttam, for courage, shown by those who fought and survived the 1971 war. By what fiction could any Court maintain that Taher's trial was lawful? 
19.Five years ago, when I spoke at the Teacher- Student Center at Dhaka University, I made the following observation: "Thirty years have now passed. We are all aware of what

happened. Today marks the 30th anniversary of Taher's execution. It is time in many view for a public act by the state and judicial authorities to publicly declare that Abu Taher was wrongfully tried and wrongfully executed. The verdict of July 17, 1976 should be vacated and a public acknowledgment should be made that Taher's civil and legal rights were grossly violated by the government which put him on trial Appropriate mechanisms to accomplish this task need to be found. Justice requires that the verdict be formally overturned and that there be an official acknowledgement that the entire so-called 'trial of Abu Taher' was a violation of proper legal procedure and represented a violation of the fundamental rights of the accused to due process My own view is that some future government [or Court] will act in a moral and ethical way on this issue. We must not rest until the verdict in the Taher case has been overturned. It is, my friends, a matter of justice." ("The Trial of Abu Taher", Keynote Address by Lawrence Lifschultz, Dhaka University, The Daily Star, July 24, 1976. See also "Colonel Taher, Lifschultz & Our Collective Guilt" by Syed Badrul Ahsan, The Daily Star, July 26, 1976.) 

20. Justice Shamsuddin and Justice Hossain, you have before you a great moral and legal challenge. Whatever you decide in this case will have historic significance. The Taber case in my view has important international implications. The petitioners in this case have been on a long journey. It is a journey that for so many men and women is painfully elusive. To find justice at the end of such a long road for an event that had shaken one's life happens so rarely in human experience. I know each of the petitioners in this case. They deserve our profound respect and respect of the world. There is only one way to provide that respect to them. It is to provide them a sense that finally at the end of a journey of more than three decades, justice has been done. This is your task.
