full_judgment:
Mr. Sheikh Abdul Awal, J.:- These First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 63 of 1995 and First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 64 of 1995 are directed against the judgment and order dated 9.02.1995 passed by the then Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Chittagong in Miscellaneous Case No. 49 of 1993 analogously heard with Miscellaneous Case No. 50 of 1993 under Order 9, Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure rejecting the prayer for setting aside the ex-parte preliminary decree dated 27.8.1991 and final decree dated 5.8.1992 passed in Partition Suit No.79 of 1990.

2. These two appeals are being disposed of by this single judgment inasmuch as both these appeals arose out of same judgment and order dated 9.02.1995 passed by the then Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Chittagong.

3. Material facts of the case, briefly, are that the respondent nos. 1-10 as plaintiffs instituted a suit being Partition Suit No.79 of 1990 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Chittagong against the defendant appellant and others. Ultimately, the said Partition Suit was decreed ex parte in preliminary form on 27.8.91 and final decree was drawn up on 5.8.92 ex parte. Against which the defendant appellant Sirajul Haque ( now deceased), the predecessor of the appellants filed Miscellaneous Case No.49 of 1993 and Miscellaneous Case No.50 of 1993 respectively under Order 9, Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the Court of then Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Chittagong on the ground, inter alia, that no summons/ notices of the suit were served upon the defendants and the ex parte decree was obtained by the plaintiffs on practicing fraud upon the Court in collusion with the process server. It has been also alleged that after preliminary decree an Advocate Commissioner was appointed although the Advocate Commissioner without serving any notice upon the defendants and without visiting the suit land submitted a report as desired by the plaintiff respondents and on the basis of the said report final decree was drawn up on 5.8.1992 and thereafter, the decree holder plaintiffs put the decree into execution by filing other Execution Case No.11 of 1992 beyond the knowledge of the defendant appellant, who heard about the said ex parte decree for the fast time from one Sheikh Nurul Alam and then on search definitely came to know about the ex parte decree on 13.5.1993 and hence, the case.

4. Plaintiff- respondents contested the miscellaneous cases by filing a written objection denying the allegations of the defendant-appellant and contending, inter alia, that the summons were duly served upon the defendants and that there was no suppression of the summons and the suit was decreed in due course of law.

5. At the trial both the parties led evidence to prove their respective cases.

6. The Trial Court after closing of the evidence and hearing argument of the parties by the impugned judgment and order dated 9.02.1995 disallowed both the miscellaneous cases on the findings that summons were duly served on the parties and the cases were barred by limitation.

7. Being aggrieved thereby the present appellants preferred these two First Miscellaneous Appeals before this Court.

8. Mr. Habibul Islam Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellants in both the appeals submits that the learned Subordinate Judge erred in law in rejecting the miscellaneous cases under Order 9, Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure without properly considering the scope of a proceeding under Order 9, Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the case made out by the defendant-appellant and the same has occasioned failure of justice.

9. Drawing my attention to the case record, Mr. Bhuiyan submits that due service of summons upon the defendants is a condition precedent for passing an ex parte order/ decree and the Court before passing an ex parte order/ decree is required to satisfy itself that summons were duly served upon the parties and there were good reasons for passing the ex parte order or decree, although in this case the learned Subordinate Judge did not record any satisfaction as to service of summons upon the defendants. The learned Advocate further submits that under Order 9, Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the ex parte decree the whole onus is upon the plaintiff to prove that summons/ notices of the suit were duly served upon the defendants, though in this case the plaintiffs to discharge their onus neither examined the process server nor examined any attesting witness and as such it cannot be said that the plaintiffs have discharged their onus to prove that the summons were duly served upon the defendants. Finally, Mr. Bhuiyan submits that in this case there is nothing on record to show that the summons were duly served upon the defendants or the defendants deliberately did not turn to contest the suit and as such the impugned judgment is liable to be set-aside. Mr. Habibul Islam Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate in support of his submission has relied on the decisions reported in 54 DLR(AD) 108, AIR 2001(SC) 1253, 35 DLR (AD) 162, 1 BLC (AD) 179, 40 DLR 313 and 3 BLC 412.

10. Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-respondents, on the other hand, supports the impugned judgment and contends that the teamed Subordinate Judge was perfectly justified in refusing the defendant-appellant's prayer for setting aside the ex parte decree on the clear finding that summons were duly served upon the defendants in the suit.

11. Relying on the decision reported in 40 DLR (AD) 193, Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan argues that examination of process server is mandatory when he has simply submitted his report about the service of summons without any verification or declaration that he had served the summons but when he made a declaration to this effect then his examination as a witness is not mandatory and it is apparent from the record that in this case the process server made a declaration that he went to the residence of defendant No.1 and the inmates of the house of defendant No.1 refused to accept the summons and then he served the summons/ notices by hanging in presence of local witnesses and as such the defendant-appellants are not entitled to get any benefit for non-examination of process server.

12. Mr. Wadud Bhuiyan further argues that the miscellaneous cases under Order 9, Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure were hopelessly barred by limitation inasmuch as those cases filed for setting aside the ex parte decree long 8(eight) months after passing the Final decree and in that view of the matter the learned Subordinate Judge rightly held that the cases were barred by limitation as per Article 164 of the Limitation Act. Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan to fortify his argument has relied on the decisions reported in 7 BLT (AD) 19, 17 BLT (AD) 206 and 16 DLR (SC) 438.

13. I have considered the submission of the learned Advocates for both the sides and perused the record. The main point for consideration is, as already noticed, whether the trial Court below has committed any illegality in disallowing the miscellaneous cases under Order 9, Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure on the ground that summons were duly served upon the parties and the cases were barred by limitation as well.

14. It is found that PW- 1 , Md. Rafiul Alam son of defendant appellant, Md. Sirajul Haque stated in his deposition that his father is aged about 75/76 years who filed both the miscellaneous cases. This witness also stated that his father due to sickness executed a power of attorney in favour of him to take necessary steps in both the cases. This witness also stated that:

“১-১০ নং প্রতিপক্ষগন বাদী হইয়া আত্রাদালতের অপর ৭৯/৯০ বিভাগের (Partition) মোকদ্দমা দায়ের করে। কিন্তু উযধশক্ত মামলার কোন সমন নোটিশ প্রার্থীকের উপর নিজারত যোগে বা ডাক যোগে জারী করা হয় নাই। এমনকি এই প্রার্থি দরখাস্তকারী হইয়া স্থানীয় নোয়াপাড়া ইউনিয়ন পরিষদে বাদী প্রতিপক্ষের বিরুদ্ধে ৪০/৯০ নম্বর মামলা আনয়ন করে এবং সেই মামলায় বাদী প্রতিপক্ষ হাজির হইয়াছিল কিন্তু সেখানে অত্রাদালতের মুল ৭৯/৯০ মামলার সম্পর্কে কোন কিছু প্রকাশ করে নাই।

O.P.W. 2, Md. Shamsul Islam Chowdhury stated in his deposition that he was appointed as Advocate Commissioner in Partition Suit No. 40 of 90 and after completion of commission work he submitted a report. This witness in his cross-examination admitted that: “মুল বিবাদীদের আমি চিনি না। বিবাদীদের প্রতি কমিশন সম্পর্কে আমি কোন নোটিশ দেইনি।”

<u>15. On a perusal of the whole order-sheet it appears that summons were allegedly served, upon the defendant no.1 by hanging. The record also shows that the learned Subordinate Judge did not record any satisfaction as to service of summons upon the defendants before fixing the suit for ex-parte hearing. Further, reading the evidence as a whole I find no reason to hold that the defendant no. 1 was noticed about the suit or summons were duly served upon him.</u>

16. Now, let me see the cited decisions for having a better view of the dispute in question.

<u>17. In the case of Abdur Rashid and another Vs. Abdul Barik and another reported in 35 DLR(AD) 162, it has been held that:</u>

<u>"Under Order IX, Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure, if summons is not duly served on the defendant, that is a good ground for setting aside an ex parte decree. On a perusal of the relevant provisions of the Civil Procedure Code it would be apparent, that due service of summons is an essential condition, which must be satisfied before the Court can proceed to give a judgment and under Order IX, Rule 13 if a party satisfies a Court that summons were not duly served upon him, the Court is bound to set-aside an ex parte decree. In such a case question of knowledge is not at all relevant and ex parte decree will be set-aside even if the defendant had knowledge of institution of a suit. No provision of law could be pointed out by the learned Counsel for the respondent, which dispenses with the necessity of proper service of summons.</u>

<u>" In the case of Syed Ameenul Huq Vs. M.H. Arif and others reported in 40 DLR 314, it has been held that:</u>

<u>"When the defendant Nos.1 and 2 filed two miscellaneous cases under Order 9, Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure setting aside the ex parte decree, an enquiry was conducted by the learned Subordinate Judge in pursuance of an application from the plaintiff No. 1- respondent as to whether summons was served or not. The Nayeb-Nazir reported on 16.4.86 (at page 61 of the lower Court's records) that summons were served and returned to the sherista of the Court of the learned Subordinate Judge on 18.9.85 on due receipts. These returns are not in the record. It was also the Court's order dated 17.8.85 that the defendants were to be served additionally by registered post with acknowledgement due. The postal acknowledgement receipts are also not in the lower Court's records. From the order sheet we do not find any attempt on the part of the learned Subordinate Judge to satisfy himself before fixing the suit for ex parte hearing, that the other defendants were served with the summons of the suit."</u>

<u>In the case of Abu Zafor Miah (Md.) Vs. Abdul Motaleb and another reported in 3 BLC 412, it has been held that:</u>

<u>"On a perusal of the whole order-sheet up to the date 3.4.85 it does not at all appear that summons was at all served. There is nothing on record to show what happened to those summons issued upon the defendants. From the above materials it becomes manifestly clear that summons upon the defendants were not at all served. If it is seen that no summons had been served not to speak of "duly served" the ex parte decree is liable to be shot down. If is worthy to state that the elements of fraud and collusive is manifested in procuring the ex parte decree by the plaintiff."</u>

<u>In the case of Naresh Chandra Agarwal Vs. Bank of Baroda and others reported in AIR 2001 (SC) 1253, it has been held that:</u>

<u>" When a party is sought to be impleaded in a legal proceedings service of notice on such party cannot be a mere formality but should, in fact, be a reality. In the instant case, neither the trial Court nor the High Court gave any definite finding as to the service of notice on the appellant."</u>

18. In an application under order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying for setting aside the ex parte decree the whole onus is upon the plaintiff to prove that summon was duly served on the defendant. It appears that in this case neither the process server was examined nor any attesting witness was examined to prove that summons/notices of the suit were duly served on the defendants, although the learned trial Judge mechanically held that the summons alleged to have been served upon the defendants.

It is now well established principle of law that fraud vitiates all judicial proceedings. Thus contravention of the provision of law cannot be a valid ground for allowing an order obtained by fraud to stand. In this case an ex parte decree is challenged on the ground that it was obtained by practicing fraud upon the court and some elements of fraud and collusion are found on the record, the trial court below ought to have set aside the ex parte decree even if an application seeking for setting-aside of the ex parte decree is barred by limitation. When the fraud is proved then there is no question of limitation and time will run from the date when the fraud is detected and so the question of limitation does not arise in the present case.

19. In the given facts and circumstances of the case and the uniform decisions of the highest Court as cited above, I have no hesitation to hold that the impugned judgment does not deserve to be sustained.

20. From the facts and circumstances of the case and the materials on record it cannot be held that summons were duly served on the defendant appellant, either by the process server or by registered post. Under such circumstances, it must be found that the defendant appellant was prevented by sufficient cause for not appearing before the Court when the ex-parte decrees in question were passed respectively. Since the dependent-appellant filed the present cases under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure shortly after coming to know about the impugned ex-parte decrees it must be held to be within time and there is no reason why he should not get the relief, as prayed for. Since due service of summons is an essential requirement of law justifying an ex-parte decree and the plaintiffs failed to prove due service of summons upon the defendants, the learned Subordinate Judge evidently erred in law in rejecting the applications under Order 9 rule 13 C.P.C and in maintaining the ex-parte decrees passed in Partition Suit No. 79 of 1990. The learned Subordinate Judge was palpably wrong in passing the impugned judgment without at all applying his judicial mind into the facts and circumstances of the case and the materials on record.

21. By the way, it may be mentioned that the cases relied upon by the respondents have also no manner of application in the facts and circumstance of the case inasmuch as the facts of the instant case are quite distinguishable from the facts of those cases.

22. In view of my discussions made in the foregoing paragraphs it is by now clear that the instant appeals must succeed.

23. In the result, both the appeals are allowed. The impugned judgment and order dated 9.02.1995 passed by the then Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Chittagong in Miscellaneous Case No. 49 of 1993 analogously heard with Miscellaneous Case No. 50 of 1993 under Order 9, Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure disallowing the miscellaneous cases are set-aside and accordingly, the prayer for setting aside the ex parte preliminary decree dated 27.8.1991 and final decree dated 5.8.1992 passed in Partition Suit No. 79 of 1990 are allowed.

24. In view of the fact that since the appeals are allowed, the connected Rule being Civil Rule No. 118 (F.M.) of 1995 is disposed of.

25. Since, the Partition Suit No.79 of 1990 has been dragging over a period of 24 years, I am inclined to direct the trial Court concerned to hear and, dispose of the suit as early as possible preferably within 6(six) months from the date of receipt of this judgment without giving any adjournment to any of the parties.

26. Let a copy of this judgment along with the lower Court's record be sent down at once.

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1564 of 2004
lawyer:
Md. Tafazzlur Rahman, Advocate instructed by Sufia Ahmed, Advocate-on-Record. ------ For the Petitioner 
A.J. Mohammad Ali, Senior Advocate, instructed by Haridus Paul, Advocate-on-Record ----- For Respondents 
Respondent Nos. 2-5 ------ Not represented
parties:
Rafique Ahmed ------ Petitioner
VS
Managing Director, Bangladesh Overseas Employment & Service Ltd. and others ----- Respondents.
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 11th March, 2003 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 2889 of 2002)
full_judgment:
Md. Tafazzul Islam J: Delay of 13 days is condoned.

2. This civil petition for leave to appeal arises out of the judgment dated 11.3.2003 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 2889 of 2002 making absolute the Rule obtained against the judgment and decree dated 23.5.2002 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 4th Court, Dhaka in Title Appeal No. 82 of 2001 reversing those of dated 15.1.2001 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 270 of 2000 dismissing the suit.

<u>3. The petitioner instituted the above suit (previously Title Suit No. 98 of 2000) seeking declaration that the order dated 12.9.1999 passed by the defendant No.2, the respondent No.1 herein, terminating his service is illegal and void and also for further declaration that he being still in service as Deputy General Manager is entitled to emolument and other service benefits on the averments that he, on 9.5.1996, was appointed as the Deputy General Manager of Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Ltd (BOESL), a public limited company fully owned by the Government on the basis of an open competitive process and he joined in his service on 18.5.1996 and since then he had been working with reputation and without any blemish; in the year 1998 the defendant No.2, an erstwhile army officer, joined BOESL as its Managing Directors; the primary task of BOESL is to arrange overseas employment for Bangladesh nationals for which service charge at fixed rate is realizable from the candidates selected for getting employment abroad; the defendant No.2 since his joining engaged himself in all ill practices to extort money from the Bangladeshi nationals seeking overseas employment and other subordinate officials of BOESL namely Mr. Obaidul Haque Chowdhury (General Manager) Md. Shahidul Huq Chowdhury (Asst. General Manager, Foreign Employment) Mr. Mosarraf Hossain, (Manager, Foreign Employment), Mr. Enamul Haque (Manager, Accounts) participated with him for making the above illegal gains the petitioner having refused to involve himself with the said persons in such ill practice they were looking for an opportunity to cause harm to him who was primarily responsible for protocol and administrative duties and had no connection at all with matters relating to overseas employment which was looked after jointly by the defendant Nos. 1 and 2; in order to remove the petitioner from service the defendant No.2, in conspiracy with the defendant Nos. 3, 4 and 5, got some false complaints filed against the petitioner by the defendant Nos. 3 and 4 and on the basis of two such allegations against the petitioner the Board of BOESL, in its meeting held on 9.9.1999, took decision to terminate his service without giving him any opportunity to defend him and then by Memo dated 12/9/1999 issued under the signature of defendant No.2 the service of the petitioner was terminated in violation of the Service Rules of BOESL and also in violation of the principles an natural justice. The defendant Nos. 1 and 2 contested the suit by filing a written statement contending, inter alia, that the action taken against the petitioner was lawful and correct; BOESL is an institution and is guided by its rules and procedure and the allegation of conspiracy against the petitioner is baseless; the petitioner was simply terminated as per provision of Rule 57(B) of Chapter VII of the Service Rule of BOESL as the service of the petitioner was no longer required, that the petitioner joined in the service of BOESL following a written agreement in which he agreed to comply with all the rules and procedure of BOESL and therefore of the BOESL Employees Service Rules was violated and the service benefits have been duly sent to the account of the petitioner in due course of time.</u>

4. The learned Senior Assistant Judge after hearing, dismissed the suit. The petitioner then preferred Title Appeal No. 82 of 2001 which, after hearing, was allowed. The defendants then moved the High Court Division and obtained Rule in Civil Revision No. 2889 of 2002 and after hearing, the High Court Division made the Rule absolute.

5. The learned counsel for the petitioner submits that the High Court Division failed to consider that the appellate Court referring to exhibit 5, the resolution taken in the Board meeting of BOESL regarding the termination of the petitioner, found that Regulation 57 (B) of the BOESL Employees Service Regulation was used as a camouflage for hiding the real purpose of the respondents in inflicting upon the petitioner major punishment for his alleged insubordination, corruption, inefficiency etc. without initiating any proceeding; the High Court Division wrongly relied on the decision reported in 46 DLR (AD) 1 ignoring the subsequent decision on the same point of law as enunciated in the decision reported in 47 DLR (AD) 66; the facts and circumstances of the case reported in 46 DLR (AD) 1 on which the High Court Division relied is quite distinguishable from the facts of the present case; the subsequent decision reported in 47 DLR (AD) 66 was not a decision "per-incurrium", the High Court Division erroneously held that the decision taken by the Board of BOESL was not malafied even though the head line of Ext. 5 clearly shows that the decision to terminate the service of the petitioner was taken on the allegation of insubordination, corruption and inefficiency of the petitioner.

<u>6. As it appears the learned Assistant Judge dismissed the suit mainly on the ground that the order of termination was a termination simpliciter passed under Rule 57(B) of Chapter 7 of BOESL Employees Service Regulation giving him the service benefit and so there was nothing to be interfered with. But the appellate court decreed the suit relying on the decision reported in 47 DLR (AD) 66 and also upon exhibit 5, i.e. the minutes of the meeting of the Board of Directors of the BOESL, which shows that although the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 termed the order of termination passed against the petition as termination simpliciter but from the contents of said exhibit it is clear that order of termination was in fact passed as a measure of punishment. However the High Court Division made the Rule absolute holding that the decisions reported in 46 DLR (AD) 1 and 47 DLR (AD) 66 are quite consistent on the question of the legal and factual implication of an order of termination simpliciter and that though in paragraphs 6 and 8 of the plaint of the present suit allegations of malafide were made but the law requires that mere allegation of malafide is not enough and such allegation has to be substantiated by adducing evidence and further though in paragraphs 6 and 8 of the plaint the petitioner alleged conspiracy against him by as many as four persons, namely, Mr. Obaidul, General Manager, Mr. Shahidul Haque, Assistant General Manager (Foreign employment), Mr. Mosharraf Hossain, Manager (Foreign employment) and Mr. Enamul Haque, Manager Accounts of BOESL but none of them were made parties in the suit and no paper or document was filed to show their enmity with the petitioner of that they were instrumental behind the termination of the petitioner and moreover there is also nothing on record to show that at any point of time defendant No.2 or any other officers of BOESL acted against the petitioner on filed any complaint against him and further Ext.5, the minutes of the meeting of the Board of Directors of BOESL, was never communicated to the petitioner and that decision taken in Ext. 5, being an internal matter of the BOESL, the petitioner was not entitled to use the same to prove his case of malafide or to make out a case of camouflage by the respondent No.2 to pass an order of major punishment by way of terminating him from service; Ext.5 primafacie shows that the decision to terminate the petitioner from his service was taken by the Board of BOESL and when Board took the decision then how can it be said that it is the defendant No.2 who in a malafide manner took the decision to terminate the services of the petitioner as a measure of punishment particularly when the petitioner failed to produce any paper showing any pervious enmity or other bad feeling between him and the defendant No.2 and further Ext.5, on the face of it does not show that the decision to terminate the petitioner was taken as a measure of punishment and on the other hand it shows the decision to terminate the service of the petitioner was taken on other grounds and moreover Exhibit-4, the letter of termination, is a termination simpliciter without entailing any stigma on the petitioner and also without referring to any allegation made against the petitioner.</u>

7. We are of the view that the High Court Division on proper consideration of the materials on record arrived at a correct decision and there in no cogent reason to interfere with the same.

8. The petition is dismissed.

End.

lawyer:
Mr. Fida M. Kamal with Mr. Md. Jamal Uddin Ahmed, Advocates ------ For the petitioner 
Mr. Shaheed Alam, Advocate ------ For respondent No.2 
Mr. A.F. Hassan Arif with Mr. Monirumman, Advocate ------ For respondent No.3
parties:
Shahabuddin Ahmed ------ Petitioner
Versus
Joint District Judge, Artha Rin Adalat, Narayangonj and another ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Ms. Nazmun Ara Sultana, J:  This Rule Nisi was issued calling in question the order dated 11.1.2009 passed by the Artha Rin Adalat, Narayangonj in Mortgage Execution Case No.59 of 1994 rejecting this petitioners application for cancellation of the auction sale of his mortgaged property. 

2. The facts relevant for the purpose of disposal of this rule, as appear from the writ petition, several supplementary affidavits filed by the well petitioner, the affidavits-in-opposition filed by the respondent No.2 and 3 and several supplementary affidavits-in-opposition filed by the respondent No.3 are as follows:

The petitioner took loan of Tk.11,87,000/- (Eleven lac eighty seven thousand) only from the respondent No.2 Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation in the year 1979 for construction of a multistoried building on his land measuring .18 decimals situated within Narayangonj town and with that loan money the petitioner constructed a four storied building on that loan and had been living there with his family. As security of that loan the petitioner mortgaged the said building along with the land to the Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation. The petitioner failed to repay the said loan as per stipulation and consequently the respondent No.2 Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation filed a Miscellaneous Case being No.16 of 1989 under Article 27 of P.O. 7 of 1973 against this petitioner. Subsequently, that Miscellaneous Case No. 16 of 1989 was transferred to the Artha Rin Adalat, Narayangonj for disposal and it was then renumbered as Artha Rin Mortgaged Suit No.152 of 1991. The said Artha Rin Adalat disposed of that mortgage suit decreeing that in favour of the Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation. On the basis of said decree the decree holder Bangladesh House Building. Finance Corporation filed Execution Case No.59 of 1994 for realization of the decreetal money by selling the mortgaged property in auction. In that execution case this petitioner appeared and entered into agreement with the decree holder Bangladesh House Building Finance

 Corporation and the said execution case was disposed of in terms of the solenama filed by both the parties. But subsequently since this petitioner failed to repay the outstanding loan as per terms and conditions of the said solenama the said execution case was revived on the prayer of the decree holder Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation as per the terms and condition of that solenama and ultimately the mortgaged property was put in auction on 10.11.2008. In that auction three bidders participated of whom the present added respondent No.3 Md. Salim Hossain became the highest bidder offering price of Tk.28 (Twenty eight) lac only. The decree holder Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation filed an application before the execution Court concerned praying for canceling the said auction on the ground of low price, but that application was rejected. Thereafter, this present petitioner also, on 24.11.2008, filed an application praying for cancellation of the said auction stating that the respondent No.2 Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation had already allowed re-schedulement for payment of outstanding loan and he had been paying the outstanding loan according to that re-schedulement and alleging also that the auction price was too low that the actual price of the property in question was initially assessed by the Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation at Tk. 87 (Eighty seven) lac, but that application also was rejected by the Judge of the Adalat by the impugned order dated 11.01.2009. The decree holder Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation filed a Miscellaneous Case also being No.28 of 2008 under Order XXI Rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure for cancellation of the said auction sale which also was rejected by the executing Court and against that rejection order the respondent No.2 Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation filed as Miscellaneous Appeal being No.6 of 2009 before the learned District Judge, Narayangonj which is still pending. 

3. However, the petitioner has filed this writ petition challenging the impugned order dated 11.01.2009 rejecting his application for cancellation of the auction sale on the main contention that the judgment and decree passed in Artha Rin Mortgaged Suit No.16 of 1989 by the Artha Rin Adalat, Narayangonj was without jurisdiction and as such a nullity since the Artha Rin Adalat had no jurisdiction to try a case filed under Article 27 of P.O. 7 of 1973 and in the circumstances this judgment and decree is not executable at all and therefore the execution case in question is illegal and the auction held therein and the impugned order along with all other orders passed in that execution are of no legal effect. 

4. Respondent No.2, Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation has filed an affidavit-in-opposition, however, praying for making the Rule absolute stating that the value of the property in question is Tk.87 lac but it was sold in auction at Tk.28 lac only which was shockingly low and that the respondent No.2 filed a Miscellaneous Case before the Artha Rin Adalat concerned praying for setting aside that auction sale on the ground of low price, but that Miscellaneous Case was rejected and against that order of rejection the respondent No.2 has filed Miscellaneous Appeal No.6 of 2009 before the learned District Judge, Narayangonj which is pending for disposal. 

5. Respondent No.3 has contested this Rule by filing an affidavit-in-opposition and also several supplementary affidavits-in-opposition. This respondent has denied the material case and all the allegations of the writ petitioner and has submitted that there is no illegality either in the judgment and decree passed by the Artha Rin Adalat in Artha Rin Mortgaged Suit No.152 of 1989 or in the execution case started on the basis of said decree or in the auction sale of the mortgaged property in question held in that execution case, that the auction sale of the mortgaged property was held quite in accordance with law and there is no reason at all for setting aside this auction sale and as such the impugned order does not suffer from any illegality. 

6. However, we have heard the learned Advocates for all the contesting parties in details. 

7. Mr. Fida M. Kamal, the learned senior counsel for the writ petitioner has made elaborate arguments in support of the writ petitioner's case and contention. He has showed us the certified copies of all the relevant orders passed in the proceeding of the case in question which have been submitted from the side of both the contesting parties. The learned senior counsel for the petitioner has drawn our attention to annexure-26 the certified copy of the order sheets of Miscellaneous Case No.16 of 1989 which show that initially the said case was filed as per provision of Article 27 of P.O. 7 of 1973 before that learned District Judge, Narayangonj on payment of Court fee of Tk.2 (two) only and it was registered as a Miscellaneous Case on 27.6.1989. But subsequently after promulgation of Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 the said Miscellaneous Case was transferred of the Artha Rin Adalat, Narayangonj as per Section 9 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 and it was renumbered as Artha Rin Mortgaged Suit No.152 of 1991, but no advaluram Court fee was paid ever. The learned counsel for the writ petitioner has argued that this transfer of a Miscellaneous Case filed under Article 27 of P.O. 7 of 1973 to the Artha Rin Adalat; Narayangonj and the disposal of the same by the Artha Rin Adalat was illegal. He has contended that Section 9 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 does not contemplate transfer of any Miscellaneous Case filed under the provision of P.O. 7 of 1973 to Artha Rin Adalat and as such the transfer of the same to the Artha Rin Adalat was illegal. Mr. Fida M. Kamal has contended that Section 9 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 says for transfer of suits only filed by any financial institution for realization of outstanding loan and not any Miscellaneous Case. He has argued also that a Artha Rin Adalat can entertain suits for realization of outstanding loan on payment of advaluram Court fee and on presentation of plaint, but in the present case there was no plaint and no advaluram Court fee was paid at all. Referring to the decision of Appellate Division reported in 49 DLR (AD) at page 80 the learned counsel has submitted that the Apex Court of the country has already decided that Miscellaneous Case under Article 27 of P.O. 7 of 1973 filed before District Judge cannot be termed as Suit MITD and as such it cannot be transferred to the Artha Rin Adalat as per Section 9 of the Artha Rin Adalat AM, 1990. The learned counsel has argued that the transfer of the Miscellaneous Case No.16 of 1989 filed under Article 27 of P.O. 7 of 1973 from the Court of District Judge, Narayangonj to the Artha Rin Adalat, Narayangonj was illegal and that the Artha Rin Adalat had no jurisdiction to try that Miscellaneous Case and as such the decree passed by the Artha Rin Adalat in that Miscellaneous Case was without jurisdiction and as such null and void. The learned Advocate has argued that since, the execution case in question was started on the basis of a null and void decree the whole proceeding of that execution case including the auction sale of the mortgaged property have been illegal. 

8. Mr. A. F. Hassan Arif, the learned senior Counsel for the auction purchaser-respondent No.3 has mainly argued to the effect that the auction purchaser is an innocent third party purchaser and he has purchased the property in question in auction held in accordance with the law and as such this auction-purchaser's right cannot be denied now. Mr. A.F. Hassan Arif has argued also that this writ petitioner himself appeared in the Artha Rin Suit in question and also in the execution case long before and he also entered into an agreement with the decree holder respondent No.2, Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation in the execution case admitting the decree a valid one and as such he cannot be allowed now to raise any objection as to validity of the said decree. The learned counsel has argued also that according to Section 9 of the Artha Rin Adalat AM, 1990 (as amended on 10 July, 1990) all the proceedings filed by the financial institutions for realization of outstanding loan in any Court stood transferred to the Artha Rin Adalats of competent jurisdiction and that the transfer of Miscellaneous Case No.16 of 1989 filed by the respondent No.2 Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation to the Artha Rin Adalat, Narayangonj was in accordance with Section 9 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 and as such it was not illegal at all and the Artha Rin Adalat, Narayangonj also had jurisdiction to try and dispose of this case. 

9. Mr. Shaheed Alam, the learned Advocate for the respondent No.2, Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation has stated before us that the writ petitioner has already paid off the entire outstanding dues of Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation and Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation has no objection in making this Rule absolute. 

10. We have considered the submission of the learned Advocates of all the parties and gone through the writ petition, the supplementary affidavit submitted by the writ petitioner, the affidavits-in-opposition and also the supplementary affidavits-in-opposition and the papers submitted by all the parties. From the above stated cases of the contesting parties and also the arguments advanced by the teamed Advocates of both the sides it is evident that in this case the main questions for determination are whether the transfer of Miscellaneous Case No.16 of 1989 under Article 27 of P.O. 7 of 1973 from the Court of District Judge, Narayangonj to the Artha Rin Adalat, Narayangonj as per Section 9 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 was legal and whether the disposal of the said case by the Artha Rin Adalat, Narayangonj was within its jurisdiction. It appears that both these, two questions have already been answered by the Apex Court of the country in the case of Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation Vs. Jahanara Akhter and others reported in 49 DLR (AD) at page 80. It requires to be mentioned here that Section 9 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 as amended on 31st July, 1990 provided that all the “মামলা” filed by any financial institution for realization of outstanding loan pending in any Court shall be transferred to the Artha Rin Adalat of competent jurisdiction. The relevant portion of Section 5(1) of the same Ain also requires to be quoted here; 

৫। অর্থঋণ আদাললতের ক্ষমতা ও এখতিয়ার।– (১) অন্য কোন আইনে যাহা কিছুই থাকুক না কেন, আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠানের ঋণ আদায় সংক্রান্ত যাবতীয় মামলা অর্থঋণ আদালতে দায়ের করিতে হইবে এবং উক্ত আদালতেই উহা নিস্পত্তি করা হইবেঃ
	
তবে শর্ত থাকে যে, কোন আইন দ্বারা আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠান প্রতিষ্ঠা করা হইয়া থাকিলে এবং উক্ত আইনে উহার ঋণ আদায়ের জন্য কোন বিশেষ বিধান বা পদ্ধতি থাকিলে সেই বিধান বা পদ্ধতি এই ধারার দ্বারা ক্ষুন্ন হইবে না।  

11. In the cited case of 49 DLR the Appellate Division has clearly held that the word 01001 used in this Section 5(1) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain 1990 refers to suit only and not all legal proceedings. Their Lordships held also that a Miscellaneous Case filed under Article 27 of P.O. 7 of 1973 was not a suit and it could not be transferred to the Artha Rin Adalat as per Section 9 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 and the Artha Rin Adalat has no jurisdiction to try any such Miscellaneous Case. 

12. Mr. Hassan Arif, the learned senior counsel for the respondent No.3 auction purchaser has argued to the effect that in this judgment of 49 DLR their Lordships relied on the 4th schedule of the Constitution where the word "মামলা" has been used to mean suits only and not all the legal proceedings-to give meaning to the word “মামলা” used in Section 5(1) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 and has contended that since this 4th schedule of the Constitution has been declared void by the judgment on 5th amendment of the constitution this decision of the 49 DLR cannot be relied on now. But we are unable to accept this contention of the learned senior counsel for the respondent No.3 auction purchaser. We have gone through the entire judgment of the 49 DLR (AD) 80. In this judgment their Lordships made observation "an application under Article 27 cannot be equated with a suit, for in an application under that article none of requirements as in a suit is attracted. No plaint, no court fee, no limitations, no written statement, no other necessary steps, no decree, nothing, the financial institution will get the relief or reliefs in a summary manner which is not available in the form of a Suit. It cannot, therefore, but be said that Article 27 is a special provision or procedure for realization of loan which comes squarely within the provisio to Section 5(1) of the Act"....."The action contemplated under Article 27 is, therefore, outside the concept of “মামলা” which we have found to correspond with suit as provided in the main part of Section 5(1) of the Act." 

13. From the above quoted observation of - their lordships in the judgment of 49 DLR (AD) 80 it is evident that for coming to the decision that the word “মামলা” used in section 5(1) of the Artha Rin Adalat AM, 1990 refers to suit and the proceedings under Article 27 of P.O. 7 of 1973 are not suits their lordships did not at all base on the 4a schedule of the Constitution, rather taking into consideration the requirements of a suit and also the nature of a proceeding under Article 27 of P.O. 7 of 1973 and also taking into consideration the provisio to Section 5(1) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 their lordships formed their independent opinion that the word “মামলা” used in section 5(1) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 refers to suit only and the proceeding under Article 27 of P.O. 7 of 1973 is not a suit and as such cannot be transferred to Artha Rin Adalat as per Section 9 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 and that Artha Rin Adalat can try suit only and not may proceeding under Article 27 of P.O. 7 of 1973. 


14. However, we are of the opinion that after the above decision of our Appellate Division reported in 49 DLR (AD) at page 80 there cannot be any scope for argument that the word “মামলা” used in section 9 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 includes all legal proceedings including a Miscellaneous Case under Article 27 of P.O. 7 of 1973. So, obviously the transfer of the Miscellaneous Case No.I6 of 1989 filed by the respondent No.2 Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation under Article 27 of P.O. 7 of 1973 to the Artha Rin Adalat, Narayangonj as per Section 9 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 and the disposal of the same by that Adalat have been illegal and therefore the decree passed in that Case by the Artha Rin Adalat, Narayangonj is without jurisdiction and as such a nullity. 

15. It has been argued from the side of the auction-purchaser that this petitioner did not raise any objection as to jurisdiction of the Artha Rin Adalat, Narayangonj rather admitting the validity of the decree passed by the Artha Rin Adalat this petitioner entered into an agreement with the Bangladesh House Finance Corporation and field solenama in the execution case. The contention of the auction- purchaser is that since the petitioner did not raise any objection as to jurisdiction of the Artha Rin Adalat rather accepted the decree passed by the Artha Rin Adalat by filling a solenama at execution stage the petitioner is now estopped from raising any question as to validity of the said decree. But we are unable to accept this contention made by respondent No.3 action-purchaser, for, "Jurisdiction of courts is created by statutes; it can neither be conferred nor taken away by agreement or concession of parties to a litigation or of their lawyers" (vide 36 DLR (AD) at page 1). This petitioner though, at earlier stage, entered into an agreement with the decree-holder Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation having no knowledge about the legal position but subsequently, before the execution court, he, by filling an application, raised this question of jurisdiction and prayed for setting aside of the action-sale on that very ground also. 

However, from the above discussion it is evident that the decree passed in Artha Rin Mortgaged Suit No.I52 of 1991 being without jurisdiction is a nullity and as such it is not executable. So the whole proceeding of the Execution Case No.59 of 1994 started on the basis of that decree is illegal and consequently the auction sale of the mortgaged property in question also held in that execution case has been illegal. 

16. The learned advocate for the auction purchaser respondent has made some submission to the effect also that even if the decree was without jurisdiction the 3rd party auction purchaser's right which he acquired in the execution of that decree cannot be denied now-the auction sale of the property in question in that execution proceeding being held quite in accordance with law. But this submission also of the learned advocate is not acceptable. A decree passed without jurisdiction being void is not executable and as such an auction sale held in execution of any such void decree also is void and consequently the auction purchaser cannot acquire any right in the purchased property. The claim that the auction was held quite in accordance with law also cannot be accepted in view of the admitted facts that the price of the mortgaged property was assessed at Tk.87 (eighty seven) lac but the auction price of this property was only Tk.28 (twenty eight) lac and that both the decree—holder and the judgment debtor made complain of this shockingly low price immediate after the auction, but both those were rejected. 

17. However, in view of above discussion it is evident that this Rule deserves to be made absolute. 

18. In the circumstances, the Rule is made absolute on contest without any order as to costs. 

19. The proceeding of Mortgaged Execution Case No.59 of 1994 of the Artha Rin Adalat, Narayangonj be declared illegal. Consequently the auction-sale of the mortgaged property in question held in that execution case also be declared illegal. The possession of the mortgaged property in question be resorted to the petitioner. 

20. The auction purchaser respondent No.3 will get return of the entire auction money which he deposited.

21. Arbitration is public policy as in law it can be said to alternative dispute resolution which has been accepted whole over the World. When agreement having an arbitration clause it is settle principle of law that before instituting any suit parties must or shall invoke the arbitration proceeding. Civil court has a hand to part to play as unless award may make rule of the court, award has no value.

22. In the text book. Jurisdiction and Arbitration Agreements and Their Enforcement, first Edition by David Joseph Q.C-2005, the author look into limitations on bringing of an application as: "Section 9(3): Limitations on the bringing of an application No application can be made prior to acknowledgment of service. This is straightforward and requires' no amplification. The application must thereafter be made prior to taking any, step in the proceedings to answer the substantive claim, which in most cases will mean within the time for the service of the defence, namely 28 days after the service by the claimant of the particulars of claim.

Bys 9(3), the defendant is not entitled to bring an application under s.9(1) after he has taken a step in the proceedings to answer the substantive claim. The expression was considered by the Court of Appeal in Patel vs. Patel(2000)QB 551CA. The decision in that case was that a party who had issued an application (1) (2000 QB 554) to set aside a default judgment, (OP.Cit Para 6.13 and see to same effect Mustill & Bagd. P.472) (2) to be granted permission to bring a counterclaim, and (3) (Pitchers Ltd. Vs Plura (Queensbury) Ltd. (1940) IAll ER 151) for consequential directions to be given, was not precluded from applying to stay proceedings under s.9 of the Arbitration Act 1996. The affidavit in support indicated that the defendant intended to apply for a stay. The application to answer the substantive Claim. The potential difficulty created was the inclusion in the application notice of a claim for permission to counterclaim and for consequential directions. Lord Woolf MR, however, considered that the applicant did not need permission to counterclaim and therefore had sought otiose relief, and that, further, the application for directions was entirely neutral. Lord Woolf M.R considered that a party ought not be taken to have abandoned the tight to apply for a stay by making a claim for otiose relief. The judgments of Lord Woolf M.R. and Lord Justice Otton contain important guidance to practitioners under s. 9(3) of the Arbitration Act. Lord Woolf Law which referred to the latest time for challenge being the submission of his first statement on the substance of the dispute. Lord Justice Otton approved a passage in professor Merkin's Arbitration Law equating the loss of the right to apply for a stay with the defendant taking some step amounting to an invocation of the court's jurisdiction and an unequivocal representation that he did not intend to refer issues in dispute to arbitration. Where a party in his affidavit states that he intends to apply for a stay, this test will not be satisfied. Likewise, the test will not be satisfied where a party seeks a stay of proceedings and summary judgment conditional upon the dismissal of the stay application.

23. In practical terms, the right to apply under s. 9(3) will be lost by reason of the filing of the defence. However, the right might be lost any other unequivocal act which invokes the jurisdiction of the court to deal with the substance of the claim without a proper reservation of rights. Care, therefore should be taken expressly to indicate the intention to apply for a stay and to reserve all rights, when seeking an extension of time for the service of a defence or in appearing in court on the return date of an injunction for interim relief.

24. Section 9 (4): "the court shall grant a stay unless satisfied that the arbitration agreement is null and void, inoperative, or incapable of being performed".

It should first be remembered that the nature of the remedy is a stay and not a compulsory reference to arbitration. This distinction is important (as was pointed out in para. 11.01 above) and this linguistic formula permits the courts to stay court proceedings which are the subject of an arbitration agreement but which are required to be submitted to an expert (or some other alternative dispute resolution forum) prior to arbitration. Although the remedy does not compel arbitration, the remedy is mandatorily imposed. The court is obliged to grant a stay if the requirements of section 9(1) are fulfilled, unless the court is satisfied that the arbitration agreement is null and void, inoperative or incapable of being performed. There is no discretion to refuse a stay on general grounds of forum non convenient or the desire to avoid multiple proceedings. As regards this last point, this distinguishes arbitration agreements from choice of court agreements.

25. The burden of proof in each case rests with the party opposing a stay. This is in contrast to the position under s. 9(1). The burden rests with, the applicant to demonstrate the existence and scope of the arbitration agreement. The stay, of proceedings refers to all any interim freezing injunction or other, security process. The words in s. 9(4) are themselves derived from Art. 11.3 of the New York Convention. It is noted, by Professor Van den Berg in his authoritative word on the New York Convention that the summary Records of the New York Conference of 1958 do not reveal any discussion regarding these words. It is suggested that the words ought to be interpreted in the same manner as other English statutory provisions giving effect to international treaty obligations. In the present context, it is suggested that the exceptions to mandatory referral to arbitration ought to be narrowly construed in order to give effect to the overall scheme of the New York Convention.

26. The court is only concerned here with the arbitration agreement. If therefore an issue is: raised as to whether the substantive contract is illegal, null or void, the court will have to consider the nature of the allegation, whether it impeaches the arbitration agreement (as opposed to the substantive contract), and whether the dispute in question falls within the scope of the arbitration agreement. Section 7 of the Arbitration Act 1996 expressly embraces the doctrine of the reparability of the arbitration agreement. An arbitration agreement is not to be regarded as invalid, non-existent or ineffective because the substantive agreement is so held. Reparability has been considered in Ch.4 above. A respondent to an application under s.9 separate the agreement to arbitration from the governing procedural rules. Likewise, neither a change of the name of the identified institution nor a change to its governing rules will ordinarily render the agreement incapable of being performed. Further, the nonexistence of an appointing authority will not render the arbitration agreement incapable of being performed as the parties can approach the court for the appointment of an arbitrator. If the arbitration clause itself contains some pathological contradiction, the court might conclude that it is incapable of being performed, or might conclude that there is no agreement at all on the grounds of uncertainty.

27. The court has inherent jurisdiction to stay its proceedings in the interests of justice. The long-established inherent power of the court contrasts with the less developed and more questionable inherent power of a tribunal under the Arbitration Act 1996 to stay its own proceedings in the interest of justice. The power of the court obviously applies to cases where the English court is not forum convenience or where proceedings have been brought in breach of an agreement to bring proceedings in another forum. The power, however, also applies in cases where court and arbitral claims proceed in parallel. It is appropriate to, have regard to the clear statement of principle from the eminent US Supreme Court judge. Mr Justice Cardozo in Landis v North American co.''

28. A potential area for the exercise of the inherent jurisdiction is where it is plain that the arbitration agreement only covers part of the claims brought in court by a claimant against the defendant. In such a case, the court taking into account all the circumstances might well conclude that the balance of the court proceedings not caught by the arbitration agreement ought to be stayed pending the determination of the arbitral tribunal. The argument in favour of such an order will be more powerful if the conclusions of the arbitral tribunal are likely to affect or even be determinative of the remaining matters to be decided in court.

29. In our Arbitration Act of 2001 law says that:

Section 7-of Arbitration Act of 2001 give jurisdiction to Court as "Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, where any of the parties to the arbitration agreement files a legal proceedings in a Court against the other party, no judicial authority shall hear any legal proceedings except in so far as provided by his Act."

30. Our law says if there be any arbitration clause in any contract or agreement then whether it is invoke or not, Court has a duty to see whether parties to the agreement proceed to resolve the dispute by arbitration. Arbitration is alternative forum i.e. alternative dispute resolution, which at present is intends to relieve the court from deciding, in lengthy legal proceeding. 32. This section uphold the sanctity of the arbitration clause signed by the parties as if any party filed any suit, the court has duty that as soon the court find there is arbitration clause signed by the parties to resolve the dispute by arbitration then a duty cast upon the court to stay the legal proceeding pending before the Court. Khoksha Ltd. (1994) 1 Arb.LR 506(SC), wherein it has been held that ad interim order or granting injunction should not he allowed. 33. We have read the plaint and satisfy that this requirement of law has not clearly spelt out. 34. In the decision of AIR 1951 (Punj) 173 it has been held that Section 34 however does not prohibit the filing of the written statement pending the decision of an application for stay of the proceeding. Hence, there is no irregularity if the. Court calls upon such applicant to put in a written statement before deciding the application for stay. It is settled principle that the question is to be decided as to when the dispute in the suit and when dispute in the arbitration clause covered if suit be filed for damage of breach of contract and non delivery of goods then the suit can proceed otherwise suit cannot proceed. The Court shall keep their hands off till decisions arrive by arbitrator.

35. The Contract No.315510058 dated 31.1.2011 specifically stipulates that all disputes shall be referred to arbitration in accordance with the Rules and By-Laws of the International Cotton Association shall be for any technical or quality dispute. Bylaw 300(1) of the Rules and Bylaws of the International Cotton Association states as follows:

"Quality arbitrations will deal with disputes arising from the manual examination of the quality of cotton and/or the quality characteristics which can only be determined by instrument testing. Bylaws especially applicable to quality arbitrations and appeals are set out in part.2. Technical arbitrations will deal with all other disputes. Bylaws especially applicable to technical arbitrations and appeals are set out in Part 1."

36. Question calls for determination as to whether suit should be stayed pending disposal of arbitration proceeding. In the case of PLD 1978 Lah. 475 and ILR 1953 Hyd.727 (DB), it is held that by commencing arbitration proceeding right to sue is not ousted. The suit can proceed as per PLD 1982 Kar. 778(DB) if the existence of an arbitration agreement or its validity is challenged and thereafter, if the court found have seen from the decision of Indian Jurisdiction in the Case of Dresser S.A. vs. K.G. Khoksha Ltd. (1994) I Arb.LR 506(SC), wherein it has been held that ad interim order or granting injunction should not he allowed. The suit so long an arbitration proceedings continue, can be stayed as per section 10 of the Arbitration Act unless the agreement is void. inoperative or is incapable of determination by arbitration that the agreement is valid and agreement is in existence then allowed the parties to proceed with the arbitration proceeding.

37. In the case of 1982 CLC 1039 it is held that when the subject matter of the suit and the arbitration agreement is the same, the parties are bound to refer the matter to arbitration and the court would, therefore, stay the suit. In the case of AIR 1956 (A11)194 a Division Bench of Allahabad held if a person, who has been a party to an arbitration agreements, brings, a suit ignoring that agreement, the defendant's remedy, if he wants to rely on that agreement, , is to proceed under section 34 and to ask for stay of the suit.

38. It appears that both plaintiff and defendant to the contract in open eyes go through the clauses of the contract and put their signature as such filing of the suit instead of proceeding of arbitration by plaintiff is unthinkable. It is also seen defendant and plaintiff did not raise question of validity of the arbitration agreement or did not raise anything as regard fraud practice, the proceeding as we see can continue. The award if so facto does not give any fear upon the person against whom the award goes as the suit, ultimate decision, rest with civil court.

39. In the case of lagatheesan vs. Veerammal MLJ (1980) (3(Mad) 802 it was held that:

1. It is true that the word "arbitrator" has not been used in the partnership deed, but one has to see what the parties contemplated at the time of entering into the partnership.

2. If the obvious intention between the parties was to refer the matter in dispute between them to Panchayatdars without report to court then it can easily be assumed that the intention of the parties was to settle the matters in their entirety  by arbitration.

3. Therefore, so long as the parties repudiate the terms of the contract relating wanted to have the dispute determined to arbitration, white seeking to rely on the contract in support of his claim by approaching the Panchayatdars outside the court, the intention that the disputes must be referred to arbitration, can be easily inferred.

40. Where a dispute, though not arising under the contract, is inextricably connected with or indisputably linked up with the contract which contains an arbitration clause, it can be said that the dispute is connected with the contract. In the case of Firm Harjas Rai vs. Tek Chand, 101 IC 786, AIR (Lah) 465 it has been held that section 34 cannot apply unless:

(a) The plaintiff is a party to the agreement to refer;

(b) The defendant, desiring stay of the suit, has the right to apply to the court to stay it; and

(c) The subject-matter of the dispute is the same before the arbitrator and the court.

<u>41. The guiding principle for determining whether the clause as to arbitration in the contract applies or not, is that the dispute is referable to arbitration in cases where the avoidance of the contract arises out of the terms of the contract itself. Where, however, a party seeks to avoid the contract for reasons dehors it, the arbitration clause cannot be resorted to, as it, together with the terms of the contract, is set aside. A party cannot rely on a term of the contract to repudiate it and still say that the arbitration clause should not apply. If he relies on the resort to court, then it can easily be contract, he must rely on it for all purposes assumed that the intention of the parties Therefore, where the plaintiff sues to was to settle the matters in their entirety recover the price under the contract, as a by arbitration valid and binding contract, he cannot repudiate the terms of the contract relating to arbitration, while seeking to rely on the contract in support of his claim.</u>

42. In the case of Lewis W. Fernandes vs. Jivtalal, 29 IC 568; It has held that in order to give the arbitrators jurisdiction to make a valid award, the party claiming arbitration must show (i) the existence of a dispute between him and the opposite party, arising out of or in relation to a contract, entered into between them, and (ii) a clear, valid and subsisting arbitration agreement within the meaning of this section.

43. In the case of Jai Narain vs. Narain Das, 69 IC 583; Gopi Ram vs. Pokhar Das, 154 IC 7; It has been held that a private tribunal, such as an arbitrator, cannot oust the jurisdiction of the court, but an arbitration becomes functus officio when the Court has refused to stay an action, or the defendant has abstained from asking it to do so. This rule only applies when the dispute before the two tribunals is identical.

44. In the case of Gopi Ram vs. Pokhar Das, 154 IC 7; it has further held that when the arbitrator has become functus officio in respect of the dispute which forms the subject matter of a suit, he becomes functus officio regarding the whole dispute including that portion of it which formed the subject-matter of the second suit, if the subject-matter of the second suit was the same as the subject-matter of the first suit.

45. Now if the court did not want to stay the proceeding what is its effect.

46. In the case of Gul. Mohammed vs. Fata Bibi, AIR 1956 J & K 122, it is held that when the court refuses to stay the proceedings, it means that the suit will be heard on merits by the Court. If the suit is to proceed, the work of the arbitrator, ipso facto, comes to an end and his authority is revoked, and there is no more a valid reference before him.

47. In the case of Muhammad Mohideen vs. Muhammed Naina, 177 IC 440, it is held that in that case, the court should not renounce its powers and ditties in disposing of the suit. It should exercise as much control as it can under the law over the proceedings before the arbitrator. The court should see that the parties do not delay the disposal of the arbitration proceedings and that, as far as possible, they prosecute those proceedings.

48. In the case of Hukum Chand vs. T.M. Kaisha Ltd. 190 IC 596, it is held that the arbitration proceeding can legally continue on the stay of the suit, even though the court has decided that the award already made is a nullity.

In the proceeding of the suit Court shall see-

(1) An arbitration agreement between parties to the dispute.

(2) A Reference before arbitrators duly appointed by the parties under the arbitration agreement, and

(3) An award properly made by such arbitrators.

49. Where a suit is stayed under this section, the matter is referred to arbitration; but if, during the arbitration proceedings, some mistake is found to have been made, and an application is made to the Court to correct it, and the court orders the mistake to be corrected, the suit does not become a new suit and the jurisdiction of the arbitrators is not lost.

<u>50. On an overall consideration of the entire materials on record before LIS, on considerations of the decisions as referred to above we have already seen that there is a valid agreement between plaintiff and defendant with arbitration clause, pursuant to the agreement an arbitration proceeding has already commenced before arbitration tribunal at Liverpool, the suit is subsequent to the arbitration proceeding, written statement has been filed by the defendant can be treated as information to the court pending arbitration before Liverpool. It is also seen that arbitrators have no jurisdiction over the court but court has jurisdiction over the arbitration. The decisions of the arbitration is subject to review by the court, either at the time of mistake of some rules of the court or on the application of any of the parties. We also seen that there is arbitration proceeding which arrived in the contract by the parties by signing it in open eyes and there is no allegation of fraud practice upon the plaintiff, we are of the view that as per Section 10(2) of the Arbitration Act when it is found that there is arbitration proceeding, Court should keep its hands off from the proceeding pending before the court. We find substance in this rule.</u>

51. In that view of the matter ends of justice would be met if we stay the proceeding of Title Suit No.73 of 2012. Proceedings of Title Sui No.73 of 2012 is stayed till disposal of arbitration proceeding.

52. In the result, this rule is disposed of.

53. Parties are directed to settle the matter through arbitration expeditiously.

The order of injunction granted earlier by the trial court is hereby vacated.

End.
